subjects.name: Calculus 1
subjects.desc: Functions, limits, continuity, derivative rules, curve sketching, optimization, and definite/indefinite integrals.

subjects.name: Calculus 2
subjects.desc: Techniques of integration, improper integrals, infinite sequences, series convergence, and power series.

subjects.name: Differential Equations
subjects.desc: First and higher-order ordinary differential equations, exact ODEs, Laplace transforms, and series solutions.

subjects.name: Linear Algebra
subjects.desc: Matrices, Gaussian elimination, determinants, vector spaces, linear independence, eigenvalues, and eigenvectors.

subjects.name: Numerical Methods
subjects.desc: Root finding algorithms (Newton-Raphson, Bisection), interpolation, numerical differentiation, and numerical integration.

subjects.name: Probability and Statistics
subjects.desc: Probability theory, discrete/continuous random variables, normal distribution, and statistical inference.

subjects.name: Physics 1 (Mechanics)
subjects.desc: Classical mechanics, vectors, 1D/2D kinematics, Newton's laws, work, energy, momentum, and rotational dynamics.

subjects.name: Physics 2 (Electricity & Magnetism)
subjects.desc: Coulomb's law, electric fields, Gauss's law, electric potential, capacitance, DC circuits, magnetic forces, and induction.

subjects.name: General Chemistry
subjects.desc: Atomic structure, stoichiometry, gas laws, chemical bonding, thermochemistry, and acid-base equilibrium.

subjects.name: C++ Programming
subjects.desc: Structured programming, pointers, references, dynamic memory management, arrays, and basic OOP in C++.

subjects.name: Object-Oriented Programming (OOP)
subjects.desc: Encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, virtual functions, abstract classes, operator overloading, and exception handling.

subjects.name: Data Structures & Algorithms
subjects.desc: Asymptotic complexity, linked lists, stacks, queues, binary search trees, heaps, hash tables, and graph algorithms.

subjects.name: Assembly Language
subjects.desc: x86 processor architecture, register conventions, arithmetic/logical instructions, memory addressing, interrupts, and subroutines.

subjects.name: Computer Architecture
subjects.desc: Instruction set architecture (ISA), pipelining stages, hazards, branch prediction, memory hierarchy, and cache design.

subjects.name: Artificial Intelligence
subjects.desc: Search algorithms (BFS, DFS, A*), adversarial search (Minimax, Alpha-Beta pruning), CSP, and logic representation.

subjects.name: Machine Learning
subjects.desc: Supervised vs unsupervised learning, regression, classification, gradient descent, decision trees, SVM, and regularization.

subjects.name: Computer Skills
subjects.desc: Computer hardware, operating systems, networking basics, spreadsheets, number systems, and digital literacy.

subjects.name: Electrical Circuits 1
subjects.desc: Ohm's law, Kirchhoff's laws, nodal and mesh analysis, Thevenin and Norton theorems, and first-order RL/RC transients.

subjects.name: Electrical Circuits 2
subjects.desc: AC sinusoidal steady-state analysis, phasors, impedance, power factor, balanced three-phase systems, and resonance.

subjects.name: Electronics
subjects.desc: Semiconductor diodes, rectifiers, Zener regulators, BJT DC biasing and AC small-signal models, and MOSFET amplifiers.

subjects.name: Digital Logic Design
subjects.desc: Boolean algebra, Karnaugh maps, combinational logic (adders, decoders, multiplexers), and sequential circuits (flip-flops, counters).

subjects.name: Signals and Systems
subjects.desc: LTI systems, continuous/discrete convolution, Fourier transform, Laplace transform, and frequency response.

subjects.name: Control Systems
subjects.desc: Feedback control systems, transfer functions, block diagrams, transient response, Routh-Hurwitz stability, root locus, and PID tuning.

subjects.name: Telecommunications
subjects.desc: Analog and digital modulation (AM, FM, PM, PCM, QPSK), sampling theorem, channel capacity, and noise analysis.

subjects.name: Computer Networks
subjects.desc: OSI 7-layer model, TCP/IP protocol suite, subnetting (CIDR), routing algorithms (OSPF, RIP), transport protocols, and DNS/HTTP.

subjects.name: Cloud Computing
subjects.desc: Cloud service models (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS), hypervisors, virtualization, elasticity, AWS/Azure architectures, and cloud security.

subjects.name: Circuits Lab
subjects.desc: Hands-on breadboard wiring, DMM measurements, oscilloscope waveform analysis, KCL/KVL verification, and RC transients.

subjects.name: Digital Logic Lab
subjects.desc: Wiring 74xx TTL logic gates, decoders, multiplexers, latches, flip-flops, and counter circuits.

subjects.name: Electronics Lab
subjects.desc: Laboratory measurements of diode I-V curves, rectifiers, filter circuits, Zener regulators, and BJT amplifiers.

subjects.name: Data Structures Lab
subjects.desc: Practical C++ programming assignments: linked lists, stack evaluation, queue buffers, BST traversals, and sorting algorithms.

subjects.name: Assembly Lab
subjects.desc: Writing, assembling, and debugging x86 assembly routines with DOSBox/EMU8086 and interrupt handling.

subjects.name: Architecture Lab
subjects.desc: Simulating ALU datapaths, register files, and single-cycle MIPS CPU architectures using Logisim and ModelSim.

subjects.name: Physics Lab
subjects.desc: Vernier caliper/micrometer measurements, simple pendulum experiments, vector force table, and energy conservation.

subjects.name: Chemistry Lab
subjects.desc: Volumetric titration experiments, determination of unknown acid molarity, safety protocols, and empirical formula analysis.

subjects.name: Control Lab
subjects.desc: MATLAB and Simulink modeling of transfer functions, transient response analysis, root locus plotting, and PID controller tuning.

subjects.name: English Communication 1
subjects.desc: Reading comprehension, academic vocabulary, grammatical accuracy, subject-verb agreement, and sentence structure.

subjects.name: English Communication 2
subjects.desc: Advanced academic reading, argumentative writing, synthesizing sources, academic integrity, and formal presentations.

subjects.name: Technical Writing
subjects.desc: Engineering technical reports, executive summaries, proposal writing, documentation formatting, and professional correspondence.

subjects.name: Engineering Economics
subjects.desc: Time value of money, compound interest, cash flow diagrams, present/annual worth analysis, rate of return, and depreciation.

subjects.name: Islamic Culture
subjects.desc: مفهوم الثقافة الإسلامية، خصائص الشريعة، الكليات الخمس، النظام الأخلاقي والاجتماعي، وموقف الإسلام من العلم والعمل.

subjects.name: National Education
subjects.desc: التربية الوطنية، مفاهيم المواطنة والدستور الأردني، السلطات الدستورية الثلاث، ودور المؤسسات الوطنية.

subjects.name: Military Science
subjects.desc: العلوم العسكرية، تاريخ الجيش العربي وبطولاته، معركة الكرامة، الأمن الوطني الشامل، والضبط والربط العسكري.

subjects.name: Islamic History
subjects.desc: تاريخ الخلافة الراشدة، الفتوحات الكبرى، التطور الإداري والقضائي، وإسهامات الحضارة الإسلامية العلمية.

subjects.name: Entrepreneurship & Innovation
subjects.desc: إدارة الأعمال الريادية، مخطط نموذج العمل التجاري BMC، دراسة الجدوى، والملكية الفكرية وبراءات الاختراع.

subjects.name: Engineering Workshops
subjects.desc: السلامة والصحة المهنية، مشغل التمديدات الكهربائية والتأريض، مشغل اللحام بالأكسي-أسيتيلين، ومشغل الخراطة.

questions.explanation: MGF of normal is e^(μt + σ²t²/2). Here σ²/2 = 2 => σ² = 4.

questions.question: Chebyshev's Inequality states that for any distribution, P(|X - μ| ≥ k σ) is at most:
questions.explanation: P(|X - μ| ≥ kσ) ≤ 1/k² for any k > 1.

questions.question: A paired t-test is used when:

options.text: Observations are paired or matched (e.g., before-and-after measurements on the same subjects)

questions.explanation: Reduces to a one-sample t-test on the differences d_i = x_{1i} - x_{2i}.

questions.question: The coefficient of determination R² in simple linear regression represents:

options.text: The slope of the regression line
The proportion of total variation in Y explained by the linear regression model with X

questions.explanation: R² = SSR / SST = 1 - (SSE / SST).

questions.question: In simple linear regression y = β₀ + β₁ x + ε, the least squares estimator b₁ for slope is:
questions.explanation: b₁ = Σ(x - x̄)(y - ȳ) / Σ(x - x̄)².

questions.question: What is the sum of the residuals Σ (y_i - ŷ_i) in an OLS regression that includes an intercept?
questions.explanation: Normal equations guarantee residuals sum to zero.

questions.question: The joint probability density function f(x, y) of independent RVs X and Y satisfies:
questions.explanation: Independence factorizes the joint density.

questions.question: The marginal PDF f_X(x) is obtained from joint PDF f(x, y) by:

options.text: Integrating out y: ∫_{-∞}^∞ f(x, y) dy

questions.explanation: Marginalization integrates over the unwanted variable.

questions.question: If X ~ N(0, 1), what is the distribution of X²?

options.text: Chi-Square distribution with 1 degree of freedom (χ²₁)

questions.explanation: Square of a standard normal is chi-square with df = 1.

questions.question: The sum of k independent squared standard normal variables Σ_{i=1}^k Z_i² has:

options.text: Chi-Square distribution with k degrees of freedom (χ²_k)

questions.explanation: Definition of the Chi-Square distribution.

questions.question: The ratio [Z / √(V / k)] where Z ~ N(0, 1) and V ~ χ²_k are independent follows:

options.text: Student's t-distribution with k degrees of freedom

questions.explanation: Exact mathematical definition of Student's t-distribution.

questions.question: The ratio (U / d₁) / (V / d₂) of two independent chi-square variables divided by their degrees of freedom follows:

options.text: Snedecor's F-distribution with (d₁, d₂) degrees of freedom

questions.explanation: Definition of the F-distribution.

questions.question: A 99% confidence interval is:

options.text: Wider than a 95% confidence interval for the same sample

questions.explanation: Higher confidence requires a larger critical value Z or t, widening the interval.

questions.question: Which of the following is a fundamental base unit in the SI system?
questions.explanation: Kilogram, meter, and second are base SI units; Newton and Joule are derived.

questions.question: The dimensional formula for acceleration is:
questions.explanation: Acceleration is velocity/time = (L/T)/T = L T⁻².

questions.question: Given vector A = 3i + 4j, its magnitude |A| and direction angle θ with the +x axis are:
The scalar (dot) product of two perpendicular vectors A and B is:
The magnitude of the vector (cross) product |A x B| is maximum when the angle between A and B is:
questions.explanation: |A x B| = |A||B| sin θ, which is maximum at θ = 90°.

questions.question: A car accelerates uniformly from rest to 20 m/s in 5 seconds. Its acceleration is:
How far does the car travel during those 5 seconds of uniform acceleration from rest?
An object is dropped from rest from a cliff. Neglecting air resistance (g = 9.8 m/s²), its velocity after 3 seconds is:
How far has the dropped object fallen after 3 seconds?
A ball thrown vertically upward reaches its highest point. At that instant, its velocity and acceleration are:
questions.explanation: Velocity is momentarily zero at the apex, but gravity acts constantly downward.

questions.question: In ideal projectile motion, the horizontal component of velocity v_x:

options.text: Decreases to zero at the peak

questions.explanation: Neglecting air drag, horizontal acceleration a_x = 0.

questions.question: The launch angle that yields the maximum horizontal range on flat ground is:
questions.explanation: R = (v₀² sin 2θ)/g; sin 2θ is maximized at 2θ = 90° => θ = 45°.

questions.question: Two projectiles launched at the same speed have identical ranges if their launch angles are:
Newton's First Law of Motion states that an object continues in its state of rest or uniform motion unless acted upon by:
questions.explanation: Law of inertia.

questions.question: The net force on an object moving with CONSTANT VELOCITY in a straight line is:

options.text: Equal to its mass times velocity

questions.explanation: Constant velocity means acceleration a = 0, so F_net = ma = 0.

questions.question: A 5 kg block experiences a net force of 20 N. Its acceleration is:
Newton's Third Law states that every action force has an equal and opposite reaction force. These two forces:

options.text: Act on different interacting bodies and never cancel each other out
Act on the same body and cancel each other
Are not equal if one object is heavier

questions.explanation: Action and reaction act on two distinct objects: F_{A on B} = -F_{B on A}.

questions.question: The apparent weight of a person of mass m standing on a scale in an elevator accelerating UPWARD with acceleration a is:
questions.explanation: Normal force N - mg = ma => N = m(g + a).

questions.question: If the elevator cable snaps and it goes into free fall (a = g downward), the scale reads:
The maximum force of static friction f_{s,max} is related to the normal force N by:
questions.explanation: Definition of coefficient of static friction.

questions.question: For almost all material pairs, the coefficient of static friction μ_s and kinetic friction μ_k satisfy:
questions.explanation: It takes more force to initiate motion than to maintain it.

questions.question: A block resting on an incline of angle θ begins to slip when tan θ equals:
questions.explanation: mg sin θ = μ_s mg cos θ => tan θ = μ_s.

questions.question: In uniform circular motion with radius r and speed v, the acceleration is directed:

options.text: Radially inward toward the center (centripetal acceleration a_c = v² / r)

questions.explanation: Centripetal acceleration changes direction of velocity toward center.

questions.question: The centripetal force required to keep a mass m in a circular path of radius r at speed v is:
questions.explanation: F_c = m a_c = m v² / r.

questions.question: If the speed of a car rounding a curve is DOUBLED, the required centripetal force:
questions.explanation: F_c is proportional to v² => (2v)² = 4v².

questions.question: The banking angle θ of a frictionless curve of radius r for speed v satisfies:
questions.explanation: N sin θ = mv²/r and N cos θ = mg => tan θ = v²/(rg).

questions.question: Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation states that the gravitational force between masses m₁ and m₂ separated by r is:
questions.explanation: Inverse-square law of gravity.

questions.question: If the distance between two planets is doubled, the gravitational attraction between them becomes:
questions.explanation: Inverse-square: 1/(2r)² = 1/(4r²).

questions.question: The acceleration due to gravity at the surface of a planet with mass M and radius R is:
questions.explanation: mg = G M m / R² => g = G M / R².

questions.question: An Atwood machine consists of two masses m₁ > m₂ connected by a light string over a frictionless pulley. The acceleration is:
questions.explanation: Net force (m₁ - m₂)g divided by total mass (m₁ + m₂).

questions.question: The period T of uniform circular motion with radius r and speed v is:
questions.explanation: Distance of one revolution (2πr) divided by speed v.

questions.question: A 2 kg mass is moving at 10 m/s. Its momentum is:
The work done by a constant force F acting through displacement d is defined as:
questions.explanation: Definition of mechanical work.

questions.question: If a force acts perpendicular to the displacement (θ = 90°), the work done by this force is:
questions.explanation: cos 90° = 0. Example: centripetal force does zero work.

questions.question: The kinetic energy of an object of mass m moving with speed v is:
questions.explanation: Kinetic energy formula.

questions.question: The Work-Kinetic Energy Theorem states that the net work done on an object equals:

options.text: The change in its kinetic energy: W_net = ΔK = K_f - K_i

questions.explanation: Fundamental theorem connecting work and kinetic energy.

questions.question: A force is conservative if:

options.text: The work done moving between two points is independent of the path taken
The work done around a closed loop is non-zero

questions.explanation: Work depends only on endpoints; ∮ F · dr = 0.

questions.question: Which of the following is a non-conservative force?
questions.explanation: Friction dissipates mechanical energy into thermal energy.

questions.question: The gravitational potential energy of mass m near Earth's surface at height y is:
questions.explanation: Work done against constant gravity.

questions.question: Hooke's Law for an ideal spring gives the restoring force F_s as:
questions.explanation: Linear restoring force directed toward equilibrium.

questions.question: The elastic potential energy stored in a spring stretched by distance x is:
questions.explanation: ∫₀^x k s ds = (1/2) k x².

questions.question: In an isolated system with only conservative forces acting, the total mechanical energy E = K + U is:
questions.explanation: Law of conservation of mechanical energy.

questions.question: Power is defined as the rate at which work is done. Its instantaneous expression is:
questions.explanation: P = dW/dt = F · (dr/dt) = F · v (unit: Watt = J/s).

questions.question: Linear momentum p of an object is defined as:
questions.explanation: Definition of momentum vector.

questions.question: The impulse J delivered by a force F over time interval Δt equals:

options.text: J = ∫ F dt = Δp (change in momentum)

questions.explanation: Impulse-Momentum Theorem.

questions.question: In the absence of external forces, the total linear momentum of a system of particles is:

options.text: Conserved in all collisions (both elastic and inelastic)

questions.explanation: Conservation of momentum holds universally when F_ext = 0.

questions.question: An elastic collision is characterized by:

options.text: Conservation of momentum only, with loss of kinetic energy
Conservation of BOTH total linear momentum and total kinetic energy

questions.explanation: Kinetic energy is completely conserved in elastic collisions.

questions.question: In a completely (perfectly) inelastic collision:

options.text: The objects bounce apart with equal speeds
The colliding bodies stick together and move with a common final velocity (maximum kinetic energy lost)

questions.explanation: Sticking together maximizes mechanical energy loss.

questions.question: The center of mass position r_cm for two masses m₁ at x₁ and m₂ at x₂ is:
questions.explanation: Mass-weighted average position.

questions.question: The angular velocity ω is related to linear velocity v for a point at distance r from the axis of rotation by:
questions.explanation: Arc length s = rθ => v = ds/dt = r(dθ/dt) = rω.

questions.question: The tangential acceleration a_t is related to angular acceleration α by:
questions.explanation: a_t = dv/dt = r(dω/dt) = rα.

questions.question: The rotational kinetic energy of a rigid body with moment of inertia I rotating with angular speed ω is:
questions.explanation: Rotational analog of (1/2)mv².

questions.question: The moment of inertia of a point mass m at distance r from the rotation axis is:
questions.explanation: Definition of moment of inertia.

questions.question: The moment of inertia of a uniform solid cylinder (or disk) of mass M and radius R about its central axis is:
questions.explanation: Standard integral formula for solid disk.

questions.question: The moment of inertia of a uniform solid sphere of mass M and radius R about any diameter is:
questions.explanation: Standard formula for solid sphere.

questions.question: The Parallel-Axis Theorem states that the moment of inertia I about any axis parallel to an axis through the center of mass is:
questions.explanation: Steiner's parallel axis theorem.

questions.question: Torque τ produced by force F applied at position r relative to pivot is defined as:

options.text: τ = r x F = |r| |F| sin θ

questions.explanation: Rotational analog of force.

questions.question: Newton's Second Law for rotational motion about a fixed axis is:
questions.explanation: Net torque equals moment of inertia times angular acceleration.

questions.question: Angular momentum L of a rigid body rotating about a fixed principal axis is:
questions.explanation: Rotational analog of linear momentum p = mv.

questions.question: In the absence of external torque (Σ τ_ext = 0), the total angular momentum of a system is:
questions.explanation: Law of conservation of angular momentum (e.g. spinning figure skater pulling in arms).

questions.question: The two necessary conditions for static equilibrium of a rigid body are:

options.text: Σ F = 0 (translational equilibrium) and Σ τ = 0 (rotational equilibrium)

questions.explanation: Zero net force and zero net torque about any pivot.

questions.question: A uniform meter stick of mass 0.2 kg is pivoted at its center (50 cm). Where must a 0.4 kg mass be placed to balance a 0.8 kg mass at the 20 cm mark?

options.text: At the 110 cm mark (cannot balance on stick) or at 30 cm on opposite side: distance = 60 cm from pivot

questions.explanation: τ₁ = 0.8 * 30 = 24. For 0.4 kg: 0.4 * d = 24 => d = 60 cm from pivot.

questions.question: A solid cylinder and a hoop of identical mass and radius roll without slipping down an incline. Which reaches the bottom first?

options.text: Both reach at the exact same time
The solid cylinder, because it has a smaller moment of inertia ((1/2)MR² < MR²)

questions.explanation: Smaller moment of inertia channels more energy into translation rather than rotation.

questions.question: In simple harmonic motion (SHM) of a mass-spring system, the angular frequency is:
questions.explanation: ω² = k/m => ω = √(k/m).

questions.question: The period T of a simple pendulum of length L in a gravitational field g is:
questions.explanation: Independent of the mass of the bob for small amplitudes.

questions.question: In simple harmonic motion, the acceleration is proportional to displacement and directed:

options.text: In the same direction as displacement
Opposite to the displacement: a(t) = -ω² x(t)

questions.explanation: Defining equation of SHM: d²x/dt² + ω²x = 0.

questions.question: At the equilibrium position (x = 0) of simple harmonic motion:

options.text: Speed is zero; acceleration is maximum
Speed and kinetic energy are maximum; potential energy and acceleration are zero

questions.explanation: All energy is kinetic at equilibrium.

questions.question: A 1000 kg car traveling at 20 m/s hits a wall and comes to a stop in 0.2 s. The average stopping force is:
Escape velocity from the surface of a planet of mass M and radius R is given by:
Kepler's Third Law of planetary motion states that the square of orbital period T is proportional to:

options.text: The square of semi-major axis: T² ∝ a²
The cube of the semi-major axis: T² ∝ a³

questions.explanation: Harmonic law of planetary orbits.

questions.question: A ball of mass 0.5 kg moving at 6 m/s collides head-on elastically with an identical stationary ball. After collision, the first ball:

options.text: Comes to rest, and the second ball moves away at 6 m/s
Both stick together and move at 3 m/s

questions.explanation: Equal masses exchange velocities in 1D elastic collisions.

questions.question: The work done stretching a spring from x = 0 to x = 0.1 m with spring constant k = 200 N/m is:
Total energy of a rolling sphere (mass M, radius R, v = Rω) without slipping is:
The SI unit of torque is:
questions.explanation: N·m (kept separate from Joule to distinguish from energy scalar).

questions.question: The SI unit of linear momentum is:
questions.explanation: Mass times velocity: kg * m/s.

questions.question: The SI unit of angular momentum is:
questions.explanation: r × p gives meters times kg·m/s = kg·m²/s.

questions.question: A mass on a spring oscillates with amplitude A. If amplitude is doubled to 2A, the total mechanical energy:
questions.explanation: Total energy E = (1/2) k A² is proportional to amplitude squared.

questions.question: What is the work done by gravity on a satellite in a circular orbit around Earth during one full revolution?
questions.explanation: Gravity is always perpendicular to instantaneous displacement in circular orbit.

questions.question: The slope of a potential energy curve U(x) versus position x gives:
questions.explanation: Conservative force relation F = -dU/dx.

questions.question: A point where dU/dx = 0 and d²U/dx² > 0 corresponds to a point of:

options.text: Stable equilibrium (local minimum in potential energy)

questions.explanation: Minimum potential energy corresponds to stable equilibrium.

questions.question: A point where dU/dx = 0 and d²U/dx² < 0 corresponds to:

options.text: Unstable equilibrium (local maximum in potential energy)

questions.explanation: Maximum potential energy gives unstable equilibrium.

questions.question: A 4 kg rifle fires a 0.01 kg bullet at 800 m/s. The recoil velocity of the rifle is:
Work done by a variable force F(x) from x₁ to x₂ is computed as:
questions.explanation: Definite integral of force over displacement.

questions.question: The mechanical advantage of a simple machine with 100% efficiency is defined as:
questions.explanation: Ratio of load to effort.

questions.question: Coulomb's Law states that the electrostatic force between two point charges q₁ and q₂ separated by distance r is:
questions.explanation: k_e ≈ 8.99 x 10⁹ N·m²/C²; inverse-square law.

questions.question: The electrostatic constant k_e is related to the permittivity of free space ε₀ by:
questions.explanation: Standard SI definition with ε₀ ≈ 8.85 x 10⁻¹² C²/(N·m²).

questions.question: Electric charge is quantized, meaning any observed charge Q must satisfy:

options.text: Q can take any continuous real value
Q = ±n e, where e ≈ 1.602 x 10⁻¹⁹ C and n is an integer

questions.explanation: Charge exists in discrete multiples of fundamental charge e.

questions.question: The electric field E created by a point charge q at distance r is:

options.text: E = k_e q / r² directed radially away from positive charge and toward negative charge

questions.explanation: Force per unit positive test charge E = F / q₀.

questions.question: Electric field lines:

options.text: Begin on positive charges, terminate on negative charges, and never cross
Cross each other at high density

questions.explanation: Standard rules for electrostatic field lines.

questions.question: The electric flux Φ_E through an area A in a uniform electric field E is:

options.text: Φ_E = E · A = E A cos θ

options.text: q_enc / ε₀, where q_enc is the net enclosed charge

questions.question: Inside a static conductor in electrostatic equilibrium, the electric field is:

questions.question: Any excess charge placed on an isolated conductor resides:

questions.question: The electric field just outside the surface of a charged conductor is:

options.text: E = σ / ε₀, directed perpendicular to the surface

options.text: E = σ / (2 ε₀), independent of distance

options.text: ΔV = -∫ E · ds = ΔU / q₀ (change in potential energy per unit charge)

questions.explanation: Definition of electric potential difference (unit: Volt = J/C).

questions.question: The electric potential V of a point charge q at distance r (taking V(∞) = 0) is:
questions.explanation: -∫_∞^r (k_e q/s²) ds = k_e q/r.

questions.question: Electric potential is a:

options.text: Vector quantity with direction along E
Scalar quantity, so potentials from multiple charges add algebraically (V = Σ V_i)

questions.explanation: Potential is scalar; superposition is algebraic without vector components.

questions.question: An equipotential surface is a surface on which:

options.text: The electric field is zero everywhere
E is parallel to the surface
The electric potential is the same at every point, and E is always perpendicular to it

questions.explanation: No work is done moving a charge along an equipotential surface: E · ds = 0.

questions.question: The electric field component E_x is related to potential V by:
questions.explanation: Electric field is the negative gradient of potential: E = -∇V.

questions.question: Capacitance C of any capacitor is defined as:

options.text: C = Q / ΔV (ratio of charge magnitude to potential difference)

questions.explanation: Definition of capacitance (unit: Farad = C/V).

questions.question: The capacitance of an ideal parallel-plate capacitor with plate area A and separation d in vacuum is:
questions.explanation: ΔV = Ed = (Q/ε₀A)d => C = Q/ΔV = ε₀A/d.

questions.question: Inserting a dielectric with dielectric constant κ > 1 between the plates of a capacitor:

options.text: Decreases the capacitance to C₀ / κ
Increases the capacitance to C = κ C₀

questions.explanation: Dielectrics increase capacitance by factor κ.

questions.question: For capacitors connected in SERIES, the equivalent capacitance C_eq is:

questions.question: Two identical capacitors of capacitance C are connected in series. Their equivalent capacitance is:

questions.question: The electric potential energy U stored in a charged capacitor is:
questions.explanation: Integrate work dw = v dq = (q/C) dq => Q²/(2C).

questions.question: The energy density u_E (energy per unit volume) stored in an electric field E in vacuum is:

questions.question: An electron (charge -e, mass m) released from rest in a uniform electric field E experiences acceleration:

options.text: a = e E / m in the direction of E
a = e E / m in the direction OPPOSITE to E

questions.question: An electric dipole consists of charges +q and -q separated by distance d. The dipole moment vector p is:

p = q d directed from negative to positive charge

questions.explanation: Convention: dipole moment points from -q to +q.

questions.question: The torque τ on an electric dipole p in an external electric field E is:
questions.explanation: Dipole tends to align parallel with electric field.

questions.question: The potential energy U of an electric dipole p in an electric field E is:
questions.explanation: Minimum energy U = -pE when aligned with field (θ = 0).

questions.question: A 10 μF capacitor is connected to a 12 V battery. The charge on the capacitor is:
questions.explanation: Q = C V = 10 μF * 12 V = 120 μC.

questions.question: Dielectric breakdown occurs when:

options.text: The electric field exceeds the dielectric strength of the material, causing it to conduct

questions.question: Electric current I is defined as the rate of charge flow through a cross-section:
questions.explanation: Definition of electric current.

questions.question: Microscopic current is related to drift velocity v_d of charge carriers by:
questions.explanation: n = carrier density, q = charge, A = area, v_d = drift speed.

questions.question: Ohm's Law states that for many materials (ohmic conductors):

options.text: The current I is directly proportional to voltage V (V = I R)
Current is constant regardless of V

questions.question: The resistance R of a wire of length L, cross-sectional area A, and resistivity ρ is:
questions.explanation: Resistance increases with length and decreases with area.

questions.question: Electrical conductivity σ is the reciprocal of resistivity ρ:

questions.question: For resistors in SERIES, the equivalent resistance R_eq is:

questions.question: For resistors in PARALLEL, the equivalent resistance R_eq is:

questions.question: Kirchhoff's Junction Rule (Current Law - KCL) is based on the conservation of:

questions.question: Kirchhoff's Loop Rule (Voltage Law - KVL) is based on the conservation of:

questions.question: In an RC charging circuit (resistor R, capacitor C, voltage source V₀), the time constant is:

questions.question: During charging of a capacitor in an RC circuit, after one time constant (t = τ), the charge reaches:

questions.question: The magnetic force F_B on a particle of charge q moving with velocity v in magnetic field B is:

questions.question: The torque τ on a magnetic dipole μ in magnetic field B is:

questions.question: The Biot-Savart Law gives the magnetic field dB produced by a current element I ds as:
questions.explanation: Fundamental differential law for magnetic fields.

questions.question: The magnetic field B at distance r from a long straight wire carrying current I is:

questions.question: Two long parallel wires carrying currents in the SAME direction:

Rusting of iron in moist air

options.text: The same total number of electrons
Similar chemical properties and the same number of valence electrons
The same number of occupied energy levels

questions.question: Avogadro's number, the number of particles in exactly 1 mole of a substance, is:
questions.explanation: Fundamental chemical counting constant.

options.text: The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in the compound
The exact number of atoms in a single molecule

The amount of product obtained experimentally in the lab

questions.explanation: Formula for percentage yield.

Total mass of products equals total mass of reactants

questions.question: Boyle's Law states that at constant temperature, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is:

options.text: Inversely proportional to pressure (P₁ V₁ = P₂ V₂)

questions.question: What is a pointer in C++?

A variable that stores the memory address of another variable

questions.question: What is a memory leak in C++?

options.text: Allocating memory with new on the heap but failing to deallocate it with delete, wasting system RAM

questions.explanation: Lost memory references that cannot be freed.

questions.question: What is a copy constructor in C++?

options.text: A function that assigns two integers
A constructor of the form ClassName(const ClassName &other) that initializes an object from another object of the same class
A method in the math library

questions.explanation: Enables deep copies when objects contain pointers.

questions.question: What is the danger of relying on the default compiler-generated copy constructor when a class contains raw pointers?

options.text: Shallow copy: both objects point to the same heap memory, causing double-free crashes on destruction

questions.explanation: Shallow copy copies the pointer value rather than allocating new heap memory.

questions.question: What is inheritance in C++?

options.text: A mechanism where a derived class acquires the properties and methods of a base class
Writing multiple functions with the same name

questions.explanation: Fundamental OOP pillar representing an "is-a" relationship.

questions.question: What is the syntax for a class Dog inheriting publicly from class Animal in C++?
questions.explanation: C++ uses a colon : followed by access specifier and base class name.

questions.question: In public inheritance, public members of the base class become:

options.text: Private members of the derived class
Protected members of the derived class
Public members of the derived class

questions.explanation: Public inheritance preserves public visibility.

questions.question: In public inheritance, private members of the base class are:

options.text: Inherited but not directly accessible by derived class member functions

questions.explanation: Private members remain strictly private to the base class.

questions.question: When a derived class object is created, in what order are constructors executed?

options.text: Base class constructor first, followed by derived class constructor
Derived class constructor first, then base class

questions.explanation: Base must be initialized before derived enhancements.

questions.question: When a derived class object is destroyed, in what order are destructors executed?

options.text: Base class destructor first, then derived
Derived class destructor first, followed by base class destructor (reverse order)

questions.explanation: Destruction proceeds in exact reverse order of construction.

questions.question: How can a derived class constructor pass arguments to its base class constructor in C++?

options.text: Calling Base(a) inside the body of Derived
Using member initializer list: Derived(int a, int b) : Base(a) { ... }

questions.explanation: Base constructors must be invoked via the initializer list.

questions.question: What is operator overloading in C++?

options.text: Giving special meaning to existing C++ operators (like +, -, <<) when applied to user-defined class objects

questions.explanation: Keyword operator followed by symbol, e.g. operator+.

questions.question: Which operator CANNOT be overloaded in C++?

options.text: The scope resolution operator (::) and member selection (.)

questions.explanation: ::, ., .*, and ?: cannot be overloaded.

questions.question: What is a friend function in C++?

options.text: A member function inherited from base class
A non-member function granted full access to the private and protected members of a class
A function that can only access public members
A function that cannot take arguments

questions.explanation: Declared with keyword friend inside class definition.

questions.question: Can friendship in C++ be inherited or transitive?

options.text: Yes, if class A is friend of B, and B of C, A is friend of C
No, friendship is neither inherited nor transitive

questions.explanation: Friendship is granted explicitly and is not inherited.

questions.question: What is a virtual function in C++ (declared with keyword 'virtual')?

options.text: A function that has no code
A function that cannot be modified
A member function in a base class that can be overridden in a derived class and supports dynamic (runtime) polymorphism

questions.explanation: Resolved at runtime via the vtable.

questions.question: What is a pure virtual function in C++?

options.text: A virtual function declared with = 0 (e.g. virtual void draw() = 0;)
A virtual function with an empty body {}

questions.explanation: = 0 declares an interface method that must be implemented by derived classes.

questions.question: A class that contains at least one pure virtual function is called:

options.text: An abstract class (cannot be instantiated directly)

questions.explanation: Abstract classes serve as blueprints; you cannot create objects of an abstract class.

questions.question: Why should a base class designed for polymorphic deletion have a virtual destructor?

options.text: To make the object smaller in memory
To prevent objects from being deleted
To ensure that the derived class destructor is properly invoked when deleting a derived object via a base pointer
It is required for compile-time constants

questions.explanation: Non-virtual destructor causes undefined behavior and resource leaks during polymorphic delete.

questions.question: What is the scope resolution operator in C++?
questions.explanation: Used to specify class scope (ClassName::methodName) or global scope (::x).

questions.question: What is a static data member in a C++ class?

options.text: A variable shared by all instances of the class (only one copy exists in memory)
A variable that cannot be changed
A variable stored on the heap for each object

questions.explanation: Belongs to the class itself rather than individual instances.

questions.question: Can a static member function in C++ access non-static class data members directly?

options.text: No, because static member functions do not have a 'this' pointer
Only if the member is public

questions.explanation: Static functions lack object instance context (*this).

questions.question: What is the arrow operator (->) used for in C++?

options.text: To access a member of an object through a pointer (ptr->member is equivalent to (*ptr).member)

questions.explanation: Syntax sugar for dereference and member access.
Default copy constructor copies member x = 5.

questions.question: What is multiple inheritance in C++?

options.text: A derived class inheriting from more than one base class (e.g. class C : public A, public B)
A class inheriting through multiple levels

questions.explanation: C++ natively allows inheriting from multiple parent classes.

questions.question: The "Diamond Problem" in C++ multiple inheritance is resolved using:
questions.explanation: Virtual base classes ensure only one shared base subobject is created.

questions.question: What is an inline function in C++?

options.text: A function defined outside a class
A function where the compiler attempts to replace the function call directly with its machine code to reduce call overhead
A function that takes no parameters

questions.explanation: inline hint reduces stack frame push/pop overhead for small functions.

questions.question: What is function overriding in C++?

options.text: Defining functions with different parameters in the same class
Hiding a function using private access
Redefining a base class virtual function in a derived class with the exact same signature

questions.explanation: Core mechanism for dynamic runtime polymorphism.

questions.question: In C++11, the 'override' specifier is used to:

options.text: Ensure that a member function is overriding a base class virtual function (compiler throws an error if it doesn't)
Prevent a function from being inherited

questions.explanation: Prevents subtle bugs from mismatched signatures.

questions.question: In C++11, the 'final' specifier on a virtual function:

options.text: Forces derived classes to override it
Prevents further derived classes from overriding that function

questions.explanation: Specifies the end of polymorphism for that method.

questions.question: What does nullptr represent in C++11?

options.text: A type-safe null pointer literal of type std::nullptr_t

questions.explanation: Replaces ambiguous NULL macro (which was 0) with a distinct pointer type.

questions.question: What is the Rule of Three in classic C++ for classes managing resources?

options.text: A class must have 3 member variables
If you define a Destructor, Copy Constructor, or Copy Assignment Operator, you should define all three

questions.explanation: Ensures correct resource lifetime management and avoids shallow-copy bugs.

questions.question: What is the syntax for defining an overloaded insertion operator (<<) for class Point?

options.text: ostream& operator<<(ostream& os, const Point& p) { ... return os; }

questions.explanation: Overloaded stream operators return stream reference for chaining.

questions.question: Can the assignment operator (operator=) be a non-member (friend) function in C++?

options.text: Yes, it can be a friend function
No, operator= MUST be a non-static member function of the class

questions.explanation: C++ standard requires operator= to be a member function.

questions.question: What is encapsulation in Object-Oriented Programming?

options.text: Writing multiple functions with the same name
Inheriting properties from a base class
Bundling data and methods into a single unit (class) while restricting direct access to internal details (data hiding)

questions.explanation: Definition of encapsulation.

questions.question: What is polymorphism in C++?

options.text: Having multiple variables of the same type
The ability of different objects to respond to the same function call in their own specific way (one interface, multiple implementations)

questions.explanation: Definition of polymorphism.

questions.question: What is early (static) binding in C++?

options.text: Resolving function calls at compile time (used for regular non-virtual functions and overloaded functions)
Resolving function calls at runtime via vtable

questions.explanation: Early binding occurs at compilation.

questions.question: What is late (dynamic) binding in C++?

options.text: Resolving function calls at runtime based on the actual type of the object pointed to (used for virtual functions)

questions.explanation: Late binding powers runtime polymorphism.

questions.question: How is dynamic dispatch implemented internally by most C++ compilers?

options.text: Through if-else statements generated at compile time
Through a Virtual Method Table (vtable) and a hidden virtual pointer (vptr) inside each object
Using string comparisons of method names

questions.explanation: vptr points to the class vtable containing function pointers.

questions.question: What is the output of: class B { public: virtual void f() { cout << "B"; } }; class D : public B { public: void f() override { cout << "D"; } }; B *ptr = new D(); ptr->f(); ?
questions.explanation: Because f() is virtual, ptr->f() dynamically resolves to D::f() based on actual object type.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the four primary pillars of Object-Oriented Programming?
questions.explanation: The four pillars are Encapsulation, Abstraction, Inheritance, and Polymorphism.

questions.question: Encapsulation is best demonstrated by:

options.text: Making member variables private and providing public getter and setter methods

questions.explanation: Data hiding combined with accessor methods encapsulates state.

questions.question: An instance of a class is known as:
questions.explanation: A class is a blueprint; an object is an instance.

questions.question: A constructor that initializes all member variables with default values when no arguments are provided is a:
questions.explanation: Invoked when an object is declared with no arguments.

questions.question: What is constructor overloading?

options.text: Defining multiple constructors with different parameter lists in the same class
Having constructors in both base and derived classes
Calling a constructor inside a loop
A constructor that calls a destructor

questions.explanation: Permits object initialization in multiple ways.

questions.question: In C++, constructor delegation (introduced in C++11) allows:

options.text: A constructor to call a destructor
A constructor to call another constructor of the same class in its initializer list
A class to delegate its construction to a global function
A derived class constructor to be private

questions.explanation: Reduces duplicate initialization code.

questions.question: The initialization list of a constructor is executed:
questions.explanation: Initializes members directly upon memory allocation.

questions.question: Which members MUST be initialized in the constructor initialization list rather than the body?
questions.explanation: References and const members must be initialized when created, not assigned.

questions.question: What is a copy constructor called for?

options.text: When an object is passed by value to a function, returned by value, or initialized from another object of the same type
When assigning an object using = operator after initialization

questions.explanation: Invoked during initialization from another instance.

questions.question: What is the signature of a standard copy constructor for class Complex?
questions.explanation: Must take by reference (typically const); passing by value would cause infinite recursion.

questions.question: A deep copy differs from a shallow copy because a deep copy:

options.text: Is automatically done by default by the compiler
Allocates new memory and copies the actual values rather than just copying pointer addresses

questions.explanation: Prevents aliasing and double-free errors.

questions.question: The "is-a" relationship in object-oriented design is modeled using:
questions.explanation: Example: Dog is-an Animal.

questions.question: The "has-a" relationship in object-oriented design is modeled using:
questions.explanation: Example: Car has-an Engine.

questions.question: In composition (strong "has-a"):

options.text: The contained object cannot exist independently of the containing object (shared lifetime)
The relationship is defined using the 'is' keyword

questions.explanation: Destroying a Car destroys its Engine subobject in composition.

questions.question: In aggregation (weak "has-a"):

options.text: The lifetime of both objects is strictly identical
The contained object can exist independently of the containing object (e.g., Department has Teachers)

questions.explanation: Teachers continue to exist even if Department is closed.

questions.question: The keyword 'explicit' on a single-parameter constructor prevents:
questions.explanation: explicit Complex(double r) prevents code like Complex c = 5.0.

questions.question: Operator overloading enables user-defined classes to:

options.text: Define custom behavior for standard operators (+, -, *, ==, <<, etc.)
Change the precedence of C++ operators

questions.explanation: Provides intuitive, readable mathematical syntax for objects.

questions.question: Which operator should return *this by reference to allow chaining (e.g. a = b = c;)?
questions.explanation: MyClass& operator=(const MyClass &rhs) { ... return *this; } allows assignment chaining.

questions.question: Why is self-assignment check (if (this == &rhs) return *this;) essential in operator=?

options.text: To prevent deleting your own heap memory before copying it
It is optional and never needed

questions.explanation: Deleting old resources in a self-assignment would destroy the source data.

questions.question: A static member function:

options.text: Has access to non-static member variables
Can be invoked using ClassName::functionName() without creating an instance of the class

questions.explanation: Static methods belong to the class, not to an instance.

questions.question: Const member functions (e.g., int getX() const;):

options.text: Promise not to modify any non-mutable member variables of the calling object
Can only be called by const objects

questions.explanation: Guarantees read-only access on *this.

questions.question: Which keyword allows a specific member variable to be modified even inside a const member function?
questions.explanation: mutable variables (e.g. cache/mutex) can be modified in const methods.

questions.question: What is the purpose of getter and setter methods?

options.text: To control and validate access to private data members (maintaining encapsulation)

questions.explanation: Enables data validation and hides internal representations.

questions.question: What is method overloading in OOP?

options.text: Re-implementing a base class method in a derived class
Defining multiple methods in the same class with identical names but different signatures

questions.explanation: Compile-time ad-hoc polymorphism.

questions.question: Can a constructor be declared as virtual in C++?
questions.explanation: An object's exact type must be known at construction time; vtable is established during construction.

questions.question: Can a destructor be declared as virtual in C++?

options.text: Yes, and base classes designed for inheritance should virtually always have virtual destructors

questions.explanation: Virtual destructor is necessary for proper cleanup via base class pointers.

questions.question: In C++, protected members of a base class are accessible by:

options.text: Member functions of the base class and member functions of derived classes

questions.explanation: Provides visibility down the inheritance hierarchy.

questions.question: What is the return type of the comparison operator operator==(const MyClass &other) const?
questions.explanation: Comparison yields true or false.

questions.question: When an object is passed BY VALUE to a function:

options.text: The copy constructor is called to create a local copy
The address of the original object is passed

questions.explanation: Pass-by-value invokes the copy constructor.

questions.question: When an object is passed BY CONST REFERENCE (const MyClass &obj):

options.text: No copy is made (efficient) and the function cannot modify the original object (safe)
The object is destroyed upon return
Only public members can be read

questions.explanation: Combines the efficiency of pass-by-reference with the safety of pass-by-value.

questions.question: What is an anonymous (temporary) object in C++?

options.text: An unnamed object created on the fly (e.g. return Complex(1, 2);)

questions.explanation: Rvalue temporary objects with lifespan of the full expression.

questions.question: The scope of an automatic object declared inside a block { ... } ends when:

options.text: Execution reaches the closing brace }, and its destructor is called automatically

questions.explanation: Automatic stack storage duration.

questions.question: Polymorphism in OOP is primarily achieved in C++ through:
questions.explanation: Virtual functions enable runtime dynamic dispatch.

questions.question: A class with at least one pure virtual function (virtual void f() = 0;) is:

options.text: An abstract class, which cannot be instantiated directly

questions.explanation: Abstract classes define interfaces for derived classes to implement.

questions.question: If a derived class does NOT override a pure virtual function inherited from an abstract base class:

options.text: The code compiles and runs using the base implementation
The pure virtual function is ignored
The derived class also becomes an abstract class and cannot be instantiated
A runtime exception is thrown on startup

questions.explanation: Failure to implement pure virtual functions leaves derived class abstract.

questions.question: What is the Virtual Method Table (vtable)?

options.text: A table of object variables in RAM
An array of function pointers maintained by the compiler for each polymorphic class to resolve virtual function calls at runtime

questions.explanation: Core mechanism of C++ runtime polymorphism.

questions.question: Every object of a polymorphic class contains a hidden pointer called:

options.text: vptr (virtual pointer), which points to the class's vtable

questions.explanation: Added to object layout to locate the vtable.

questions.question: What is an interface in object-oriented design?

options.text: A class that contains ONLY pure virtual functions and no data members, defining a contract
A class with only private members

questions.explanation: Abstract interface contract pattern.

questions.question: What does the dynamic_cast operator do in C++?

options.text: Forces a cast without any checks
Safely converts a base class pointer to a derived class pointer at runtime, returning nullptr if invalid

questions.explanation: Uses Run-Time Type Information (RTTI) to verify polymorphic downcasts.

questions.question: What does typeid operator return in C++?

options.text: The size of the object in bytes
A reference to a std::type_info object representing the runtime type of an expression

questions.explanation: Requires #include <typeinfo> and polymorphic types for runtime inspection.

questions.question: What are function templates in C++?

options.text: Blueprints for generating functions that can operate on different data types with a single codebase

questions.explanation: template <typename T> T max(T a, T b) generates type-specific functions at compile time.

questions.question: What are class templates in C++?

options.text: Generic classes parameterized by types (e.g. template <typename T> class Stack { ... };)

questions.explanation: Foundation of generic programming and the Standard Template Library (STL).

questions.question: The C++ Standard Template Library (STL) consists of which three major components?
questions.explanation: The classic STL triad.

questions.question: Which STL container represents a dynamically resizable array with contiguous memory storage?
questions.explanation: std::vector provides O(1) random access and dynamic resizing.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of accessing an element by index (vec[i]) in a std::vector?
questions.explanation: Contiguous memory allows immediate address calculation.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of inserting an element at the back of std::vector (push_back)?
questions.explanation: Capacity doubling ensures amortized constant time.

questions.question: Which STL container implements a doubly-linked list with non-contiguous memory storage?
questions.explanation: std::list is a doubly linked list with O(1) insertions anywhere given an iterator.

questions.question: Which STL container stores unique elements sorted automatically in logarithmic time?
questions.explanation: Self-balancing BST guarantees O(log n) search, insertion, and deletion.

questions.question: Which STL container stores key-value pairs sorted by key?
questions.explanation: std::map<Key, Value> stores sorted associative pairs in a Red-Black tree.

questions.question: What is an iterator in C++ STL?

options.text: An object that points to an element within a container and enables sequential traversal like a pointer

questions.explanation: Abstracts traversal across different container types.

questions.question: Which method returns an iterator pointing to the FIRST element of an STL container?
questions.explanation: begin() returns an iterator; front() returns a reference to the element.

questions.question: Which method returns an iterator pointing PAST THE LAST element of an STL container?
questions.explanation: end() points to the theoretical past-the-end position.

questions.question: In C++ exception handling, which block contains code that might throw an exception?
questions.explanation: Exceptions thrown inside a try block are caught by an associated catch block.

questions.question: Which keyword is used to signal/raise an exception in C++?
questions.explanation: throw expr; raises an exception.

questions.question: A catch(...) block with three dots in C++ catches:

options.text: Any exception of any type (catch-all handler)

questions.explanation: Default catch-all handler.

questions.question: What is RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization) in C++?

options.text: A method for initializing arrays with zeros
A programming idiom where resources (memory, file handles, sockets) are acquired in a constructor and released in the destructor

questions.explanation: Ensures exception-safe leak-free resource management.

questions.question: Which C++11 smart pointer represents exclusive ownership of a dynamically allocated object?
questions.explanation: Cannot be copied, only moved (std::move).

questions.question: Which C++11 smart pointer represents shared ownership using reference counting?
questions.explanation: Deletes object when the reference count drops to zero.

questions.question: std::weak_ptr is used in conjunction with std::shared_ptr to solve:
questions.explanation: Observes an object without incrementing its reference count.

questions.question: The Singleton design pattern ensures that:

options.text: A class has only one instance and provides a global access point to it

questions.explanation: Private constructor + static getInstance() method.

questions.question: The Factory Method design pattern is used to:

options.text: Define an interface for creating an object, but let subclasses decide which class to instantiate

questions.explanation: Decouples object creation from client code.

questions.question: In the SOLID design principles, the "S" stands for:

options.text: Single Responsibility Principle (a class should have one, and only one, reason to change)

questions.explanation: Each module/class focuses on a single responsibility.

questions.question: In SOLID principles, the "O" stands for the Open/Closed Principle, which states that software entities should be:

options.text: Open for extension, but closed for modification
Open to inheritance but closed to composition

questions.explanation: Extend behavior by adding code, not modifying tested code.

questions.question: In SOLID principles, the "L" stands for Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP), which requires that:

options.text: Classes cannot have more than 2 levels of inheritance
Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types without altering the correctness of the program

questions.explanation: Derived classes must adhere to base class contracts.

questions.question: In SOLID principles, the "I" stands for Interface Segregation Principle, meaning:

options.text: Clients should not be forced to depend on interfaces they do not use (many specific interfaces are better than one general interface)
Classes can only implement one interface

questions.explanation: Break large interfaces into smaller, cohesive ones.

questions.question: In SOLID principles, the "D" stands for Dependency Inversion Principle, which states:

options.text: High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules; both should depend on abstractions
Derived classes cannot call base methods

questions.explanation: Depend upon abstractions, not concretions.

questions.question: Which STL algorithm is used to sort a container in ascending order?
questions.explanation: std::sort uses introsort (quick/heap/insertion hybrid) running in O(n log n).

questions.question: Which STL algorithm performs binary search on a pre-sorted container?
questions.explanation: Returns true/false in O(log n) time.

questions.question: What is a lambda function in C++11?

options.text: An anonymous inline function that can capture variables from its enclosing scope [captures](params){body}
A function defined in a separate header

questions.explanation: Convenient callable objects used with algorithms.

questions.question: In a C++11 lambda [=](int x) { return x + a; }, the capture clause [=] means:

options.text: Capture all local variables used in the lambda BY VALUE

questions.explanation: [=] captures by value; [&] captures by reference.

questions.question: What does std::move do in C++11?

options.text: Casts an lvalue to an rvalue reference (T&&), enabling move semantics instead of expensive deep copying
Copies an object to the heap

questions.explanation: Unlocks move constructors and move assignment operators.

questions.question: What is the benefit of move semantics in C++11?

options.text: It eliminates the need for constructors
Resources (e.g. heap memory pointers) are transferred from temporary objects without expensive deep copying

questions.explanation: Move constructors transfer ownership in O(1) pointer swaps.

questions.question: The Observer design pattern is ideal for:

options.text: A one-to-many dependency where when one object changes state, all its dependents are notified automatically
Ensuring only one instance of a class exists

questions.explanation: Core pattern for event handling and MVC architecture.

questions.question: The Adapter design pattern is used to:

options.text: Convert the interface of a class into another interface clients expect, enabling incompatible classes to work together

questions.explanation: Structural wrapper pattern.

questions.question: What is the purpose of std::stack container adapter in STL?

options.text: Provides Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) access with push(), pop(), and top() operations

questions.explanation: Restricts operations to LIFO discipline.

questions.question: What is the purpose of std::queue in STL?

options.text: Provides First-In, First-Out (FIFO) access with push(), pop(), front(), and back()

questions.explanation: Standard FIFO queue.

questions.question: What is std::priority_queue in STL based on by default?

options.text: A Max-Heap where top() always returns the largest element

questions.explanation: Default priority_queue is a max-heap.

questions.question: In C++ templates, template specialization allows:

options.text: Restricting a template to only integers
Providing a customized implementation of a template for a specific data type

questions.explanation: e.g. template <> class Vector<bool> specialized for bit packing.

questions.question: What is slicing in C++?

options.text: Dividing an array into two halves
Assigning a derived object to a base object by value, which strips off (slices away) the derived members

questions.explanation: Occurs when assigning Base b = derived_obj; avoided by using pointers or references.

questions.question: An abstract class can have:

options.text: Only pure virtual functions and nothing else
Constructors, member variables, normal member functions, and pure virtual functions

questions.explanation: Abstract classes can have normal state and methods for derived reuse.

questions.question: What is the output of std::min(10, 20) in <algorithm>?
questions.explanation: Returns the smaller of two values.

questions.question: What happens if an exception is thrown in C++ but never caught by any catch block?

options.text: The program ignores the error and continues
std::terminate() is called, terminating the program abnormally
The operating system restarts the function

questions.explanation: Uncaught exceptions invoke std::terminate.

questions.question: Why should destructors never throw exceptions in C++?

options.text: If another exception is already active during stack unwinding, throwing another terminates the program immediately
It is a syntax error to write try-catch in a destructor

questions.explanation: Two simultaneous exceptions trigger immediate std::terminate.

questions.question: The Strategy design pattern allows:

options.text: Defining a family of algorithms, encapsulating each one, and making them interchangeable at runtime

questions.explanation: Enables switching behavioral algorithms dynamically.

questions.question: What does Big-O notation O(f(n)) describe in algorithm analysis?

options.text: An asymptotic upper bound on the growth rate of running time or space as input size n grows
The exact number of CPU clock cycles
The lower bound on execution time
The average number of lines of code

questions.explanation: Big-O represents worst-case asymptotic upper bound.

questions.question: Which of the following time complexities grows the SLOWEST as n approaches infinity?
questions.explanation: Logarithmic growth is strictly slower than linear or polynomial growth.

questions.question: Which time complexity represents quadratic growth?
questions.explanation: n² is quadratic.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of searching for an element in an UNSORTED array of size n?
questions.explanation: In the worst case, every element must be inspected.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of Binary Search on a SORTED array of size n?
questions.explanation: Each comparison halves the remaining search space.

questions.question: A Stack is an abstract data structure that follows which principle?
questions.explanation: The last element pushed is the first one popped.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of push and pop operations on a stack implemented with an array or linked list?
questions.explanation: Accessing and modifying the top of the stack is O(1).

questions.question: What condition occurs when attempting to pop from an empty stack?
questions.explanation: Popping from empty stack is underflow.

questions.question: What condition occurs when attempting to push onto a full array-based stack of fixed capacity?
questions.explanation: Exceeding allocated capacity is overflow.

questions.question: Which data structure is primarily used to evaluate arithmetic postfix (Reverse Polish) expressions?
questions.explanation: Operands are pushed onto a stack; operators pop two operands and push result.

questions.question: Evaluate the postfix expression: 5 3 + 2 *
A Queue is an abstract data structure that follows which principle?
questions.explanation: Elements are enqueued at rear and dequeued from front.

questions.question: In a standard linear queue implemented with a fixed array, what problem arises after multiple enqueues and dequeues?

options.text: False overflow: rear reaches the end of the array while front space is empty

questions.explanation: Linear array queue wastes vacated front spaces.

questions.question: How does a Circular Queue solve the false overflow problem of linear queues?

options.text: By shifting all elements forward on every dequeue
By wrapping the indices around using the modulo operator: (rear + 1) % MAX_SIZE
By dynamically doubling array size each time

questions.explanation: Modulo arithmetic wraps around to reuse front positions in O(1).

questions.question: In a singly linked list, each node contains:

options.text: Data and pointers to both next and previous nodes
Data and a pointer/reference to the next node in the list

questions.explanation: Singly linked list has a single forward pointer.

A tree with all leaves on the left

When two distinct keys produce the same hash code/index from the hash function

questions.question: The load factor α of a hash table with n elements and m buckets is defined as:

questions.explanation: DFS is a LIFO exploration strategy.
