questions.question: The repeat prefix REP in front of a string instruction (e.g. REP MOVSB) repeats the operation until:

options.text: CX reaches 0 (decrementing CX on each step)

questions.explanation: Repeats string operations CX times.

questions.question: The REPE (or REPZ) prefix repeats the string comparison instruction (e.g. CMPSB) as long as:

options.text: CX ≠ 0 AND Zero Flag ZF = 1 (elements are equal)

questions.explanation: Repeat while equal.

questions.question: What is a macro in assembly language?

options.text: A named block of code expanded inline by the assembler preprocessor during compilation
A procedure called at runtime via CALL and RET

questions.explanation: Macros replace text at assemble time; procedures use stack at runtime.

questions.question: How does a macro differ from a procedure in execution and memory?

options.text: A macro is slower than a procedure
A macro generates inline code every time it is invoked (larger code size, no CALL/RET overhead); a procedure exists in one memory location
A macro uses the stack for return addresses

questions.explanation: Classic code size vs speed trade-off.

questions.question: Which instruction disables maskable hardware interrupts in 8086 by clearing the Interrupt Flag (IF)?
questions.explanation: CLI ignores INTR line.

questions.question: Which instruction enables maskable hardware interrupts in 8086 by setting the Interrupt Flag (IF)?
questions.explanation: STI responds to INTR line.

questions.question: The NOP instruction in 8086 performs which action?

options.text: No Operation: consumes 1 byte and 3 clock cycles without modifying registers or flags

questions.explanation: Used for timing delays or padding machine code.

questions.question: The HLT instruction causes the 8086 processor to:

options.text: Halt execution and enter an idle state until an external interrupt or reset occurs

questions.explanation: Processor halts until hardware interrupt arrives.

questions.question: In 8086, I/O ports are accessed using which dedicated instructions?

options.text: IN and OUT (e.g., IN AL, 60h; OUT 20h, AL)

questions.explanation: Isolated I/O uses IN/OUT instructions.

questions.question: What does the LOOP label instruction do in 8086?

options.text: Decrements CX by 1, and jumps to label if CX ≠ 0

questions.explanation: CX = CX - 1; if (CX != 0) goto label.

questions.question: What is the function of the IRET instruction?

options.text: Returns from an Interrupt Service Routine by popping IP, CS, and FLAGS from the stack

questions.explanation: IRET restores IP, CS, and FLAGS saved by INT.

questions.question: A 16-bit word stored in memory at address 1000h as [12h, 34h] (where 12h is at 1000h and 34h is at 1001h) evaluates in little-endian to:
questions.explanation: Little-endian: lower byte at lower address (12h is low byte, 34h is high byte => 3412h).

questions.question: Which register can be used with XLAT (Translate) instruction to perform table lookups?

options.text: BX (holding table base address) and AL (holding index)

questions.explanation: XLAT replaces AL with byte at DS:[BX + unsigned AL].

questions.question: Which flag is set if the number of 1-bits in the low byte of an arithmetic result is EVEN?
questions.explanation: Even parity sets PF to 1.

questions.question: In the classic Von Neumann architecture, programs and data:

options.text: Share the same physical memory space and system bus
Are stored in physically separate memories with separate buses
Are stored only inside CPU registers

questions.explanation: Shared memory for instructions and data is the hallmark of Von Neumann.

questions.question: In the Harvard architecture:

options.text: Separate physical memories and buses are used for instructions and data

questions.explanation: Allows simultaneous instruction fetch and data read/write.

questions.question: The CPU instruction execution cycle consists of which sequence of phases?

options.text: Fetch -> Decode -> Execute -> Memory Access -> Write Back

questions.explanation: Standard 5-stage instruction cycle.

questions.question: The Program Counter (PC) register holds:

options.text: The result of the last arithmetic operation
The base address of the stack
The memory address of the next instruction to be fetched

questions.explanation: Incremented after every fetch or updated by jumps/branches.

questions.question: The Instruction Register (IR) holds:

options.text: The instruction that was just fetched from memory while it is being decoded and executed

questions.explanation: IR stores the fetched machine instruction word.

questions.question: The Memory Address Register (MAR) holds:

options.text: The actual data read from memory
The memory address to which data will be sent or from which data will be fetched

questions.explanation: MAR connects directly to the address bus.

questions.question: The Memory Data Register (MDR or MBR) holds:

options.text: The data read from memory or data ready to be written to memory

questions.explanation: MDR connects directly to the data bus.

questions.question: The Control Unit (CU) of a CPU is responsible for:

options.text: Generating control signals to orchestrate the movement of data and operations across components

questions.explanation: The "brain" directing datapath components.

questions.question: A hardwired control unit generates control signals using:

options.text: Fixed combinational logic circuits and sequential state machines (faster, but inflexible)

questions.explanation: Hardwired logic maximizes speed in RISC processors.

questions.question: A microprogrammed control unit generates control signals by:

options.text: Reading microinstructions sequentially from a Control Read-Only Memory (Control ROM)

questions.explanation: Microcode provides flexibility and easier modification for complex CISC instructions.

questions.question: In MIPS architecture, all instructions have a fixed length of:
questions.explanation: Uniform 32-bit instruction encoding in classic MIPS.

questions.question: The three instruction formats in MIPS architecture are:
questions.explanation: R (register-to-register), I (immediate/branch/load), J (jump).

questions.question: In MIPS R-type instructions (e.g. add $rd, $rs, $rt), the opcode field is:

options.text: 6 bits of all zeros (000000), with the specific operation specified by the funct field

questions.explanation: All MIPS R-type arithmetic/logical instructions share opcode 0 and use funct.

questions.question: In MIPS R-format, how many bits are allocated for each register specifier (rs, rt, rd)?
questions.explanation: 5 bits can address any of the 32 general-purpose registers ($0 to $31).

questions.question: What is the special property of MIPS register $0 ($zero)?

options.text: It is hardwired to the constant value 0 and cannot be overwritten

questions.explanation: Reading $0 always returns 0; writes to $0 are ignored.

questions.question: In MIPS I-type instructions (like lw, sw, addi, beq), the immediate field has a length of:
questions.explanation: 6 bits opcode + 5 rs + 5 rt + 16-bit immediate = 32 bits.

questions.question: In MIPS, memory is byte-addressable, and words are aligned at addresses that are multiples of:
questions.explanation: A 32-bit word consists of 4 bytes; word addresses must end in 00 binary.

questions.question: The ALU control unit in a MIPS single-cycle datapath generates ALU control signals based on:

options.text: The 2-bit ALUOp signal from main control and the 6-bit funct field of the instruction

questions.explanation: Two-level decoding simplifies main control.

questions.question: In a single-cycle datapath, the clock cycle time is determined by:

options.text: The critical path (the longest latency instruction, typically Load Word 'lw')

questions.explanation: Clock must accommodate the slowest instruction that uses all stages.

questions.question: A multi-cycle datapath improves on the single-cycle design by:

options.text: Allowing different instructions to take different numbers of shorter clock cycles

questions.explanation: Faster instructions (like R-type) take 4 cycles, while lw takes 5 cycles.

questions.question: In MIPS, the instruction `beq $s1, $s2, Label` performs branch target calculation using:
questions.explanation: Branches are relative to PC+4 and word-aligned (shifted left by 2).

questions.question: In MIPS, the instruction `j Target` uses which addressing mode?

options.text: Pseudodirect addressing: upper 4 bits of PC+4 concatenated with 26-bit target << 2

questions.explanation: 26-bit field shifted by 2 fills 28 bits; remaining 4 bits from PC+4.

questions.question: A bus that connects the CPU, memory, and I/O devices consists of three sets of lines:

options.text: Power bus, Ground bus, and Signal bus
Serial bus, Parallel bus, and Optical bus
Address bus, Data bus, and Control bus
Input bus, Output bus, and Clock bus

questions.explanation: Standard three-bus architecture.

questions.question: The width of the address bus determines:

options.text: The maximum directly addressable memory capacity

questions.explanation: n address lines can address 2^n memory locations.

questions.question: The width of the data bus determines:

options.text: The number of bits transmitted between CPU and memory in a single read/write cycle

questions.explanation: Defines word throughput per transfer.

questions.question: A synchronous bus operates using:

options.text: Handshaking request and acknowledge lines without a clock
A shared central clock signal to synchronize all bus transactions

questions.explanation: Clock edges govern all transfers.

questions.question: An asynchronous bus operates using:

options.text: Handshaking protocols (e.g. Ready and Acknowledge signals) without a shared clock

questions.explanation: Permits connecting devices with widely varying response speeds.

questions.question: Little-Endian byte ordering means:

options.text: The most significant byte (MSB) is stored at lowest address
Bytes are stored in random order
The least significant byte (LSB) is stored at the lowest memory address

questions.explanation: x86 and ARM (by default) use Little-Endian.

questions.question: Big-Endian byte ordering means:

options.text: The most significant byte (MSB) is stored at the lowest memory address
LSB is stored at lowest address

questions.explanation: Network protocols (IP) and older Motorola processors use Big-Endian.

questions.question: Which register in MIPS is designated as the Stack Pointer?
questions.explanation: $sp ($29) points to the top of the stack.

questions.question: Which register in MIPS stores the return address during a `jal` (Jump and Link) instruction?
questions.explanation: jal automatically saves PC + 4 into $ra.

questions.question: Memory-Mapped I/O means that:

options.text: I/O devices use dedicated special CPU instructions like IN and OUT
All I/O is stored in the cache
I/O device registers are assigned regular memory addresses and accessed using standard memory instructions (e.g. lw, sw)

questions.explanation: No separate address space for I/O; memory and devices share the same bus.

questions.question: Pipelining in computer architecture improves performance by:

options.text: Increasing instruction throughput (number of instructions completed per unit time)
Decreasing the execution time (latency) of an individual instruction

questions.explanation: Overlaps execution of multiple instructions like an assembly line.

questions.question: In an ideal 5-stage pipeline with balanced stages and no stalls, the theoretical speedup over a non-pipelined processor is:

options.text: Equal to the number of stages (5x)

questions.explanation: Speedup = (k * n) / (k + n - 1) → k as n becomes large.

questions.question: What is a STRUCTURAL HAZARD in a pipeline?

options.text: A resource conflict where two instructions require the same hardware component at the same time

questions.explanation: e.g., single memory accessed simultaneously for instruction fetch and data read.

questions.question: How is the structural hazard for simultaneous instruction and data memory access resolved in modern pipelines?

options.text: Using separate L1 Instruction Cache and L1 Data Cache (Harvard architecture at L1)

questions.explanation: Split L1 caches provide independent ports for IF and MEM stages.

questions.question: What is a DATA HAZARD in a pipeline?

options.text: When an instruction depends on the result of a previous instruction that is still in the pipeline (e.g. Read-After-Write - RAW)

questions.explanation: Pipeline tries to read an operand before it is written back.

questions.question: Which data hazard is the most common in standard in-order pipelines?

options.text: RAW (Read After Write / True data dependency)

questions.explanation: A later instruction needs data calculated by an earlier instruction.

questions.question: How does Forwarding (Bypassing) resolve data hazards without stalling the pipeline?

options.text: By waiting for the result to be written to the register file in stage 5
By routing the result directly from an internal pipeline register (EX/MEM or MEM/WB) back to the ALU input

questions.explanation: Result is available at ALU output before reaching the register file.

questions.question: A Load-Use Data Hazard occurs when:

options.text: Two store instructions occur back to back
An instruction immediately follows a Load instruction and uses the loaded register as an operand

questions.explanation: Memory data is not available until end of MEM stage, requiring 1 stall cycle even with forwarding.

questions.question: What is a CONTROL HAZARD (branch hazard) in a pipeline?

options.text: A delay caused by branch/jump instructions where the target address or outcome is not known in time for the next fetch

questions.explanation: The pipeline fetches instructions before knowing if the branch is taken.

questions.question: In static branch prediction, the common heuristic used for loops is:

options.text: Always predict all branches as taken
Predict backward branches as TAKEN, and forward branches as NOT TAKEN
Always predict all branches as not taken

questions.explanation: Loop branches jump backward and are taken repeatedly.

questions.question: Dynamic branch prediction uses a Branch History Table (BHT) containing 2-bit saturating counters to:

options.text: Require a branch to mispredict twice in a row before changing its prediction

questions.explanation: Prevents anomalous single-instance exits in loops from flipping the prediction.

questions.question: A Branch Target Buffer (BTB) is a cache that stores:

options.text: The predicted target instruction address for a branch instruction

questions.explanation: Enables fetching target instruction immediately during IF stage.

questions.question: The principle of Locality of Reference states that programs tend to reuse data and instructions near recently accessed ones, comprising:

options.text: Temporal Locality (recently referenced items likely referenced soon) and Spatial Locality (items nearby likely referenced soon)

questions.explanation: Core principle making cache hierarchies effective.

questions.question: Loop execution exhibits high:

options.text: Temporal Locality (same code executed repeatedly) and Spatial Locality (consecutive instructions fetched)

questions.explanation: Loops access the same instructions and array sequences continuously.

questions.question: Arrange the memory hierarchy levels in order from FASTEST / SMALLEST to SLOWEST / LARGEST:

options.text: Main Memory -> L1 Cache -> Registers -> Disk
Registers -> L1 Cache -> L2 Cache -> L3 Cache -> Main Memory (DRAM) -> Solid State Drive / Hard Disk

questions.explanation: Standard pyramid of memory hierarchy.

questions.question: In a DIRECT-MAPPED cache, a main memory block maps to:

options.text: Any cache line in the entire cache
Any line within a specific set of 4 lines
Exactly ONE specific cache line, determined by: (Block Address) % (Number of Cache Lines)

questions.explanation: Direct mapping: unique designated slot per address.

questions.question: In a FULLY ASSOCIATIVE cache, a main memory block can be placed in:

options.text: ANY line in the cache, requiring all tags to be searched in parallel
Only lines determined by modulo arithmetic
Only the least recently used set

questions.explanation: Maximum placement flexibility, but requires expensive parallel comparator hardware.

questions.question: In an N-WAY SET ASSOCIATIVE cache:

options.text: There are N total lines in the cache
The cache is divided into sets, each containing N lines; a block maps to a specific set and can occupy any of the N lines within that set
Blocks are mapped randomly across N caches

questions.explanation: Balanced compromise between direct-mapped and fully associative designs.

questions.question: A 32-bit memory address in a cache system is partitioned into which three fields?

options.text: Tag, Set Index (or Line Index), and Byte Offset

questions.explanation: Offset selects byte within block; Index selects cache set; Tag verifies block identity.

questions.question: What is a CACHE HIT?

options.text: The data must be fetched from disk
The requested memory data is found in the cache level being accessed

questions.explanation: Data delivered immediately with low latency.

questions.question: What is a CACHE MISS?

options.text: The requested data is NOT in the cache, requiring a fetch from a lower level in the memory hierarchy

questions.explanation: Incurs a miss penalty to retrieve the block.

questions.question: Average Memory Access Time (AMAT) is calculated as:

options.text: AMAT = Hit Time + (Miss Rate * Miss Penalty)

questions.explanation: Standard formula for evaluating cache memory performance.

questions.question: In cache write policies, WRITE-THROUGH means:

options.text: Writes update only the cache, and memory is updated only upon block eviction
Every write updates BOTH the cache line and the underlying main memory simultaneously

questions.explanation: Simpler and memory is always consistent, but consumes more write bandwidth.

questions.question: In cache write policies, WRITE-BACK (copy-back) means:

options.text: Memory is updated on every write
Writes update ONLY the cache line; a "dirty bit" is set, and memory is updated only when the block is evicted

questions.explanation: Drastically reduces memory bus write traffic.

questions.question: The "3 C's" model categorizes cache misses into which three types?
questions.explanation: Mark Hill's classification of cache miss sources.

questions.question: Which replacement policy evicts the cache block that has not been accessed for the longest time?
questions.explanation: LRU exploits temporal locality effectively.

questions.question: Virtual Memory provides which major advantages?

options.text: Eliminates the need for hard drives
Allows processes to exceed physical RAM size, provides memory protection, and simplifies program loading via isolated address spaces

questions.explanation: Hardware abstraction translating virtual addresses to physical frames.

questions.question: What is a PAGE FAULT in virtual memory?

options.text: A syntax error in source code
An interrupt triggered when a program accesses a virtual page that is currently not mapped into physical RAM (present bit = 0)

questions.explanation: OS handles page fault by loading the missing page from disk (swap space) into RAM.

questions.question: The Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) is:

options.text: A special high-speed cache inside the CPU that stores recent virtual-to-physical page table translations
A storage area on hard disk

questions.explanation: TLB hit avoids visiting the page table in memory.

questions.question: A RISC (Reduced Instruction Set Computer) architecture is characterized by:

options.text: Complex variable-length instructions with many addressing modes
Simple instructions of uniform fixed length, load/store architecture, and single-cycle execution of basic instructions

questions.explanation: RISC emphasizes hardware simplicity, pipelining, and compiler optimization.

questions.question: A CISC (Complex Instruction Set Computer) architecture (like x86) is characterized by:

options.text: All instructions executing in 1 clock cycle
Rich instruction sets with variable lengths, complex memory-to-memory addressing modes, and microcoded control units

questions.explanation: CISC aims to reduce code size and provide high-level operations in single instructions.

questions.question: A Superscalar processor achieves Instruction-Level Parallelism (ILP) by:

options.text: Issuing and executing multiple instructions per clock cycle using multiple parallel execution units (ALUs)

questions.explanation: IPC (Instructions Per Cycle) > 1.

questions.question: A VLIW (Very Long Instruction Word) processor achieves parallelism by:

options.text: Relying on the compiler to bundle multiple independent operations into a single long instruction word executed in parallel

questions.explanation: Static scheduling performed entirely by compiler.

questions.question: Amdahl's Law calculates the theoretical speedup of a system when only a fraction P of the workload is parallelized on N processors as:
questions.explanation: Diminishing returns dictated by the sequential portion (1 - P).

questions.question: RAID 0 (Striping) provides:

options.text: High data throughput by striping blocks across multiple disks, but NO fault tolerance or redundancy

questions.explanation: Failure of any single drive results in complete data loss.

questions.question: RAID 1 provides:

options.text: Disk Mirroring: data is duplicated identically onto two or more disks for redundancy and fault tolerance

questions.explanation: High reliability; can survive failure of half the drives.

questions.question: RAID 5 provides a balance of performance, capacity, and redundancy by using:

options.text: Block-level striping with distributed parity across at least 3 disks (tolerating 1 disk failure)

questions.explanation: Distributed parity prevents the parity bottleneck of RAID 4.

questions.question: What is a DMA (Direct Memory Access) controller used for?

options.text: Transferring data directly between I/O devices and main memory without continuous CPU intervention

questions.explanation: Frees the CPU from copying bytes individually.

questions.question: Interrupt-driven I/O differs from Programmed I/O (polling) because:

options.text: The CPU must continuously check status registers in a loop
The device alerts the CPU via an interrupt line when data is ready, freeing the CPU from busy-waiting

questions.explanation: Eliminates wasted CPU polling cycles.

questions.question: In Flynn's taxonomy, standard multi-core processors executing independent threads belong to:
questions.explanation: Each core executes its own instruction stream on its own data.

questions.question: SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) architecture is extensively used in:

options.text: GPUs and vector processors for graphics, matrix operations, and scientific computing

questions.explanation: One instruction operates on multiple vector elements simultaneously.

questions.question: Cache coherence protocols (such as MESI) solve the problem of:

options.text: Ensuring that multiple processor cores with private caches see a consistent view of shared memory

questions.explanation: Modified, Exclusive, Shared, Invalid states prevent stale cache reads.

questions.question: In out-of-order execution processors, Register Renaming is used to eliminate:

options.text: False data dependencies: WAR (anti-dependencies) and WAW (output dependencies)

questions.explanation: Maps architectural registers to a larger pool of physical registers.

questions.question: The Reorder Buffer (ROB) in an out-of-order processor ensures that:

options.text: Instructions are fetched in reverse order
Instructions commit and update architectural state in strict program order, preserving precise exceptions

questions.explanation: Speculative instructions retire in order.

questions.question: The CPI (Cycles Per Instruction) of an ideal single-cycle CPU is:
questions.explanation: Every instruction takes exactly one long cycle.

questions.question: If a program executes 10^9 instructions on a 2 GHz processor with an average CPI of 1.5, its execution time is:
questions.explanation: CPU Time = (Instruction Count * CPI) / Frequency = (10⁹ * 1.5) / (2 * 10⁹) = 0.75 s.

questions.question: MIPS (Million Instructions Per Second) is considered a flawed metric for comparing different CPU architectures because:

options.text: It does not account for differences in instruction set complexity (a CISC instruction does more work than a RISC instruction)
It only applies to graphics cards

questions.explanation: Different architectures do different amounts of work per instruction.

questions.question: Which component performs address translation from virtual page number to physical frame number in hardware?
questions.explanation: Hardware component of the CPU handling virtual memory.

questions.question: In dynamic RAM (DRAM), bits are stored using:

options.text: A single transistor and a tiny capacitor per bit (requiring periodic refresh cycles)

questions.explanation: Capacitor charge leaks away and must be refreshed thousands of times per second.

questions.question: Static RAM (SRAM) differs from Dynamic RAM (DRAM) because SRAM:

options.text: Is denser and cheaper than DRAM
Is faster, does not require refresh cycles, but uses more transistors per bit (used for CPU caches)

questions.explanation: SRAM uses 6T cells; high speed, low density, high cost.

questions.question: What is a cold (compulsory) cache miss?

options.text: A miss caused by insufficient cache capacity
A miss caused by two blocks competing for the same set
The very first access to a memory block that has never been in the cache before
A miss caused by low temperature

questions.explanation: Cannot be avoided regardless of cache size.

questions.question: Thrashing in a virtual memory system occurs when:

options.text: The system spends more time swapping pages between disk and RAM than executing instructions, due to insufficient physical memory

questions.explanation: Total working sets of active processes exceed available physical frames.

questions.question: The Turing Test, proposed by Alan Turing in 1950, is designed to evaluate:

options.text: Whether a computer can exhibit intelligent behavior indistinguishable from that of a human
The processing speed of a quantum computer
Whether a program can compile without syntax errors
The storage capacity of neural networks

questions.explanation: A human interrogator attempts to distinguish between human and machine responses.

questions.question: In Artificial Intelligence, a rational agent is defined as an entity that:

options.text: Thinks and behaves exactly like a human being in every situation
Acts so as to achieve the best expected outcome based on its performance measure and percept sequence
Always knows the future with 100% certainty (omniscient)

questions.explanation: Rationality means maximizing expected performance, not perfection or human imitation.

questions.question: The PEAS framework for characterizing task environments stands for:

options.text: Performance measure, Environment, Actuators, and Sensors

questions.explanation: Standard formulation for defining agent environments.

questions.question: An environment is fully observable if:

options.text: The agent has to guess parts of the state (e.g. Poker)
The environment changes while the agent is deliberating
The agent's sensors give it access to the complete state of the environment at each point in time (e.g. Chess)

questions.explanation: Complete environmental information is available.

questions.question: An environment is deterministic if:

options.text: The next state of the environment is completely determined by the current state and the agent's action
There is randomness or uncertainty in action outcomes (stochastic)
Multiple agents compete against each other

questions.explanation: No random chance involved in state transitions.

questions.question: In a static environment:

options.text: The environment changes continuously (e.g. driving a car)
The environment does not change while the agent is choosing an action (unlike a dynamic environment)

questions.explanation: Static environment waits for the agent.

questions.question: A search problem is formally formulated by which components?

options.text: Initial state, Actions, Transition model, Goal test, and Path cost

questions.explanation: Classic formal state-space search formulation.

questions.question: Breadth-First Search (BFS) explores the state space using which data structure for the frontier?
questions.explanation: FIFO queue ensures shallowest unvisited nodes are expanded first.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of Breadth-First Search (BFS) with branching factor b and shallowest goal depth d?
questions.explanation: Generates up to b^d nodes at depth d.

questions.question: What is the space complexity of Breadth-First Search (BFS)?

options.text: O(b^d) (stores all frontier nodes in memory, which is often its biggest practical limitation)

questions.explanation: Exponential memory consumption limits BFS application.

questions.question: Is Breadth-First Search (BFS) optimal when all step costs are equal?

options.text: No, it can find sub-optimal paths
Yes, it is guaranteed to find the shallowest goal node

questions.explanation: Shallowest goal corresponds to minimum cost when all edge weights are identical.

questions.question: Depth-First Search (DFS) explores the search tree using which data structure for the frontier?
questions.explanation: LIFO stack expands deepest node first.

questions.question: What is the space complexity of Depth-First Search (DFS) with branching factor b and maximum depth m?

options.text: O(b * m) (linear space, which is its primary advantage over BFS)

questions.explanation: Only needs to store path from root plus siblings at each level.

questions.question: Is standard Depth-First Search (DFS) complete in infinite state spaces or spaces with loops?

options.text: No, it can get trapped in infinite paths or cycles without visiting the goal
Complete only if b is prime

questions.explanation: Can traverse forever down an infinite branch.

questions.question: Depth-Limited Search (DLS) addresses the infinite path problem of DFS by:

options.text: Using a queue instead of a stack
Imposing a fixed maximum depth limit l beyond which nodes are not expanded

questions.explanation: Prevents descending past depth l.

questions.question: Iterative Deepening Depth-First Search (IDDFS) combines the benefits of BFS and DFS by:

options.text: Storing all generated nodes in a database
Repeatedly running DLS with increasing depth limits (l = 0, 1, 2, ...), achieving BFS optimality with DFS O(b*d) space

questions.explanation: Preferred uninformed search method for large state spaces with unknown depth.

questions.question: Uniform-Cost Search (UCS / Dijkstra) expands nodes in order of:

options.text: Path cost g(n) from the initial state, using a Priority Queue

questions.explanation: Expands node with minimum path cost g(n); optimal for general positive edge costs.

questions.question: In informed (heuristic) search, a heuristic function h(n) represents:

options.text: The exact cost from the start state to node n
An estimate of the cheapest path cost from node n to a goal state
The number of children of node n
The execution time of the algorithm

questions.explanation: Domain-specific estimate guiding the search toward the goal.

questions.question: Greedy Best-First Search evaluates and expands nodes based purely on:

options.text: f(n) = h(n) (the estimated cost to reach the goal)

questions.explanation: Greedily chooses the node that appears closest to goal; not guaranteed to be optimal.

questions.question: The A* search algorithm evaluates nodes using the evaluation function:

options.text: f(n) = g(n) + h(n) (known path cost from start + estimated cost to goal)

questions.explanation: Core formula balancing past path cost and future estimated cost.

questions.question: A heuristic function h(n) is called ADMISSIBLE if:

options.text: It NEVER overestimates the true cost to reach the goal (h(n) ≤ h*(n) for all n, with h(goal) = 0)
It is strictly greater than the true cost

questions.explanation: Admissibility guarantees A* tree search optimality.

questions.question: A heuristic function h(n) is called CONSISTENT (or monotonic) if for every node n and successor n' generated by action a:

options.text: h(n) ≤ c(n, a, n') + h(n') (satisfies the triangle inequality)

questions.explanation: Consistency ensures f(n) values are monotonically non-decreasing along any path, guaranteeing A* graph search optimality.

questions.question: Does consistency imply admissibility in heuristic search?

options.text: No, consistent heuristics are never admissible
Yes, every consistent heuristic is admissible (provided h(goal) = 0)

questions.explanation: Mathematical proof by induction on path length to goal.

questions.question: If h₁(n) and h₂(n) are both admissible heuristics, which combination is guaranteed to be admissible and DOMINATING?
questions.explanation: The maximum of two admissible heuristics never overestimates and expands fewer or equal nodes.

questions.question: In the 8-puzzle problem, which of the following is an admissible heuristic?

options.text: Number of misplaced tiles (and Manhattan distance)
Number of misplaced tiles multiplied by 10

questions.explanation: Both misplaced tiles and Manhattan distance never overestimate moves needed.

questions.question: The Manhattan distance heuristic for a tile at (x₁, y₁) and goal (x₂, y₂) is:
questions.explanation: Sum of horizontal and vertical distances.

questions.question: Which search algorithm uses O(1) memory and moves only in the direction of increasing value (steepest ascent)?
questions.explanation: Greedy local search moving to the highest-scoring neighbor.

questions.question: Hill-climbing search can get stuck on:
questions.explanation: Standard failure modes of local greedy search.

questions.question: Simulated Annealing avoids getting stuck in local maxima by:

options.text: Allowing occasional "downhill" moves with a probability that decreases over time (temperature schedule T)

questions.explanation: Analogy to physical metallurgical annealing; P = e^(ΔE / T).

questions.question: Genetic Algorithms solve optimization problems using operations inspired by natural evolution:
questions.explanation: Evolves a population of candidate chromosome solutions.

questions.question: In a genetic algorithm, the fitness function plays the role of:

options.text: Evaluating how good or suitable a candidate solution is (objective function to be maximized)

questions.explanation: Higher fitness implies higher probability of selection for reproduction.

questions.question: Beam search is a heuristic search algorithm that:

options.text: Retains all nodes in memory like BFS
Retains only the k best states (beam width) at each level, discarding all other candidate nodes

questions.explanation: Heuristic variant that limits memory by pruning to top k states.

questions.question: In game playing (adversarial search) for zero-sum, two-player games with perfect information, the standard algorithm is:
questions.explanation: MAX aims to maximize utility; MIN aims to minimize utility.

questions.question: What is the optimal strategy for the MAX player in a Minimax tree?

options.text: Choose the action that leads to the state with the MAXIMUM value among MIN's best responses
Assume MIN will make a mistake

questions.explanation: Minimax assumes optimal counter-play by the opponent.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of the Minimax algorithm for game tree with branching factor b and maximum depth m?
questions.explanation: Traverses the entire game tree down to terminal leaves.

questions.question: Alpha-Beta pruning improves the Minimax algorithm by:

options.text: Approximating the minimax value with random guesses
Changing the rules of the game
Pruning branches that cannot possibly influence the final decision, without altering the optimal outcome

questions.explanation: Computes the exact same minimax decision while skipping unneeded subtrees.

questions.question: In Alpha-Beta pruning, the parameter α (alpha) represents:

options.text: The best (highest) value that the MAX player can guarantee so far along the path
The depth of the search tree

questions.explanation: Alpha is the lower bound on score for MAX.

questions.question: In Alpha-Beta pruning, the parameter β (beta) represents:

options.text: The best (lowest) value that the MIN player can guarantee so far along the path

questions.explanation: Beta is the upper bound on score for MIN.

questions.question: A branch is PRUNED in Alpha-Beta pruning whenever:

options.text: α ≥ β (alpha is greater than or equal to beta)

questions.explanation: Condition α ≥ β indicates that this branch will never be selected by a rational opponent.

questions.question: With optimal move ordering (best moves evaluated first), Alpha-Beta pruning reduces time complexity to:

options.text: O(b^(m / 2)), effectively doubling the searchable depth in the same time

questions.explanation: Evaluates roughly the square root of the number of nodes.

questions.question: In games with large search spaces (like Chess), how is the Minimax algorithm adapted to run in real time?

options.text: By cutting off search at a fixed depth and evaluating non-terminal states with a Heuristic Evaluation Function
By evaluating all terminal states to the end of the game

questions.explanation: Evaluation function approximates the win probability from non-terminal states.

questions.question: A Constraint Satisfaction Problem (CSP) is defined by which three components?

options.text: Variables X, Domains D, and Constraints C

questions.explanation: Standard formal definition: X = variables, D = domains of values, C = constraint relations.

questions.question: The basic uninformed search algorithm used to solve CSPs is:

options.text: Backtracking Search (depth-first search that assigns one variable at a time)

questions.explanation: Assigns values incrementally and backtracks upon constraint violation.

questions.question: In CSPs, the Minimum Remaining Values (MRV) heuristic chooses the next variable to assign as the one with:

options.text: The most constraints on other variables
The fewest legal remaining values in its domain ("most constrained variable")

questions.explanation: Fails early if a variable has few options (fail-first principle).

questions.question: In CSPs, the Degree Heuristic is used as a tie-breaker for MRV by selecting the variable that:

options.text: Is involved in the largest number of constraints with other unassigned variables ("most constraining variable")

questions.explanation: Constrains future variables the most.

questions.question: In CSPs, the Least Constraining Value (LCV) heuristic orders values for an assigned variable by choosing the one that:

options.text: Rules out the fewest choices for neighboring unassigned variables

questions.explanation: Leaves maximum flexibility for remaining variables.

questions.question: Forward Checking in CSPs works by:

options.text: Checking future constraints after full assignment
Tracking remaining legal domain values for unassigned variables and terminating early if any variable's domain becomes empty

questions.explanation: Detects dead ends before descending into doomed subtrees.

questions.question: Arc Consistency algorithm AC-3 ensures that for every directed arc X_i → X_j:

options.text: X_i and X_j have only 1 value
For every value x in D_i, there exists at least one legal value y in D_j satisfying the constraint between X_i and X_j

questions.explanation: Prunes unsupported values from D_i.

questions.question: In Propositional Logic, a sentence is VALID (a tautology) if:

options.text: It is true in ALL possible models (interpretations)
It is true in at least one model
It is false in all models

questions.explanation: e.g. P ∨ ¬P is universally valid.

questions.question: In Propositional Logic, a sentence is SATISFIABLE if:

options.text: It is true in all models
It is true in AT LEAST ONE model (interpretation)

questions.explanation: A model exists where the sentence evaluates to true.

questions.question: In Propositional Logic, Modus Ponens states that from P and P → Q, we can infer:
questions.explanation: Classic inference rule: if P is true, and P implies Q, then Q is true.

questions.question: In Propositional Logic, Modus Tollens states that from ¬Q and P → Q, we can infer:
questions.explanation: If Q is false and P implies Q, P must be false.

questions.question: The Resolution Rule states that from clauses (A ∨ B) and (¬B ∨ C), we can infer:
questions.explanation: Complementary literals B and ¬B cancel out, yielding A ∨ C.

questions.question: Proof by Resolution refutes a sentence α from knowledge base KB by:

options.text: Generating truth tables of all variables
Adding ¬α to KB, converting to Conjunctive Normal Form (CNF), and resolving until the EMPTY CLAUSE (contradiction) is derived

questions.explanation: Proof by contradiction: KB ∧ ¬α |= False.

questions.question: Conjunctive Normal Form (CNF) represents a logical sentence as:

options.text: A conjunction (AND) of one or more clauses, where each clause is a disjunction (OR) of literals

questions.question: Horn clauses are logical clauses that contain at most:
questions.explanation: Enables linear-time inference using Forward Chaining and Backward Chaining.

questions.question: Forward Chaining inference in a rule-based system begins with:

options.text: Known facts and applies inference rules to extract new facts until the query goal is reached (data-driven)
The goal and searches backwards for supporting facts

questions.explanation: Data-driven bottom-up reasoning.

questions.question: Backward Chaining inference in a rule-based system begins with:

options.text: The goal/query and works backward searching for rules whose conclusions match the goal, verifying their premises (goal-driven)

questions.explanation: Goal-driven top-down reasoning (e.g. used by Prolog).

questions.question: First-Order Logic (FOL) extends Propositional Logic by introducing:

options.text: Objects, Predicates, Functions, and Quantifiers (Universal ∀ and Existential ∃)

questions.explanation: Expressive power for relationships and quantified assertions.

questions.question: The Universal Quantifier (∀x P(x)) asserts that:

options.text: P(x) is true for at least one object x
P(x) is false for all x
P(x) is true for ALL objects x in the domain of discourse

questions.explanation: ∀ represents "for all".

questions.question: The Existential Quantifier (∃x P(x)) asserts that:

options.text: P(x) is true for AT LEAST ONE object x in the domain of discourse
P(x) is true for all objects x

questions.explanation: ∃ represents "there exists".

questions.question: Negating a universally quantified statement ¬(∀x P(x)) is logically equivalent to:
questions.explanation: De Morgan's law for quantifiers: "Not all are P" = "There exists at least one that is not P".

questions.question: In First-Order Logic, the process of finding substitutions that make two different logical terms identical is called:
questions.explanation: UNIFY(p, q) = θ such that SUBST(θ, p) = SUBST(θ, q).

questions.question: Skolemization in First-Order Logic is used to eliminate:

options.text: Existential quantifiers (∃) by replacing variables with Skolem constants or Skolem functions

questions.explanation: Necessary step in converting FOL sentences to Clause Form for resolution.

questions.question: A Markov Decision Process (MDP) models sequential decision making under uncertainty using which components?

options.text: States S, Actions A, Transition probabilities P(s' | s, a), Rewards R(s, a, s'), and Discount factor γ
Initial state, Goal state, and Heuristic

questions.explanation: Standard formal definition of an MDP.

questions.question: The Bellman Equation for the optimal state value function V*(s) in an MDP is:

options.text: V*(s) = max_a Σ_{s'} P(s' | s, a) [ R(s, a, s') + γ V*(s') ]

questions.explanation: Fundamental recursive optimality equation for dynamic programming.

questions.question: The discount factor γ (where 0 ≤ γ < 1) in an MDP ensures that:

options.text: Future rewards are discounted compared to immediate rewards, guaranteeing convergence of infinite-horizon sums

questions.explanation: Mathematical convergence and preference for immediate utility.

questions.question: In Reinforcement Learning, Q-Learning is an algorithm that learns:

options.text: The transition probability table P(s'|s,a) first
The action-value function Q(s, a) directly without requiring a model of transition probabilities (model-free, off-policy)

questions.explanation: Model-free temporal difference control algorithm.

questions.question: The Exploration vs Exploitation dilemma in Reinforcement Learning refers to:

options.text: The trade-off between trying new actions to discover better rewards versus choosing the best known action to maximize reward

questions.explanation: Commonly addressed using ε-greedy action selection.

questions.question: An Expert System typically consists of two primary modules:

options.text: Knowledge Base (rules and facts) and Inference Engine (reasoning mechanism)

questions.explanation: Classic knowledge-based AI architecture.

questions.question: In fuzzy logic, a truth value:

options.text: Can range continuously between 0 and 1 (degrees of truth), rather than being strictly binary {0, 1}

questions.explanation: Models uncertainty and vague linguistic terms (e.g. "warm", "tall").

questions.question: A Bayesian Network (Belief Network) is a graphical model that represents:

options.text: A set of random variables and their conditional dependencies via a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)

questions.explanation: Compact probabilistic representation exploiting conditional independence.

questions.question: In a Bayesian Network, a variable X is conditionally independent of all its non-descendants given:
questions.explanation: Markov condition in Bayesian networks.

questions.question: Naïve Bayes classifier makes which strong assumption about feature variables given the class label?

options.text: All features are conditionally independent of each other given the class

questions.explanation: The "naïve" conditional independence assumption P(X|C) = Π P(x_i|C).

questions.question: Ontology in Knowledge Representation refers to:

options.text: A formal naming and definition of the types, properties, and interrelationships of entities in a domain of discourse

questions.explanation: Formal conceptualization of a domain for knowledge sharing.

questions.question: Frame representation in AI represents knowledge as:

options.text: Collections of attributes (slots) and associated values or default procedures (fillers)

questions.explanation: Marvin Minsky's frame theory.

questions.question: Semantic Networks represent knowledge using:

options.text: Nodes representing concepts/objects connected by labeled directed edges representing relationships (like "is-a", "has-a")

questions.explanation: Graph-based knowledge representation.

questions.question: The Frame Problem in classical AI logic refers to the challenge of:

options.text: Representing what remains UNCHANGED in the world when an action is taken, without listing endless non-effects

questions.explanation: Classical challenge in formalizing dynamic worlds in first-order logic.

questions.question: STRIPS is a classical planning language that represents actions using:

options.text: Preconditions, Add-list (effects added), and Delete-list (effects removed)

questions.explanation: Standard representation in automated planning.

questions.question: Case-Based Reasoning (CBR) solves new problems by:

options.text: Adapting solutions that were used to solve similar problems in the past (Retrieve, Reuse, Revise, Retain)

questions.explanation: Reasoning by analogy from a case library.

questions.question: In natural language processing, Tokenization is the process of:

options.text: Breaking a stream of text into individual words, phrases, or symbols (tokens)

questions.explanation: First fundamental preprocessing step in NLP.

questions.question: Stop words in natural language processing refer to:

options.text: Common words (e.g. "the", "is", "at") frequently filtered out because they carry little unique semantic meaning

questions.explanation: Removed to reduce dimensionality and focus on informative keywords.

questions.question: Stemming and Lemmatization in NLP are techniques used to:

options.text: Reduce words to their base or root forms (e.g. "running", "runs" -> "run")

questions.explanation: Normalizes morphological variants of words.

questions.question: Which search algorithm is guaranteed to be COMPLETE and OPTIMAL for any positive step costs?

options.text: Uniform-Cost Search (and A* with an admissible/consistent heuristic)

questions.explanation: UCS and A* guarantee minimum-cost path.

questions.question: In Supervised Learning, the training dataset consists of:

options.text: Input features paired with corresponding ground-truth output labels (targets)
A reward signal from the environment only

questions.explanation: Learning from labeled examples: (x, y).

questions.question: In Unsupervised Learning, the algorithm attempts to:

options.text: Discover hidden patterns, structures, or clusters in unlabeled data without explicit targets

questions.explanation: No labels y provided; examples include K-Means and PCA.

questions.question: A machine learning problem where the target variable y is a CONTINUOUS real value (e.g. predicting house prices) is:
questions.explanation: Continuous targets = Regression; Discrete categories = Classification.

questions.question: A machine learning problem where the target variable y is a DISCRETE category (e.g. spam vs non-spam) is:
questions.explanation: Discrete class assignment = Classification.

questions.question: In Simple Linear Regression y = θ₀ + θ₁ x, the standard cost (loss) function to minimize is:

options.text: Mean Squared Error (MSE): J(θ) = (1 / 2m) Σ (h_θ(x^(i)) - y^(i))²

questions.explanation: Ordinary Least Squares minimizes sum of squared residuals.

questions.question: Gradient Descent updates model parameters θ in the direction of:

options.text: The negative gradient of the cost function: θ = θ - α * ∇J(θ)

questions.explanation: Moves in direction of steepest descent to find a local minimum.

questions.question: In Gradient Descent, the parameter α (alpha) is called the:
questions.explanation: Controls how large a step is taken along the gradient.

questions.question: What happens if the learning rate α in Gradient Descent is set TOO LARGE?

options.text: The cost function may oscillate wildly, fail to converge, or diverge to infinity

questions.explanation: Overshoots the minimum and diverges.

questions.question: What happens if the learning rate α in Gradient Descent is set TOO SMALL?

options.text: The algorithm will take very tiny steps and convergence will be extremely slow

questions.explanation: Needs excessive iterations to reach minimum.

questions.question: Batch Gradient Descent computes the gradient using:

options.text: A single randomly chosen training example
The entire training dataset in every single update step

questions.explanation: Batch uses all m examples per step; stable but slow for massive data.

questions.question: Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) updates parameters using:

options.text: Exactly ONE training example chosen randomly per step

questions.explanation: Fast and noisy updates that can jump out of local minima.

questions.question: Mini-Batch Gradient Descent strikes a balance by updating parameters using:

options.text: A small random subset (mini-batch) of training examples (e.g. 32, 64, or 128) per step

questions.explanation: Standard practice in modern deep learning exploiting GPU vectorization.

questions.question: Feature Scaling (standardization or normalization) is important before gradient descent because:

options.text: It ensures the cost surface contours are spherical rather than elongated, allowing faster and smoother convergence
It increases the number of features
It eliminates the need for labels

questions.explanation: Normalized features prevent oscillation across wide axes.

questions.question: In Logistic Regression for binary classification, the Sigmoid (logistic) function maps any real number z to:
questions.explanation: S-shaped curve interpreting output as class probability P(y = 1 | x).

questions.question: The decision boundary in standard Logistic Regression is:
questions.explanation: Separates feature space into two halves with a hyperplane.

questions.question: The standard loss function used to train Logistic Regression is:
questions.explanation: Ensures a convex cost function without flat plateau local traps.

questions.question: Overfitting occurs when a machine learning model:

options.text: Learns the noise and specific details of the training data too well, failing to generalize to new unseen test data
Is too simple to capture the underlying trend (high bias)
Has zero training error and zero test error
Runs out of memory during training

questions.explanation: High variance: low training error but high test error.

questions.question: Underfitting occurs when a machine learning model:

options.text: Is too simple to capture the underlying pattern in the data, performing poorly on both training and test data

questions.explanation: High bias: poor performance on both train and test.

questions.question: The Bias-Variance Tradeoff states that:

options.text: Bias and variance are completely independent
High bias always means high variance
Increasing model complexity decreases bias but increases variance; optimal models balance both to minimize total error
Both bias and variance can be simultaneously reduced to 0 on noisy data

questions.explanation: Total Error = Bias² + Variance + Irreducible Error.

questions.question: Which technique is used to prevent overfitting by penalizing large parameter weights in the cost function?
questions.explanation: Shrinks weights toward zero to constrain model complexity.

questions.question: L2 Regularization (Ridge) adds which penalty term to the cost function?

options.text: λ Σ θ_j² (sum of squared weights)

questions.explanation: Shrinks coefficients smoothly toward zero without setting them exactly to zero.

questions.question: L1 Regularization (Lasso) differs from L2 because L1 penalty (λ Σ |θ_j|):

options.text: Can drive parameter weights exactly to ZERO, performing automatic feature selection
Causes the cost function to be non-convex

questions.explanation: L1 produces sparse models by zeroing out irrelevant features.

questions.question: K-Fold Cross-Validation evaluates model generalization by:

options.text: Training K different models on the test set
Testing only on the training set
Splitting data into K folds, training on K - 1 folds, and testing on the remaining fold, repeating K times
Running gradient descent K times on fold 1

questions.explanation: Ensures every data point is used for validation once, reducing evaluation variance.

questions.question: A Decision Tree splits nodes based on the feature that maximizes:

options.text: Information Gain (or reduction in Impurity such as Gini Impurity or Entropy)

questions.explanation: Greedy recursive splitting selects highest purity gain.

questions.question: Entropy H(S) in information theory measures:

options.text: The amount of uncertainty or impurity in a set of examples
The physical temperature of the CPU

questions.explanation: H(S) = -Σ p_i log₂(p_i). Equal distribution = maximum entropy.

questions.question: If a node in a decision tree contains examples belonging entirely to a SINGLE class (pure node), its Entropy is:
questions.explanation: -1 * log₂(1) = 0. No uncertainty remains.

questions.question: Gini Impurity for a node with class proportions p_i is calculated as:
questions.explanation: Alternative impurity measure used by CART decision trees.

questions.question: To prevent decision trees from growing too deep and overfitting the training data, one should apply:

options.text: Pruning (pre-pruning with max_depth, or post-pruning with cost-complexity)

questions.explanation: Limits tree complexity to improve generalization.

questions.question: In evaluation of classification models, a Confusion Matrix contains which four counts?

options.text: True Positives (TP), False Positives (FP), True Negatives (TN), and False Negatives (FN)

questions.explanation: Foundation of classification metrics.

questions.question: Accuracy is defined as:
questions.explanation: Overall fraction of correct predictions.

questions.question: Why is Accuracy an unreliable metric for highly IMBALANCED datasets (e.g. 99% negative, 1% positive)?

options.text: A trivial classifier predicting "negative" for everything achieves 99% accuracy while finding zero positives

questions.explanation: Accuracy paradox on skewed data.

questions.question: Precision is defined as the fraction of positive predictions that were actually correct:
questions.explanation: Precision measures quality of positive assertions.

questions.question: Recall (Sensitivity or True Positive Rate) is defined as:
questions.explanation: Fraction of actual positive cases successfully caught by the model.

questions.question: The F1-Score combines Precision and Recall into a single metric using their:
questions.explanation: Harmonic mean penalizes extreme imbalances between precision and recall.

questions.question: The Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve plots which metrics against each other at various thresholds?

options.text: True Positive Rate (Recall) vs False Positive Rate (FPR = 1 - Specificity)

questions.explanation: Evaluates trade-off between TPR and FPR across all decision thresholds.

questions.question: The Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC-ROC) of a perfect classifier is:
questions.explanation: AUC = 1.0 is perfect separation; AUC = 0.5 is no discriminative ability.

questions.question: Support Vector Machines (SVM) find the optimal decision hyperplane by:

options.text: Maximizing the margin (distance between the hyperplane and the closest data points / support vectors)
Fitting a polynomial through all points
Averaging the coordinates of all classes

questions.explanation: Maximum-margin classifier.

questions.question: In an SVM, what are the Support Vectors?

options.text: The critical data points closest to the decision hyperplane that define the boundary and margin
The weights of the neural network

questions.explanation: Removing non-support vectors does not change the decision boundary.

questions.question: The Kernel Trick in SVM allows the algorithm to:

options.text: Classify non-linearly separable data by mapping features implicitly into a higher-dimensional space without computing coordinates

questions.explanation: Computes inner products in high-dimensional feature space via kernel function K(x, z).

questions.question: Which of the following is a widely used SVM kernel function for infinite-dimensional feature mapping?

options.text: RBF (Radial Basis Function / Gaussian kernel): K(x, z) = exp(-γ ||x - z||²)

questions.explanation: Gaussian RBF kernel handles complex nonlinear boundaries.

questions.question: K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) is an instance-based (lazy learning) algorithm because it:

options.text: Stores the entire training dataset and defers computation until a query point needs classification
Learns explicit parameters θ during training

questions.explanation: No explicit training phase; computes distances to all training points at prediction time.

questions.question: In KNN classification, an odd value of k (e.g. k = 3 or 5) is typically chosen for binary problems to:
questions.explanation: Odd k eliminates 50-50 tie situations in 2-class voting.

questions.question: What happens to the decision boundary in KNN when k = 1?

options.text: It becomes a flat straight line
It becomes highly complex and sensitive to noise/outliers (high variance, overfitting)

questions.explanation: k = 1 fits training data with 100% accuracy but overfits heavily.

questions.question: As k increases toward the total number of training samples n in KNN, the decision boundary:

options.text: Becomes smoother and simpler, eventually predicting the majority class everywhere (high bias, underfitting)

questions.explanation: Large k averages over large neighborhoods.

questions.question: K-Means is an unsupervised clustering algorithm that partitions data into K clusters by:

options.text: Iteratively assigning points to the nearest centroid and updating centroids to the mean of assigned points

questions.explanation: Lloyd's algorithm: Assign -> Update -> Repeat until convergence.

questions.question: The objective function that K-Means minimizes is:

options.text: Inertia / Within-Cluster Sum of Squares (WCSS): Σ ||x - μ_k||²

questions.explanation: Sum of squared Euclidean distances to cluster centers.

questions.question: The "Elbow Method" in K-Means is used to:

options.text: Estimate the optimal number of clusters K by plotting WCSS vs K and finding the point of diminishing returns (the elbow)

questions.explanation: Identifies the inflection point where additional clusters yield diminishing improvement.

questions.question: Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is an unsupervised technique used for:

options.text: Dimensionality reduction by finding orthogonal axes (principal components) that maximize variance

questions.explanation: Projects high-dimensional data onto eigenvectors of covariance matrix.

questions.question: In PCA, the First Principal Component (PC1) accounts for:

options.text: The largest possible variance in the dataset

questions.explanation: Direction along which data varies the most.

questions.question: All principal components in PCA are mutually:
questions.explanation: Eigenvectors of the symmetric covariance matrix are mutually orthogonal.

questions.question: What is the Artificial Neuron (Perceptron) model developed by Rosenblatt?

options.text: Computes a weighted sum of inputs plus bias, followed by a step activation function: y = f(w^T x + b)

questions.explanation: Earliest mathematical model of an artificial neural network unit.

questions.question: The single-layer Perceptron can solve only problems that are:

options.text: Linearly separable (e.g. AND, OR gates; it cannot solve XOR)

questions.explanation: Minsky & Papert (1969) proved perceptron cannot solve non-linear XOR problem.

questions.question: How do Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs / Deep Neural Networks) solve non-linearly separable problems like XOR?

options.text: By using one or more hidden layers with NON-LINEAR activation functions
By using only linear activation functions in multiple layers

questions.explanation: Non-linear activations allow composing complex curved decision boundaries.

questions.question: Why is non-linearity essential in hidden layer activation functions?

options.text: Without non-linear activations, any multi-layer network collapses mathematically into an equivalent single linear model

questions.explanation: A composition of linear functions is strictly linear: W₂(W₁x) = (W₂W₁)x.

questions.question: Which activation function is most widely used in modern hidden layers due to mitigating the vanishing gradient problem?

options.text: ReLU (Rectified Linear Unit): f(z) = max(0, z)

questions.explanation: Gradient is 1 for positive inputs, enabling training of very deep networks.

questions.question: What is the "Dying ReLU" problem?

options.text: When a neuron's inputs are permanently negative, its output and gradient stay 0, and the neuron never updates (dies)

questions.explanation: Mitigated by Leaky ReLU (f(z) = max(0.01z, z)) or ELU.

questions.question: Which activation function is used in the output layer of a multi-class neural network classifier (K > 2 classes)?

options.text: Softmax: converts raw logits into a normalized probability distribution summing to 1

questions.explanation: Softmax(z_i) = e^(z_i) / Σ e^(z_j) generates valid probability outputs.

questions.question: The Backpropagation algorithm trains neural networks by computing gradients using:

options.text: The Chain Rule of calculus, propagating error derivatives backwards from output layer to input layer

questions.explanation: Efficient application of the chain rule to compute ∂Loss/∂w.

questions.question: The Vanishing Gradient problem during backpropagation in deep networks using Sigmoid or tanh activations occurs because:

options.text: The learning rate is too large
Derivatives of Sigmoid are < 0.25; multiplying many small fractions across layers causes gradients in early layers to vanish toward 0

questions.explanation: Early layers learn extremely slowly or stall completely.

questions.question: What is Dropout in neural networks?

options.text: A regularization technique that randomly deactivates (zeros out) a fraction p of neurons during training at each step

questions.explanation: Forces network to learn redundant robust features and prevents co-adaptation.

questions.question: What is Early Stopping in training machine learning models?

options.text: Halting training when validation loss stops improving and begins to increase, preventing overfitting
Stopping when the computer gets warm

questions.explanation: Captures model weights at peak validation performance.

questions.question: Ensemble Learning improves predictive performance by:

options.text: Using a single very large decision tree
Combining the predictions of multiple individual base models (learners)

questions.explanation: Aggregating models reduces variance and/or bias.

questions.question: Bagging (Bootstrap Aggregating) builds an ensemble by:

options.text: Training models sequentially where each corrects previous errors
Training multiple independent base models on different bootstrap samples (sampling with replacement) and averaging/voting results
Combining linear models with SVMs only

questions.explanation: Primary goal is variance reduction.

questions.question: Random Forest is an ensemble method that combines Bagging with:

options.text: Random feature subset selection at each node split of the decision trees

questions.explanation: De-correlates trees, leading to lower ensemble variance than plain bagging.

questions.question: Boosting (e.g. AdaBoost, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost) differs from Bagging because Boosting:

options.text: Trains models SEQUENTIALLY, with each new model focusing on correcting the mistakes (errors) of the previous models

questions.explanation: Primarily reduces bias by iterative weighted focus on hard examples.

questions.question: In AdaBoost (Adaptive Boosting), training examples that are MISCLASSIFIED by the current learner:

options.text: Have their sample weights INCREASED so the next learner focuses on them

questions.explanation: Next weak learner concentrates on the harder instances.

questions.question: Gradient Boosting algorithms (GBM, XGBoost, LightGBM) fit each new base tree to:

options.text: The original target labels y directly
The pseudo-residuals (negative gradient of the loss function) of the current ensemble

questions.explanation: Performs gradient descent in function space.

questions.question: A Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) is specifically designed for processing data with grid topology (e.g. images) using:

questions.question: A Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) is designed for sequential/time-series data by:

questions.question: The Transformer architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017) revolutionized NLP by replacing recurrence with:

The total training time in seconds

A cell column is too narrow to display the number

questions.question: What is a Computer Network?

options.text: A single computer with multiple monitors
Two or more interconnected computing devices sharing resources and information

The MAC address of the motherboard

questions.question: What does URL stand for in web navigation?
questions.explanation: Standard web address specification.

options.text: The protocol used (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure, encrypted via SSL/TLS)

questions.explanation: Secure encrypted web communication protocol.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between HTTP and HTTPS?

options.text: HTTP uses images while HTTPS uses text only
HTTPS encrypts data during transmission using SSL/TLS, preventing eavesdropping and tampering

options.text: A small text file saved on the user's computer by a website to remember session information, preferences, and login status

questions.question: What is Computer Malware?

options.text: Spreads across networks independently without human intervention (Worm)
Attaches itself to a legitimate program/file and replicates by infecting other files when executed

questions.explanation: Requires a host file and user execution to spread.

options.text: Can self-replicate and spread automatically across computer networks without human action or host files

questions.explanation: Standalone self-propagating malware.

questions.question: A Trojan Horse in computing is:

options.text: Malicious software disguised as useful or legitimate software to trick users into installing it

questions.explanation: Appears benevolent while carrying hidden malicious payload.

questions.question: Ransomware is malware that:

options.text: Encrypts the victim's personal files and demands payment (ransom) in exchange for the decryption key

questions.explanation: Extortion malware using strong cryptography.

questions.question: Phishing is a cyber attack technique that involves:

options.text: Sending fraudulent emails or messages masquerading as trustworthy entities to trick victims into revealing sensitive passwords or credit card numbers

questions.explanation: Social engineering deception.

questions.question: What is a Firewall in computer security?

options.text: A network security system that monitors and filters incoming and outgoing traffic based on predetermined security rules
Antivirus software that cleans infected files
A physical wall preventing fires in data centers

questions.explanation: Barrier controlling network traffic.

questions.explanation: High entropy resists brute-force and dictionary attacks.

questions.question: Two-Factor Authentication (2FA) enhances security by requiring:

options.text: Two passwords from the same person
Two different forms of identification (e.g. something you know like a password, and something you have like a phone SMS/code)
Logging in on two computers simultaneously

questions.question: Cloud Computing refers to:

options.text: Running programs on local USB flash drives
The on-demand delivery of computing services (servers, storage, databases, networking, software) over the Internet

options.text: Local C: Drive on your laptop

options.text: Hiding recipient email addresses from everyone else (BCC)
Sending a copy of the email to recipients who need to be kept informed, where all recipients can see who was CC'd
Deleting the email automatically after reading

options.text: Marking the email as high priority
Sending copies of the email to recipients whose addresses are HIDDEN from all other recipients

questions.explanation: Protects recipient privacy.

questions.question: In Windows, what is the Recycle Bin used for?

options.text: Temporarily holding deleted files, allowing them to be restored or permanently removed

questions.explanation: Temporary recovery storage for deleted files.

questions.question: Which shortcut permanently deletes a selected file in Windows WITHOUT sending it to the Recycle Bin?
questions.explanation: Bypasses Recycle Bin for immediate deletion.

questions.question: A Denial of Service (DoS) attack aims to:

options.text: Overwhelm a server or network with excessive fake traffic so legitimate users cannot access it

questions.explanation: Exhausts target bandwidth or system resources.

questions.question: A Botnet in cybersecurity is:

options.text: A collection of chatbots on websites
A network of private computers infected with malware and controlled as a group by an attacker without the owners' knowledge

questions.explanation: Used to launch DDoS attacks or send mass spam.

questions.question: What does the term "Spam" refer to in electronic messaging?

options.text: Unsolicited, unwanted commercial or bulk messages sent via email or messaging platforms

questions.explanation: Junk bulk communications.

questions.question: What is Cache memory inside the web browser used for?

options.text: Storing temporary copies of images, scripts, and web pages locally to speed up subsequent visits to the same site

questions.explanation: Consolidates scattered file fragments.

questions.question: In Windows, which tool provides real-time information about running processes, CPU usage, RAM consumption, and startup programs?

questions.question: Which device connects different computer networks together and routes data packets between them based on IP addresses?
questions.explanation: Routers direct packets across network boundaries.

questions.explanation: WEP is completely obsolete and broken; WPA3 is the modern secure standard.

questions.question: Ohm's Law states the relationship between voltage V, current I, and resistance R as:

questions.question: Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL) states that at any node in an electrical circuit:

options.text: The sum of voltages equals zero
The algebraic sum of currents entering the node equals the sum of currents leaving (Σ I = 0)

questions.explanation: Based on conservation of electric charge.

questions.question: Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL) states that around any closed loop in an electrical circuit:

options.text: The sum of all currents is zero
The algebraic sum of all voltages is zero (Σ V = 0)

questions.explanation: Based on conservation of electrical energy.

questions.question: Two resistors R₁ = 4 Ω and R₂ = 6 Ω connected in SERIES have an equivalent resistance of:

questions.question: The current divider rule states that the current I₁ through resistor R₁ in a two-branch parallel circuit with total current I_s is:

questions.question: Nodal Analysis is fundamentally based on the systematic application of:

options.text: Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL) and Ohm's Law at non-reference nodes

questions.question: If a circuit has N nodes, how many independent KCL nodal equations are needed to solve the circuit?
questions.explanation: One node is chosen as the reference (ground, 0 V), leaving N - 1 unknowns.

options.text: A current source is in parallel with a resistor
A voltage source (dependent or independent) is connected between two non-reference nodes

questions.explanation: Encloses the voltage source and both nodes, applying KCL to the combined surface.

questions.question: Mesh Analysis is applicable only to circuits that are:

options.text: Planar (can be drawn on a plane with no crossing branches)

questions.explanation: Meshes are defined as loops that enclose no other loops in planar graphs.

questions.question: Mesh Analysis is fundamentally based on the systematic application of:

options.text: Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL) around each independent mesh

questions.explanation: Writes KVL in terms of circulating mesh currents.

questions.question: In mesh analysis, a Supermesh is created when:

options.text: A voltage source is in series with a resistor
A current source is shared between two adjacent meshes

questions.explanation: Avoids unknown voltage across current source by bypassing the shared branch.

questions.question: The Superposition Theorem states that in any linear bilateral circuit containing multiple independent sources:

options.text: Dependent sources are deactivated one by one
The response (voltage or current) is the algebraic sum of the responses caused by each independent source acting alone

questions.explanation: Core principle of linearity; deactivates other independent sources.

questions.question: When deactivating an independent VOLTAGE source to apply superposition, it is replaced by:

options.text: A short circuit (0 V, a zero-resistance wire)

questions.explanation: Zero voltage drop across a short circuit.

questions.question: When deactivating an independent CURRENT source to apply superposition, it is replaced by:

options.text: An open circuit (0 A, broken wire)

questions.explanation: Zero current flows through an open circuit.

questions.question: Can dependent sources be deactivated (turned off) during superposition analysis?

options.text: Yes, always treated like independent sources
No, dependent sources must remain active because their values are controlled by circuit variables

questions.explanation: Dependent sources reflect internal circuit constraints.

questions.question: Source Transformation allows replacing a practical voltage source (V_s in series with R_s) by an equivalent:

options.text: Current source in series with R_s
Voltage source in parallel with R_s
Practical current source (I_s = V_s / R_s in PARALLEL with R_s)

questions.question: Thevenin's Theorem states that any linear two-terminal circuit can be replaced by an equivalent circuit consisting of:

options.text: A current source I_n in parallel with R_n
A resistor in parallel with a capacitor
An independent voltage source V_th in SERIES with a resistor R_th

questions.question: The Thevenin voltage V_th is defined as:

options.text: The open-circuit voltage across the designated load terminals (V_oc)
The source voltage inside the circuit

questions.explanation: V_th = V_open-circuit.

options.text: A voltage source in series with R_th
An independent current source I_n in PARALLEL with a resistor R_n

questions.explanation: Norton equivalent circuit.

questions.question: The Norton current I_n is defined as:

options.text: The short-circuit current flowing between the load terminals (I_sc)

questions.explanation: I_n = I_short-circuit.

questions.question: The relationship between Thevenin and Norton equivalents for the same linear circuit is:

questions.question: To find Thevenin resistance R_th for a circuit containing ONLY independent sources:

options.text: Deactivate all independent sources (turn voltage sources into short circuits, current sources into open circuits) and calculate equivalent resistance looking into the terminals
Connect a short circuit and measure voltage

questions.explanation: Direct look-back resistance with independent sources turned off.

questions.question: To find Thevenin resistance R_th for a circuit containing DEPENDENT sources:

options.text: Apply an external test source (v_test = 1 V or i_test = 1 A) at the terminals with independent sources killed, and compute R_th = v_test / i_test

questions.explanation: Test source method captures dependent source contributions.

options.text: R_L = R_th (load resistance equals Thevenin resistance of the network)

questions.question: The maximum power transferred to load R_L = R_th from a Thevenin network (V_th, R_th) is:
