questions.question: The voltage-current relationship for an ideal capacitor of capacitance C is:

questions.question: Can the voltage across an ideal capacitor change instantaneously (in zero time)?

options.text: The depletion region widens, barrier height increases, and only a tiny reverse saturation current I_s flows

questions.explanation: Applied field widens depletion layer and blocks majority carriers.

questions.question: The Shockley ideal diode equation is given by:
questions.explanation: Fundamental exponential I-V characteristic of p-n diodes.

questions.question: The thermal voltage V_T at room temperature (T = 300 K) is approximately:
questions.explanation: k = Boltzmann constant, q = electron charge; kT/q ≈ 25.9 mV.

questions.question: The dynamic (AC) resistance r_d of a forward-biased diode carrying DC current I_D is:

options.text: r_d = n V_T / I_D ≈ 26 mV / I_D

questions.explanation: r_d = dV_D/dI_D = nV_T/I_D.

questions.question: A Zener Diode is specifically designed to operate in which region of its I-V curve?

options.text: The reverse breakdown region, providing a stable constant voltage (Zener voltage V_Z)

questions.explanation: Heavy doping enables sharp, reversible reverse breakdown used for voltage regulation.

questions.question: Zener breakdown occurs predominantly in:

options.text: Lightly doped diodes at high voltages (Avalanche breakdown)
Heavily doped diodes with narrow depletion regions at low reverse voltages (< 5 V) via quantum mechanical tunneling

questions.explanation: High internal electric field causes direct band-to-band tunneling.

questions.question: Avalanche breakdown occurs predominantly in:

options.text: Lightly doped junctions with wide depletion regions at higher voltages (> 6 V) via impact ionization

questions.explanation: Thermally generated carriers accelerate and knock out secondary electron-hole pairs.

questions.question: A Half-Wave Rectifier with peak input voltage V_m and ideal diode produces an average (DC) output voltage of:
questions.explanation: (1/2π) ∫₀^π V_m sin θ dθ = V_m / π.

questions.question: A Full-Wave Rectifier (bridge or center-tapped) produces an average (DC) output voltage of:
questions.explanation: Rectifies both halves of the AC waveform: 2V_m / π.

questions.question: The output ripple frequency of a Full-Wave Rectifier with 50 Hz AC input is:
questions.explanation: Both positive and negative half-cycles produce pulses: f_ripple = 2 f_in.

questions.question: In a Bridge Full-Wave Rectifier using practical Silicon diodes (V_D = 0.7 V each), the peak output voltage is:
questions.explanation: Two diodes conduct in series during each half cycle.

questions.question: The Peak Inverse Voltage (PIV) rating of the diodes in a Full-Wave Bridge Rectifier is:
questions.explanation: Bridge rectifier diodes only need to withstand V_m, half of center-tapped (2V_m).

questions.question: A Clipper (Limiter) circuit is designed to:

options.text: Clip off (remove) portions of an input waveform above or below specified voltage reference levels without distorting the remainder
Shift the DC level of the entire waveform

questions.explanation: Uses diodes and reference voltages to truncate waveform peaks.

questions.question: A Clamper (DC Restorer) circuit is designed to:

options.text: Clip off peaks of the waveform
Shift the entire AC waveform to a different DC level by adding a DC component using a capacitor and diode

questions.explanation: Clamps peak of waveform to reference without changing peak-to-peak amplitude.

questions.question: A Bipolar Junction Transistor (BJT) consists of which three doped regions?
questions.explanation: Three terminals of a BJT.

questions.question: In a BJT, which region is the MOST HEAVILY DOPED to maximize charge carrier injection?
questions.explanation: Emitter is heavily doped to inject large carrier currents into base.

questions.question: In a BJT, the Base region is designed to be:

options.text: Extremely thin and lightly doped, so that most injected carriers pass through to the collector without recombining

questions.explanation: Minimizes recombination to keep base current small (I_B << I_C).

questions.question: For an NPN BJT to operate in the ACTIVE (linear amplification) region, its junctions must be biased as:

options.text: Base-Emitter junction: FORWARD BIASED; Base-Collector junction: REVERSE BIASED
B-E reverse biased, B-C forward biased (Reverse active)

questions.explanation: Standard forward-active biasing for linear amplification.

questions.question: When a BJT operates in the SATURATION region (both B-E and B-C junctions forward biased):

options.text: The transistor behaves as a closed switch with V_CE,sat ≈ 0.2 V

questions.explanation: Collector-emitter voltage drops to saturation value V_CE,sat ≈ 0.2 V.

questions.question: When a BJT operates in the CUTOFF region (both junctions reverse biased):

options.text: The transistor behaves as an open switch with I_C ≈ 0 and V_CE ≈ V_CC

questions.explanation: Zero base current cuts off collector current.

questions.question: The relationship between terminal currents in any BJT is:
questions.explanation: KCL applied to the transistor body.

questions.question: The common-emitter DC current gain β (or h_FE) is defined as:
questions.explanation: Current gain from base to collector.

questions.question: The common-base DC current gain α is defined as:
questions.explanation: Fraction of emitter current reaching collector (typically 0.98 to 0.998).

questions.question: The mathematical relationship between α and β is:

options.text: β = α / (1 - α), and α = β / (β + 1)

questions.explanation: Derived from I_E = I_B + I_C and I_C = β I_B.

questions.question: The Early Effect (base-width modulation) in a BJT causes:

options.text: Collector current I_C to increase slightly with increasing V_CE in the active region, due to narrowing of the effective base width

questions.explanation: Reverse-biased collector junction widens into the base, reducing base width.

questions.question: The Early Voltage V_A is extrapolated on the I_C - V_CE characteristics as:

options.text: The negative voltage intercept on the V_CE axis where all active region curves converge

questions.explanation: Output resistance r_o = (V_A + V_CE) / I_C ≈ V_A / I_C.

questions.question: In BJT DC biasing, the Voltage Divider Bias configuration is popular because:

options.text: It has the highest input impedance
Its Q-point (I_C, V_CE) is virtually independent of variations in transistor β

questions.explanation: Provides superior thermal and manufacturing stability.

questions.question: The DC load line of a common-emitter amplifier circuit plots I_C versus V_CE. Its intercepts are:

options.text: Y-intercept: I_C,sat = V_CC / (R_C + R_E); X-intercept: V_CE,cutoff = V_CC

questions.explanation: KVL around output loop: V_CC = V_CE + I_C(R_C + R_E).

questions.question: The Q-point (Quiescent operating point) of an amplifier is:

options.text: The DC voltage and current values (V_CEQ, I_CQ) when no AC input signal is applied

questions.explanation: Operating DC bias point on the load line.

questions.question: For maximum undistorted symmetrical output voltage swing in a Common-Emitter amplifier, the Q-point should be placed:

options.text: Near the middle of the AC load line

questions.explanation: Allows equal positive and negative signal swings without clipping.

questions.question: Thermal runaway in a BJT occurs when:

options.text: Increased temperature raises I_C, which increases internal power dissipation, further raising temperature destructively

questions.explanation: Positive feedback loop between temperature and leakage/collector current.

questions.question: Adding an emitter resistor R_E to a common-emitter amplifier circuit provides:

options.text: Negative feedback that stabilizes the Q-point against temperature and β changes

questions.explanation: Degenerative feedback stabilizes DC bias.

questions.question: In small-signal BJT modeling, the transconductance g_m is calculated from DC collector current I_C as:
questions.explanation: g_m = dI_C/dv_BE = I_C/V_T.

questions.question: In the small-signal hybrid-π model, the base-emitter dynamic resistance r_π is:

options.text: r_π = β / g_m = β * V_T / I_C

questions.explanation: Input resistance looking into base terminal.

questions.question: In the small-signal T-model, the dynamic emitter resistance r_e is:
questions.explanation: Resistance looking into the emitter terminal.

questions.question: The Common-Emitter (CE) amplifier configuration is characterized by:

options.text: Unity voltage gain and zero phase shift
Low input impedance and unity current gain
High voltage gain, high current gain, and a 180° phase inversion between input and output

questions.explanation: Most popular BJT amplifier configuration.

questions.question: The Common-Collector (CC / Emitter Follower) amplifier configuration is characterized by:

options.text: Voltage gain ≈ 1 (unity), high input impedance, low output impedance, and 0° phase shift
Very high voltage gain and 180° phase shift

questions.explanation: Used primarily as a buffer and impedance-matching stage.

questions.question: The Common-Base (CB) amplifier configuration is characterized by:

options.text: High current gain and low voltage gain
Unity current gain (A_i ≈ 1), high voltage gain, low input impedance, and high output impedance

questions.explanation: Used in high-frequency RF applications due to minimal Miller effect.

questions.question: In a Common-Emitter amplifier, placing a bypass capacitor C_E in parallel with R_E:

options.text: Increases AC voltage gain by shorting R_E for AC signals while maintaining DC bias stability

questions.explanation: R_E is active for DC stability but bypassed for AC gain.

questions.question: The small-signal voltage gain A_v of a loaded CE amplifier with unbypassed emitter resistor R_E is approximately:
questions.explanation: Emitter degeneration reduces gain by factor 1 + g_m R_E.

questions.question: What is the role of coupling capacitors (C_in and C_out) in an amplifier circuit?

options.text: Block DC bias voltages while passing AC signals between stages without disturbing Q-points
Act as short circuits for DC

questions.explanation: Isolates DC bias levels of adjacent stages.

questions.question: A Darlington pair consists of two BJTs connected such that:

options.text: Both collectors are tied to ground
The emitter of the first transistor drives the base of the second, resulting in total current gain β_total ≈ β₁ * β₂
Total current gain is β₁ + β₂

questions.explanation: Super-high current gain and high input impedance.

questions.question: A photodiode operates in which biasing condition to detect light?

options.text: Reverse bias, where incident light generates electron-hole pairs that increase reverse current proportionally to light intensity

questions.explanation: Reverse photocurrent is linear with optical power.

questions.question: A Light Emitting Diode (LED) emits light when:

options.text: Forward biased, as electrons and holes recombine across the bandgap, releasing energy as photons

questions.explanation: Electroluminescence in direct bandgap semiconductors (like GaAs, GaN).

questions.question: Field-Effect Transistors (FETs) differ fundamentally from BJTs because FETs are:

options.text: Voltage-controlled, unipolar devices (current carried by majority carriers only)

questions.explanation: Gate voltage controls channel conduction; uses majority carriers only.

questions.question: The three terminals of a Field-Effect Transistor (FET) are:
questions.explanation: Standard FET terminal nomenclature.

questions.question: The gate input impedance of a MOSFET is extremely high (typically > 10¹² Ω) because:

options.text: The gate is reverse biased like a diode
The gate electrode is electrically insulated from the channel by a thin layer of Silicon Dioxide (SiO₂)

questions.explanation: Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor insulation blocks DC gate current (I_G = 0).

questions.question: An Enhancement-mode N-channel MOSFET (NMOS) is normally:

options.text: OFF when V_GS = 0 V, requiring a positive gate voltage V_GS > V_th to create an inversion channel and conduct

questions.explanation: Enhancement mode devices are normally-off.

questions.question: A Depletion-mode MOSFET is normally:

options.text: ON when V_GS = 0 V (a physical channel is built-in during fabrication), turned off by applying negative V_GS

questions.explanation: Depletion mode devices conduct with zero gate bias.

questions.question: In an N-channel Enhancement MOSFET, the Threshold Voltage V_th (or V_GS(th)) is:

options.text: The minimum gate-to-source voltage required to induce the conducting channel (inversion layer)

questions.explanation: Channel forms when V_GS exceeds V_th.

questions.question: In the saturation (active) region of an NMOS, the drain current equation is:

options.text: I_D = (1/2) k_n' (W / L) (V_GS - V_th)² = (1/2) k_n (V_GS - V_th)²

questions.explanation: Square-law relationship in saturation.

questions.question: A MOSFET operates in the SATURATION (pinch-off) region when:

options.text: V_GS > V_th and V_DS ≥ V_GS - V_th (V_DS ≥ V_ov)

questions.explanation: Channel is pinched off at the drain end; current saturates.

questions.question: A MOSFET operates in the TRIODE (linear / ohmic) region when:

options.text: V_GS > V_th and V_DS < V_GS - V_th

questions.explanation: Channel is continuous from source to drain, behaving like a voltage-controlled resistor.

questions.question: In the triode region with very small V_DS, a MOSFET behaves as a:

options.text: Voltage-Controlled Resistor (VCR) whose resistance is tuned by V_GS

questions.explanation: Channel resistance r_DS = 1 / [k_n (V_GS - V_th)].

questions.question: Channel-Length Modulation in a MOSFET (analogous to the Early Effect in BJTs) is modeled by parameter λ, modifying I_D in saturation to:
questions.explanation: Finite output resistance r_o = 1 / (λ I_D).

questions.question: In a Junction Field-Effect Transistor (JFET), the gate-to-source junction must ALWAYS be:

options.text: Reverse biased (e.g. V_GS ≤ 0 for N-channel JFET)

questions.explanation: Forward biasing the gate would cause junction diode conduction, destroying FET operation.

questions.question: Shockley's equation for an N-channel JFET in saturation is:
questions.explanation: I_DSS is saturation current at V_GS = 0; V_P is pinch-off voltage.

questions.question: CMOS (Complementary MOS) technology uses pairs of:

options.text: NMOS and PMOS transistors working complementarily on the same substrate

questions.explanation: Basis of virtually all modern microprocessors and digital ICs.

questions.question: The primary advantage of CMOS digital logic circuits is:

options.text: Near-zero static power dissipation (power is consumed only during dynamic switching)

questions.explanation: One transistor is always off in any static state, blocking DC current paths.

questions.question: In a basic CMOS inverter, when the input is HIGH (Logic 1):

options.text: The PMOS is ON, and NMOS is OFF
The NMOS is ON (pulling output to GND), and PMOS is OFF

questions.explanation: Output is pulled to 0 V.

questions.question: In a basic CMOS inverter, when the input is LOW (Logic 0):

options.text: The PMOS is ON (pulling output to V_DD), and NMOS is OFF

questions.explanation: Output is pulled up to V_DD.

questions.question: The LOW-FREQUENCY roll-off in the frequency response of an audio amplifier is caused by:

options.text: Coupling capacitors (C_in, C_out) and bypass capacitors (C_E / C_S)

questions.explanation: Capacitive reactances 1/(ωC) become large at low frequencies.

questions.question: The HIGH-FREQUENCY roll-off in the frequency response of an amplifier is caused by:

options.text: Internal transistor parasitic junction capacitances (C_be, C_bc in BJT; C_gs, C_gd in FET) and wiring stray capacitances

questions.explanation: Small parasitic capacitances shunt high-frequency signals to ground.

questions.question: The Miller Effect states that an impedance Z connected between input and inverting output of an amplifier with gain -A_v is equivalent at the input to:

options.text: An effective input impedance Z_in = Z / (1 + A_v) (magnifying capacitance: C_M = C * (1 + A_v))

questions.explanation: Miller theorem: bridge feedback capacitance appears magnified at the input by (1 + |A_v|).

questions.question: The Miller Effect severely degrades the high-frequency response of which amplifier configuration?
questions.explanation: Large inverting gain multiplies C_bc, lowering input cutoff frequency.

questions.question: Why is the Common-Base (or Cascode) amplifier preferred for high-frequency RF amplification?

options.text: It has the highest input impedance
It eliminates the Miller effect because the base is AC grounded, isolating input from output

questions.explanation: No inverting feedback capacitance between input and output.

questions.question: A Cascode amplifier configuration consists of:

options.text: A Common-Emitter stage driving a Common-Base stage (or CS driving CG in MOS)

questions.explanation: Combines high input impedance of CE with high bandwidth and output impedance of CB.

questions.question: In a multistage amplifier, the overall voltage gain A_v,total in decibels (dB) is:

options.text: The product of gains in dB
The SUM of the individual stage gains in dB: A_v,total(dB) = A_v1(dB) + A_v2(dB) + ...

questions.explanation: Logarithmic dB gains add: 20 log(A₁ A₂) = 20 log A₁ + 20 log A₂.

questions.question: As more identical amplifier stages are cascaded together, the overall bandwidth:

options.text: DECREASES (narrower bandwidth than an individual stage)

questions.explanation: Shrinkage factor: BW_total = BW_single * √(2^(1/n) - 1).

questions.question: A BJT Differential Amplifier pair with tail current source I_EE has a differential voltage gain A_d equal to:
questions.explanation: Standard differential gain with balanced collector loads.

questions.question: The Common-Mode Gain A_cm of an ideal differential amplifier is:
questions.explanation: Ideally rejects all common-mode noise.

questions.question: Negative feedback applied to an electronic amplifier:

options.text: Reduces gain, increases bandwidth, stabilizes gain against component variations, and reduces distortion

questions.explanation: Classic Black feedback theorem: G_closed = A / (1 + A β).

questions.question: The four basic negative feedback topologies are:
questions.explanation: Classified by output sampling (voltage or current) and input mixing (series or shunt).

questions.question: Voltage-Series negative feedback (e.g. non-inverting op-amp):

options.text: Decreases input impedance and increases output impedance
INCREASES input impedance and DECREASES output impedance

questions.explanation: Ideal for voltage amplifiers.

questions.question: Current-Shunt negative feedback:

options.text: DECREASES input impedance and INCREASES output impedance

questions.explanation: Ideal for current amplifiers.

questions.question: The Barkhausen Criterion for sustained sinusoidal oscillation requires:

options.text: Loop gain |A β| = 1 and net loop phase shift around the feedback loop = 0° (or 360°)

questions.explanation: Two necessary conditions for sustained oscillation.

questions.question: A Wien-Bridge oscillator uses an RC bridge network and an op-amp to generate stable sine waves at frequency:
questions.explanation: At resonance, bridge attenuation is 1/3 and phase shift is 0°; op-amp needs gain of 3.

questions.question: In a Wien-Bridge oscillator, what amplifier gain A_v is required to sustain oscillations?
questions.explanation: Compensates for the 1/3 attenuation of the RC network.

questions.question: An RC Phase-Shift oscillator using a single inverting BJT amplifier requires a 3-section RC ladder network where each RC section provides:

options.text: 60° phase shift (total 180° to complement the 180° inversion of the amplifier)

questions.explanation: 3 * 60° = 180°; combined with amplifier 180° yields total 360° = 0°.

questions.question: The minimum amplifier gain required to sustain oscillations in an RC Phase-Shift oscillator with 3 identical RC sections is:
questions.explanation: Mathematical analysis of 3-mesh RC ladder shows attenuation is 1/29 at 180° phase shift.

questions.question: A Colpitts oscillator is an LC oscillator that uses a feedback network consisting of:

options.text: Two capacitors and one inductor (tapped capacitive divider)

questions.explanation: Colpitts uses capacitive divider; Hartley uses tapped inductor.

questions.question: A Hartley oscillator is an LC oscillator that uses a feedback network consisting of:

options.text: Two inductors (or a center-tapped inductor) and one capacitor

questions.explanation: Hartley uses tapped inductor.

questions.question: A Crystal Oscillator (e.g. Quartz crystal) provides superior frequency stability compared to LC or RC oscillators because:

options.text: Quartz has an extremely high Quality Factor (Q > 10,000 to 100,000) based on the piezoelectric effect

questions.explanation: Piezoelectric resonance provides ultra-stable frequency standards for clocks.

questions.question: In power amplifier classification, a Class A amplifier conducts for:

options.text: The entire 360° of the input AC cycle (conduction angle θ = 360°)

questions.explanation: Q-point is centered; zero crossover distortion, but poor efficiency.

questions.question: The maximum theoretical power conversion efficiency of a transformer-coupled Class A amplifier is:
questions.explanation: Resistive load max 25%; transformer-coupled max 50%.

questions.question: A Class B amplifier conducts for:

options.text: Exactly 180° (one half of the input AC cycle)

questions.explanation: Biased at cutoff (Q-point on X-axis).

questions.question: The maximum theoretical power conversion efficiency of a Class B push-pull amplifier is:
questions.explanation: P_out,max / P_dc = (V_m² / 2R_L) / (2 V_m² / π R_L) = π / 4 ≈ 78.5%.

questions.question: What is Crossover Distortion in a complementary symmetry Class B push-pull amplifier?

options.text: A dead-band near zero volts where neither transistor conducts because input voltage is within ±0.7 V (V_BE cutoff)

questions.explanation: Transistors need ~0.7 V to turn on; waveform exhibits flat notch at zero-crossing.

questions.question: How is crossover distortion eliminated in Class AB power amplifiers?

options.text: By providing a small forward DC pre-bias (using diodes or a V_BE multiplier) so both transistors conduct slightly at idle

questions.explanation: Class AB eliminates the 0.7 V dead band while maintaining ~70-75% efficiency.

questions.question: A Class C power amplifier conducts for:

options.text: Significantly less than 180° (typically 90° to 150°) and uses a tuned LC tank load for high RF efficiency (> 80-90%)

questions.explanation: Heavily biased in cutoff; LC tank restores sinusoidal output.

questions.question: A Class D power amplifier achieves ultra-high efficiency (> 90-95%) by:

options.text: Operating output transistors as digital on/off switches using Pulse-Width Modulation (PWM)

questions.explanation: Transistors dissipate near-zero power in cutoff (I=0) and saturation (V≈0).

questions.question: What is a V_BE Multiplier (Rubber Diode) circuit used for in power amplifiers?

options.text: Generating an adjustable, temperature-compensated DC bias voltage between the bases of push-pull output transistors

questions.explanation: V_CE = V_BE * (1 + R₁ / R₂); thermally coupled to heatsink to prevent thermal runaway.

questions.question: The 555 Timer IC configured in ASTABLE mode generates:

options.text: A continuous square-wave oscillation without external triggering
A single output pulse upon receiving a trigger (monostable)

questions.explanation: Free-running multivibrator with frequencies set by two resistors and one capacitor.

questions.question: In an astable 555 timer circuit with R_A, R_B, and C, the capacitor charges through:

options.text: R_A only and discharges through R_B
R_A + R_B, and discharges through R_B only

questions.explanation: Charging time t_high = 0.693(R_A + R_B)C; discharging time t_low = 0.693 R_B C.

questions.question: The 555 Timer configured in MONOSTABLE mode operates as:

options.text: A one-shot pulse generator: produces a single output pulse of width T = 1.1 R C when triggered

questions.explanation: Trigger input creates fixed-width output pulse.

questions.question: Thermal resistance θ_JA of a semiconductor power transistor is defined as:

options.text: The electrical resistance of the junction
The temperature rise of the junction above ambient per watt of power dissipated: θ_JA = (T_J - T_A) / P_D (°C/W)

questions.explanation: Thermal Ohm's law for heatsink sizing.

questions.question: Silicon Controlled Rectifier (SCR) is a four-layer (p-n-p-n) thyristor device that:

options.text: Latches ON when a gate current pulse is applied, and remains ON until anode current drops below the holding current I_H
Can be turned off by gate pulse at any time

questions.explanation: Bistable latching power switch.

questions.question: Which Boolean law states that A + A'B = A + B?
questions.explanation: By absorption/simplification: A + A'B = (A + A')(A + B) = 1*(A + B) = A + B.

questions.question: What is the dual of the Boolean expression: A + B * C?
questions.explanation: To find the dual, interchange + and * operators, and interchange 0 and 1 without complementing variables: A*(B+C).

questions.question: Simplify the Boolean function F = A B + A B':
How many minterms are there for a Boolean function of 4 variables?
questions.explanation: For n variables, there are 2^n possible minterms. 2^4 = 16.

questions.question: What is the standard POS (Product of Sums) term called?
questions.explanation: A sum term that contains all variables (either complemented or uncomplemented) is called a maxterm.

questions.question: Which gate is considered a universal gate because any Boolean function can be implemented using only this gate?
questions.explanation: NAND and NOR gates are universal gates because they can realize NOT, AND, and OR operations.

questions.question: What is the output of an XOR gate when both inputs are 1 (A = 1, B = 1)?
questions.explanation: XOR output is 1 only when inputs are strictly different. When A=B=1, output is 0.

questions.question: In a 3-variable Karnaugh map, how many cells (squares) are there?
questions.explanation: A 3-variable K-map has 2^3 = 8 cells.

questions.question: Adjacent cells in a Karnaugh map differ by how many bit positions?
questions.explanation: K-maps use Gray code ordering so that adjacent cells differ by exactly one literal/bit.

questions.question: In Karnaugh map minimization, a group of 4 adjacent 1s eliminates how many variables?
questions.explanation: A group of 2^k cells eliminates k variables. For 4 cells (2^2), 2 variables are eliminated.

questions.question: What is a 'Don't Care' condition in a digital circuit design?

options.text: An input that always produces a logic 1
An input that produces a clock pulse
An input combination that will never occur or whose output value does not matter

questions.explanation: Don't care conditions (X) can be assigned 0 or 1 in K-maps to maximize grouping sizes.

questions.question: A half adder adds two 1-bit inputs and produces:

options.text: Sum (A AND B) and Carry (A OR B)
Sum (A OR B) and Carry (A XOR B)
Sum (A XNOR B) and Carry (A AND B)
Sum (A XOR B) and Carry (A AND B)

questions.explanation: A half adder has Sum = A ⊕ B and Carry = A · B.

questions.question: How many half adders and OR gates are required to construct a full adder?
questions.explanation: A standard full adder consists of two half adders and one OR gate to combine the carry outputs.

questions.question: What is the primary speed limitation in a Ripple Carry Adder?

options.text: Propagation delay of the carry bit through all full adders

questions.explanation: Each stage must wait for the carry-out of the previous stage, causing a linear delay O(n).

questions.question: Which type of adder overcomes the ripple carry delay by computing carries in parallel?
questions.explanation: Carry lookahead adders calculate carry generate (G) and carry propagate (P) to compute all carries simultaneously.

questions.question: A 3-to-8 line decoder has how many input lines and output lines?
questions.explanation: An n-to-2^n decoder has n input lines and 2^n output lines.

questions.question: Which device selects one of many analog or digital input signals and forwards it into a single output line?
questions.explanation: A multiplexer acts as a digitally controlled multi-position switch.

questions.question: How many select lines are required for a 16-to-1 multiplexer?
questions.explanation: For 2^n inputs, n select lines are required. Since 16 = 2^4, 4 select lines are needed.

questions.question: Can any Boolean function of n variables be implemented using a 2^n-to-1 multiplexer directly?

options.text: No, multiplexers can only do routing
Only if the function is symmetric
Yes, by connecting function truth table values to data inputs

questions.explanation: A 2^n-to-1 MUX can implement any n-variable function by connecting variables to select lines and minterms to data inputs.

questions.question: A priority encoder resolves which problem found in standard binary encoders?
questions.explanation: A priority encoder outputs the binary code of the active input with the highest priority.

questions.question: What is the 2's complement of the 8-bit binary number 0000 1100 (decimal 12)?
questions.explanation: 1's complement of 00001100 is 11110011. Adding 1 gives 11110100 (-12 in 2's complement).

questions.question: What is the range of signed integers that can be represented with 8 bits in 2's complement?
questions.explanation: For n bits, the 2's complement signed range is -2^(n-1) to 2^(n-1) - 1. For n=8: -128 to +127.

questions.question: What is the result of binary addition 1011 + 0110?
Convert decimal 29 into binary:
Convert binary 11010111 to hexadecimal:
questions.explanation: Split into nibbles: 1101 = D (13), 0111 = 7. Result: D7.

questions.question: Which code represents each decimal digit by a 4-bit binary sequence?
questions.explanation: BCD represents each decimal digit from 0 to 9 using 4 binary bits (0000 to 1001).

questions.question: In Gray code, what is the main characteristic when progressing from one number to the next?

options.text: Two bits change at a time
Only one bit changes at a time

questions.explanation: Gray code is an unweighted code where successive values differ by only a single bit, preventing glitches.

questions.question: What is the output equation of a 2-input XNOR gate?
questions.explanation: XNOR is the equivalence gate, giving 1 when inputs are equal: F = A B + A' B'.

questions.question: According to De Morgan's theorem, (A + B + C)' is equal to:
questions.explanation: De Morgan's theorem states: The complement of a sum equals the product of the complements.

questions.question: Simplify: (X + Y)(X + Y'):
questions.explanation: Using distribution: X + Y Y' = X + 0 = X.

questions.question: What is the minimum number of NAND gates required to implement a 2-input XOR gate?
questions.explanation: A 2-input XOR requires exactly 4 two-input NAND gates.

questions.question: Which logic family is known for the lowest static power consumption?
questions.explanation: CMOS circuits draw virtually zero static current because complementary transistors are never on simultaneously in steady state.

questions.question: What distinguishes a sequential circuit from a combinational circuit?

options.text: Sequential circuits contain memory elements and their outputs depend on past inputs
Sequential circuits contain only logic gates with no feedback
Sequential circuits cannot implement Boolean algebra

questions.explanation: Sequential logic outputs depend on both current inputs and the present state stored in memory elements.

questions.question: What is the forbidden (invalid) input condition for an active-HIGH SR latch?
questions.explanation: When S=1 and R=1 in an active-high NOR latch, both Q and Q' are forced to 0 simultaneously, violating complementarity and leading to a race condition.

questions.question: How does a D flip-flop resolve the invalid state problem of an SR flip-flop?

options.text: By setting R = S' via an inverter, ensuring inputs are never both 1
By cascading two latches in parallel

questions.explanation: A D flip-flop feeds D to S and D' to R, so S and R can never be equal.

questions.question: What is the characteristic equation of a JK flip-flop?
questions.explanation: When J=1, K=0 => Q=1; J=0, K=1 => Q=0; J=K=0 => Q; J=K=1 => Q'. Thus Q(next) = J Q' + K' Q.

questions.question: What happens in a JK flip-flop when both J = 1 and K = 1 upon clock arrival?

options.text: The circuit enters an undefined state

questions.explanation: When J=1 and K=1, the flip-flop operates in toggle mode: Q(t+1) = Q'(t).

questions.question: What is the characteristic equation of a T flip-flop?
questions.explanation: A T flip-flop toggles when T=1 and holds when T=0, represented by the XOR operation Q(next) = T ⊕ Q.

questions.question: What is 'setup time' (t_su) in a flip-flop?

options.text: The time required for output to change after clock edge
The minimum time the data input must remain stable before the clock edge
The time data must be held after the clock edge

questions.explanation: Setup time is the mandatory interval preceding the active clock transition during which input data must be held constant.

questions.question: What is 'hold time' (t_h) in a flip-flop?

options.text: The time data must be stable before clock edge
The delay between Q and Q'
The minimum time data input must remain stable after the active clock transition

questions.explanation: Hold time is the duration after the active clock edge during which the data input must not change.

questions.question: What happens if setup or hold time requirements are violated in a flip-flop?

options.text: Metastability (the output may oscillate or settle unpredictably)

questions.explanation: Violating timing constraints can drive flip-flop internal nodes into a metastable intermediate voltage.

questions.question: In an edge-triggered flip-flop, state transition occurs:

options.text: Throughout the high level of the clock
Only during the rising or falling transition of the clock signal
Throughout the low level of the clock

questions.explanation: Edge-triggered devices sample inputs and update outputs strictly at the specified voltage transition.

questions.question: A Master-Slave flip-flop is designed specifically to eliminate which problem?
questions.explanation: The master latch isolates the input during clock HIGH while the slave updates output on clock LOW, preventing feedback race-around.

questions.question: How many flip-flops are required to construct a Mod-16 counter?
questions.explanation: A counter with mod N requires n flip-flops such that 2^n >= N. For N=16, 2^4 = 16, so 4 flip-flops are needed.

questions.question: What is an asynchronous (ripple) counter?

options.text: A counter where the clock of each flip-flop is triggered by the output of the preceding flip-flop
A counter where all flip-flops share a common clock
A counter that counts without any clock
A counter with no propagation delay

questions.explanation: In ripple counters, flip-flops are clocked in cascade, accumulating propagation delays across stages.

questions.question: What is the major disadvantage of an asynchronous ripple counter compared to a synchronous counter?

options.text: Accumulation of propagation delay limiting maximum operating frequency

questions.explanation: Cumulative propagation delay through cascaded flip-flops limits the clock speed and causes output glitches during transitions.

questions.question: In a synchronous counter, all flip-flops are clocked by:

options.text: The same common system clock simultaneously

questions.explanation: Synchronous counters connect the clock input of every flip-flop to the master clock line simultaneously.

questions.question: A Mod-10 counter is also commonly known as a:
questions.explanation: A counter with 10 distinct states (0 through 9) is called a decade counter or BCD counter.

questions.question: How many unused (illegal) states are there in a standard 4-bit BCD counter?
questions.explanation: A 4-bit register has 16 states. BCD uses 10 states (0 to 9), leaving 16 - 10 = 6 unused states.

questions.question: How many states does an n-bit Ring Counter have?
questions.explanation: An n-bit ring counter circulates a single 1 through n flip-flops, yielding exactly n valid states.

questions.question: How many states does an n-bit Johnson (twisted ring) Counter have?
questions.explanation: A Johnson counter feeds the inverted output Q' of the last stage back to the first, producing 2n distinct states.

questions.question: What type of shift register takes data serially on one line and outputs all bits in parallel?
questions.explanation: SIPO registers shift data in bit-by-bit serially and provide immediate parallel access to all register stages.

questions.question: What is a Mealy state machine?

options.text: A finite state machine whose outputs depend on both present state and current inputs
A machine whose outputs depend strictly on present state only
An asynchronous state machine without a clock

questions.explanation: In a Mealy machine, output = f(Present State, Current Inputs), allowing faster response but possible input glitches.

questions.question: What is a Moore state machine?

options.text: A machine whose outputs depend on inputs directly
A finite state machine whose outputs depend only on the present state

questions.explanation: In a Moore machine, output = f(Present State). Output changes occur synchronously on clock edges.

questions.question: Which state machine model typically requires fewer states to implement the same sequential specification?

options.text: Both require identical number of states

questions.explanation: Mealy machines can generate different outputs for different inputs within the same state, often needing fewer states than Moore machines.

questions.question: What is a state transition table?

options.text: A truth table for combinational logic only
A timing chart of propagation delays
A tabular representation showing present state, inputs, next state, and outputs

questions.explanation: A state table lists current states and input combinations alongside resulting next states and outputs.

questions.question: What is the purpose of state reduction in sequential circuit design?

options.text: To reduce the number of flip-flops and combinational logic required

questions.explanation: State reduction combines equivalent states to minimize hardware complexity without changing input-output behavior.

questions.question: Two states in a sequential circuit are said to be equivalent if:

options.text: For every possible input sequence, they produce identical outputs and transition to equivalent states
They share the same clock cycle

questions.explanation: States are equivalent if no input sequence can distinguish between them by observing output behavior.

questions.question: What is the excitation table of a flip-flop?

options.text: A table showing next state for given inputs
A table showing required inputs for a desired transition from present state to next state
A truth table of an inverter

questions.explanation: Excitation tables specify what inputs (e.g. J, K or D or T) must be applied to drive the flip-flop from Q(t) to Q(t+1).

questions.question: For a JK flip-flop, what are the required inputs J and K to cause a transition from Q = 0 to Q = 1?
questions.explanation: To transition 0 -> 1: J must be 1 to set or toggle, while K can be 0 or 1 (Don't care). J=1, K=X.

questions.question: For a JK flip-flop, what are the required inputs J and K for a transition from Q = 1 to Q = 1 (hold 1)?
questions.explanation: To maintain 1: J can be 0 (hold) or 1 (set), while K must be 0 (prevent reset/toggle). Thus J=X, K=0.

questions.question: For a T flip-flop, what is the required input T for a transition from Q = 1 to Q = 0?
questions.explanation: Since the state changes from 1 to 0, a toggle is required: T = 1.

questions.question: What is a static-1 hazard in combinational logic?

options.text: A glitch to 1 when output should be 0
A temporary glitch to 0 when the output is expected to remain 1

questions.explanation: A static-1 hazard occurs when an output momentarily drops to 0 due to unequal path delays while theoretically remaining 1.

questions.question: How can static hazards be eliminated from a two-level sum-of-products circuit?

options.text: By adding redundant consensus terms covering adjacent prime implicants

questions.explanation: Adding redundant product terms ensures that transitions between adjacent K-map groupings do not cause momentary 0 outputs.

questions.question: What is the fundamental difference between a PAL (Programmable Array Logic) and a PLA (Programmable Logic Array)?

options.text: PAL has a programmable AND array and fixed OR array; PLA has programmable AND and programmable OR arrays
PLA has fixed AND array; PAL has fixed OR array
PAL is volatile; PLA is non-volatile

questions.explanation: PLA offers dual programmability (both AND and OR planes), whereas PAL has a programmable AND plane feeding fixed OR gates.

questions.question: In semiconductor memories, what does volatile memory mean?

options.text: Data is lost when power is turned off
Data can only be written once

questions.explanation: Volatile memories like SRAM and DRAM require continuous power to retain stored bits.

questions.question: What is the primary memory cell mechanism used in Dynamic RAM (DRAM)?

options.text: A single transistor and a storage capacitor

questions.explanation: DRAM stores charge on a tiny capacitor accessed via an NMOS pass transistor, requiring periodic refreshing.

questions.question: Why does DRAM require periodic refreshing?

options.text: Because charge stored in the memory cell capacitor leaks away over time

questions.explanation: Capacitor dielectric leakage discharges the cell within milliseconds, requiring read-and-rewrite refresh cycles.

questions.question: Static RAM (SRAM) memory cells typically use:

options.text: A bistable latch consisting of 4 or 6 CMOS transistors
A capacitor and a single transistor

questions.explanation: SRAM uses cross-coupled CMOS inverters forming a stable latch that retains state without refresh as long as powered.

questions.question: What is the total storage capacity of a memory chip with 12 address lines and 8 data lines?
questions.explanation: 12 address lines address 2^12 = 4096 locations. Each location stores 8 bits (1 byte), giving 4096 bytes = 4 KB.

questions.question: What is the function of a tri-state buffer in digital bus architecture?

options.text: It acts as a ternary logic gate
It provides three output states: High (1), Low (0), and High-Impedance (Hi-Z)
It delays signals by 3 clock cycles

questions.explanation: Tri-state outputs allow multiple devices to connect to a shared data bus by putting inactive devices into high-impedance state.

questions.question: In digital IC specifications, what is 'fan-out'?

options.text: The cooling requirement of the chip
The maximum number of inputs connected to a gate
The maximum number of standard logic inputs that an output can drive reliably

questions.explanation: Fan-out defines how many input loads a gate output can switch while maintaining valid logic voltage levels.

questions.question: What is 'noise margin' in digital logic gates?

options.text: The maximum extraneous noise voltage added to an input that does not cause an undesirable change in circuit output
The sound level generated by switching
The ripple voltage on the power supply

questions.explanation: Noise margin quantifies gate tolerance against spurious electromagnetic noise: NM_H = V_OH - V_IH and NM_L = V_IL - V_OL.

questions.question: In CMOS logic, why is the PMOS transistor size typically wider than the NMOS transistor size?

options.text: Because hole mobility in silicon is lower than electron mobility
Because PMOS has higher breakdown voltage

questions.explanation: Electrons in silicon have ~2.5x higher mobility than holes; PMOS channel width is made wider to balance rise and fall propagation delays.

questions.question: What is an essential prime implicant in a Karnaugh map?

options.text: A minterm that cannot be grouped
A prime implicant that covers at least one minterm not covered by any other prime implicant
A prime implicant that contains don't cares

questions.explanation: Essential prime implicants are mandatory in the minimal sum of products because they alone cover specific minterms.

questions.question: Which code is commonly used in optical shaft encoders to prevent erroneous multi-bit readings during rotation?
questions.explanation: Gray code guarantees that only a single track bit changes between adjacent sectors, eliminating positioning errors caused by sensor misalignment.

questions.question: What is the radix (base) of the octal number system?
questions.explanation: Octal has base 8, using digits 0 through 7.

questions.question: In a 4-bit ripple carry adder, if each full adder has a delay of 2 ns, what is the total worst-case carry propagation delay?
questions.explanation: Delay = n * delay_per_stage = 4 * 2 ns = 8 ns.

questions.question: What type of multivibrator has no stable state and continuously oscillates between two quasi-stable states?
questions.explanation: An astable multivibrator acts as a free-running clock oscillator without requiring external triggers.

questions.question: What is a Schmitt trigger inverter used for in digital inputs?

options.text: To invert data with zero delay
To convert noisy or slowly changing analog signals into clean, sharp digital transitions using hysteresis

questions.explanation: The Schmitt trigger features distinct switching thresholds (hysteresis) that reject input noise and sharpen slow edges.

questions.question: What is the output frequency of a 4-bit binary ripple counter clocked with a 16 MHz signal?
questions.explanation: Each flip-flop divides the frequency by 2. A 4-bit counter divides frequency by 2^4 = 16. 16 MHz / 16 = 1 MHz.

questions.question: In asynchronous design, what is a 'critical race' condition?

options.text: A race between two clock lines
A state transition where the final stable state depends on which internal variable changes first, leading to erratic operation
A condition where outputs toggle at maximum speed

questions.explanation: In a critical race, unequal path delays between multiple updating state variables can cause the circuit to enter an unintended stable state.

questions.question: What is an algorithmic state machine (ASM) chart primarily used for?

options.text: Describing the flow of control and hardware operations in a digital system step-by-step

questions.explanation: ASM charts visually specify complex digital hardware control logic, states, conditional outputs, and branch conditions.

questions.question: What is the primary function of a lookahead carry generator (LCG)?

options.text: To store data bits in registers
To compute all stage carries directly from generate and propagate signals in constant time

questions.explanation: The LCG computes carries for 4 or more bits simultaneously via two-level logic, eliminating sequential carry ripple delay.

questions.question: Which of the following signals is a continuous-time energy signal?

options.text: A rectangular pulse of finite duration and amplitude

questions.explanation: Energy E = ∫ |x(t)|^2 dt is finite for pulses of bounded duration and amplitude, while periodic signals have infinite energy and finite power.

questions.question: What is the total energy E of the signal x(t) = e^(-2t) * u(t)?
What is the average power P of a periodic sinusoid x(t) = A * cos(ω_0 t + θ)?
questions.explanation: The average power of any sinusoidal waveform with peak amplitude A over a period is P = (A / √2)^2 = A^2 / 2.

questions.question: What is the sifting property of the Dirac delta function δ(t)?
questions.explanation: The sifting property extracts the exact value of the integrand at the point where the impulse argument becomes zero: x(t_0).

questions.question: What is the relationship between the unit impulse function δ(t) and the unit step function u(t)?
questions.explanation: The unit step is the integral of the unit impulse, and the unit impulse is the distributional derivative of the unit step.

questions.question: A continuous-time signal x(t) is defined as an EVEN signal if it satisfies:
questions.explanation: An even signal exhibits mirror symmetry across the vertical axis: x(-t) = x(t).

questions.question: What is the odd part x_odd(t) of any general signal x(t)?
questions.explanation: Any signal can be uniquely decomposed into even and odd components: x_odd(t) = (x(t) - x(-t)) / 2.

questions.question: If x(t) is shifted to x(t - 3), this represents:

options.text: A time advance of 3 units (shifted to the left)
A time delay of 3 units (shifted to the right)

questions.explanation: Replacing t with (t - t_0) with t_0 > 0 shifts the waveform to the right along the time axis by t_0 units.

questions.question: Given a signal x(t), the transformed signal x(2t) corresponds to:

options.text: Time compression by a factor of 2
Time expansion by a factor of 2

questions.explanation: Scaling the independent variable by a factor a > 1 compresses the signal horizontally along the time axis by 1/a.

questions.question: Is the continuous-time signal x(t) = cos(4π t) + sin(6π t) periodic, and what is its fundamental period T_0?
What is the condition for a discrete-time sinusoid x[n] = cos(ω_0 n) to be periodic?

options.text: Any discrete sinusoid is always periodic
ω_0 / (2π) must be a rational number
ω_0 must be greater than π

questions.explanation: Unlike continuous sinusoids, discrete-time sinusoids are periodic if and only if the cyclic frequency f_0 = ω_0 / (2π) = m / N is rational.

questions.question: A system described by y(t) = 3 x(t) + 5 is:
questions.explanation: Zero input gives y(0) = 5 ≠ 0, violating homogeneity (superposition). Thus it is nonlinear, but time-invariant.

questions.question: A system described by y(t) = t * x(t) is:
questions.explanation: It satisfies superposition: a x_1(t) + b x_2(t) -> a t x_1(t) + b t x_2(t). However, time delay test fails: delayed input gives t x(t-t_0) != (t-t_0) x(t-t_0).

questions.question: A continuous-time system is defined as CAUSAL if:

options.text: The output depends on future inputs
The output at any time depends only on present and past inputs
The impulse response is non-zero for t < 0

questions.explanation: Causality means the system cannot predict future inputs: y(t) depends solely on x(τ) for τ ≤ t.

questions.question: What is the necessary and sufficient condition for a continuous-time LTI system to be BIBO stable?
questions.explanation: Bounded-Input Bounded-Output stability requires the impulse response h(t) to be absolutely integrable.

questions.question: What is the convolution of any signal x(t) with a shifted impulse δ(t - t_0)?
questions.explanation: Convolving with an impulse reproduces the original signal shifted to the location of the impulse: x(t) * δ(t - t_0) = x(t - t_0).

questions.question: Compute the convolution of x(t) = u(t) with h(t) = u(t):

options.text: t * u(t) (a unit ramp function r(t))

questions.explanation: y(t) = ∫_0^t 1 * 1 dτ = t for t ≥ 0, which is the unit ramp function r(t) = t u(t).

questions.question: Which property of convolution states that x(t) * h(t) = h(t) * x(t)?
questions.explanation: Convolution is commutative; the order of input and impulse response can be interchanged without affecting output.

questions.question: If two LTI systems with impulse responses h_1(t) and h_2(t) are connected in CASCADE (series), the overall impulse response is:
questions.explanation: Cascaded LTI systems have an overall impulse response equal to the convolution of their individual impulse responses.

questions.question: If two LTI systems with impulse responses h_1(t) and h_2(t) are connected in PARALLEL, the overall impulse response is:
questions.explanation: Parallel connected systems receive the same input and their outputs are summed: h(t) = h_1(t) + h_2(t).

questions.question: What are the Dirichlet conditions for the existence of the Fourier Series of a periodic signal x(t)?

options.text: x(t) must be absolutely integrable over a period, have a finite number of maxima/minima, and finite discontinuities
x(t) must be an even function with no poles
x(t) must be differentiable at every point

questions.explanation: Dirichlet conditions guarantee convergence of CTFS except at points of discontinuity where it converges to the midpoint.

questions.question: In the exponential Fourier series x(t) = Σ a_k e^(j k ω_0 t), what does the coefficient a_0 represent?

options.text: The DC (average) value of the signal over one period
The total power of the harmonics

questions.explanation: a_0 = (1/T) ∫_T x(t) dt, which is exactly the average or DC component of the periodic waveform.

questions.question: If a periodic signal x(t) is real and even, its Fourier series coefficients a_k are:
questions.explanation: Symmetry properties state: real and even signals have purely real and even Fourier coefficients.

questions.question: If a periodic signal x(t) is real and odd, its Fourier series coefficients a_k are:
questions.explanation: Real and odd signals produce purely imaginary and odd Fourier series coefficients.

questions.question: What does Parseval's theorem for Fourier series state?

options.text: The average power of a periodic signal equals the sum of the squared magnitudes of its harmonic coefficients
Power is conserved only in LTI filters
Energy equals the Fourier transform at ω = 0

questions.explanation: Parseval's relation: P = (1/T) ∫_T |x(t)|^2 dt = Σ_{-∞}^∞ |a_k|^2.

questions.question: What is the response of a stable LTI system to a complex exponential input x(t) = e^(s t)?

options.text: y(t) = H(s) e^(s t), where H(s) is the eigenvalue (transfer function)

questions.explanation: Complex exponentials are eigenfunctions of LTI systems; the output is the same exponential scaled by the complex eigenvalue H(s).

questions.question: A causal discrete-time LTI system with impulse response h[n] is BIBO stable if:
questions.explanation: Discrete BIBO stability requires absolute summability of the unit impulse response.

questions.question: What is the step response s(t) of an LTI system with impulse response h(t)?
questions.explanation: Because u(t) is the integral of δ(t), linearity implies that the step response is the running integral of the impulse response.

questions.question: What is the fundamental frequency ω_0 of the signal x(t) = 5 cos(50π t)?
questions.explanation: In cos(ω_0 t), the coefficient multiplying t inside the argument is ω_0 = 50π rad/s.

questions.question: Compute the discrete-time convolution of x[n] = {1, 2} with h[n] = {1, 1}:
What is the length of the convolution of a sequence of length L_1 with a sequence of length L_2?
questions.explanation: The non-zero duration of the discrete convolution of two finite sequences is L_1 + L_2 - 1.

questions.question: A system is memoryless (static) if:

options.text: The output depends on the derivative of input
The impulse response has infinite duration
The system contains inductors and capacitors
The output at any instant depends only on the input at that same instant

questions.explanation: A memoryless system has y(t) = f(x(t)), meaning it does not retain any past history of inputs.

questions.question: What is the Continuous-Time Fourier Transform (CTFT) of the Dirac delta function δ(t)?
questions.explanation: F{δ(t)} = ∫_{-∞}^∞ δ(t) e^(-jω t) dt = e^0 = 1 for all frequencies.

questions.question: What is the CTFT of the constant signal x(t) = 1?
questions.explanation: By duality with F{δ(t)} = 1, the Fourier transform of a DC signal 1 is 2π δ(ω).

questions.question: What is the CTFT of x(t) = e^(-a t) u(t) where a > 0?
According to the time-shifting property of the CTFT, F{x(t - t_0)} equals:
questions.explanation: A shift in the time domain corresponds to multiplying by a linear phase shift e^(-jω t_0) in the frequency domain.

questions.question: According to the frequency-shifting (modulation) property of the CTFT, F{x(t) e^(j ω_0 t)} equals:
questions.explanation: Multiplication by a complex exponential in time shifts the spectrum in frequency: X(j(ω - ω_0)).

questions.question: What is the CTFT of the derivative of a signal, d/dt [x(t)]?
questions.explanation: Differentiation in time corresponds to multiplication by jω in the frequency domain.

questions.question: What is the convolution property of the Continuous-Time Fourier Transform?
questions.explanation: Convolution in the time domain corresponds to point-by-point multiplication in the frequency domain.

questions.question: What does the multiplication property of the CTFT state: F{x_1(t) · x_2(t)} = ?
questions.explanation: Multiplication in the time domain transforms into convolution in the frequency domain scaled by 1/(2π).

questions.question: What is the Nyquist sampling rate for a bandlimited continuous signal with maximum frequency f_max = 5 kHz?
questions.explanation: The Nyquist criterion states that the sampling rate must be at least twice the maximum frequency: f_s ≥ 2 * 5 kHz = 10 kHz.

questions.question: What phenomenon occurs when a continuous signal is sampled at a rate below its Nyquist rate (f_s < 2 f_max)?
questions.explanation: Undersampling causes higher frequency components to fold over into the baseband spectrum, creating irreversible aliasing distortion.

questions.question: What type of filter is placed before sampling to eliminate frequencies above f_s / 2?
questions.explanation: An analog low-pass anti-aliasing filter removes frequency components higher than the Nyquist limit before digitization.

questions.question: What is the bilateral Laplace transform of a continuous signal x(t)?

options.text: X(s) = ∫_{-∞}^∞ x(t) e^(-s t) dt, where s = σ + jω

questions.explanation: The bilateral Laplace transform generalizes the Fourier transform by evaluating along the complex frequency s = σ + jω.

questions.question: What is the Region of Convergence (ROC) in the Laplace transform?

options.text: The range of complex variable s values in the s-plane for which the Laplace integral converges

questions.explanation: The ROC comprises all points s in the complex plane where ∫ |x(t) e^(-σ t)| dt is finite.

questions.question: What is the Laplace transform of x(t) = e^(-a t) u(t) and its ROC?
questions.explanation: ∫_0^∞ e^(-(s+a)t) dt = 1/(s+a), requiring Re{s+a} > 0 => Re{s} > -a.

questions.question: What is the Laplace transform of the left-sided signal x(t) = -e^(-a t) u(-t) and its ROC?
questions.explanation: Left-sided exponential signals yield the same algebraic form 1/(s+a) but with a left-half ROC: Re{s} < -a.

questions.question: Can the Region of Convergence (ROC) of a rational Laplace transform contain any poles?

options.text: Yes, poles are always inside the ROC
Only if the system is stable
Only simple poles can be in the ROC
No, the ROC can never contain any poles

questions.explanation: By definition, the Laplace integral diverges at pole locations; hence the ROC cannot contain poles.

questions.question: For a causal continuous-time LTI system to be BIBO stable, what must be true about its transfer function poles?

options.text: All poles must lie strictly in the open left-half of the s-plane (Re{s} < 0)
All poles must lie on the imaginary axis
All poles must be inside the unit circle
Poles can be anywhere in the s-plane

questions.explanation: BIBO stability requires the ROC to include the jω axis; for a causal system (right-sided ROC), this means all poles have negative real parts.

questions.question: What is the Laplace transform of the Dirac delta function δ(t)?

options.text: 1 with ROC of the entire s-plane

questions.explanation: The Laplace transform of δ(t) is ∫ δ(t) e^(-st) dt = 1 for all complex s.

questions.question: What is the Laplace transform of the unit step function u(t)?
questions.explanation: L{u(t)} = ∫_0^∞ e^(-st) dt = 1/s, valid for Re{s} > 0.

questions.question: What is the Initial Value Theorem for the unilateral Laplace transform?
questions.explanation: The Initial Value Theorem allows finding x(0+) directly from the s-domain via lim_{s -> ∞} s X(s).

questions.question: What is the Final Value Theorem for the unilateral Laplace transform (assuming all poles of sX(s) are in the open LHP)?
questions.explanation: The Final Value Theorem computes steady-state value lim_{t->∞} x(t) = lim_{s->0} s X(s) provided the limit exists.

questions.question: What is the Discrete-Time Fourier Transform (DTFT) of a sequence x[n]?
questions.explanation: The DTFT maps a discrete sequence to a continuous, periodic function of discrete angular frequency Ω with period 2π.

questions.question: What is the periodicity of the DTFT spectrum X(e^(jΩ))?
questions.explanation: Because e^(-j(Ω + 2π)n) = e^(-jΩ n) e^(-j 2π n) = e^(-jΩ n), the DTFT is fundamentally 2π-periodic.

questions.question: What is the definition of the bilateral z-Transform of a discrete sequence x[n]?
questions.explanation: The bilateral z-transform is the discrete counterpart of the Laplace transform, where z = r e^(jΩ).

questions.question: What is the Region of Convergence (ROC) in the z-plane for a right-sided (causal) finite sequence?

options.text: The entire z-plane except possibly z = 0
The region inside the unit circle
The region outside the largest pole

questions.explanation: For a causal finite-length sequence, X(z) is a polynomial in z^(-1), which converges everywhere except at z = 0 where terms blow up.

questions.question: What is the z-transform of x[n] = a^n u[n] and its ROC?

options.text: 1 / (1 - a z^(-1)) = z / (z - a) with ROC |z| > |a|

questions.explanation: Σ_{n=0}^∞ (a z^(-1))^n = 1 / (1 - a z^(-1)) for |a z^(-1)| < 1, which implies |z| > |a| (exterior of circle).

questions.question: What is the z-transform of x[n] = -a^n u[-n - 1] and its ROC?
questions.explanation: Left-sided exponential sequences produce the same rational form z/(z-a) but with an interior ROC: |z| < |a|.

questions.question: For a causal discrete-time LTI system to be BIBO stable, what must be true about its transfer function poles?

options.text: All poles must lie outside the unit circle
All poles must lie on the unit circle
All poles must have negative real parts
All poles must lie strictly inside the unit circle (|p_k| < 1)

questions.explanation: BIBO stability requires the ROC to encompass the unit circle (|z| = 1); for a causal system (|z| > |p_max|), this requires all poles |p_k| < 1.

questions.question: What corresponds to the continuous-time imaginary axis (jω axis) in the discrete-time z-plane?
questions.explanation: Evaluating the z-transform on the unit circle z = e^(jΩ) yields the Discrete-Time Fourier Transform (DTFT), exactly as evaluating s = jω yields the CTFT.

questions.question: What is the z-transform of the unit impulse sequence δ[n]?

options.text: 1 with ROC of the entire z-plane

questions.explanation: X(z) = Σ δ[n] z^(-n) = 1 * z^0 = 1 for all complex z.

questions.question: What is the z-transform of the discrete unit step sequence u[n]?
questions.explanation: Applying the standard formula with a = 1 gives z / (z - 1) with ROC |z| > 1.

questions.question: According to the time-shifting property of the z-transform, Z{x[n - k]} equals:
questions.explanation: A delay of k samples in the time domain corresponds to multiplication by z^(-k) in the z-domain.

questions.question: What does the convolution property of the z-transform state: Z{x[n] * h[n]} = ?
questions.explanation: Convolution of discrete-time sequences corresponds to algebraic multiplication of their z-transforms.

questions.question: What is an ideal low-pass filter's impulse response h(t)?

options.text: A sinc function: h(t) = (ω_c / π) sinc(ω_c t / π)
An exponential decay e^(-a t) u(t)

questions.explanation: The inverse CTFT of a rectangular frequency passband of width 2ω_c is a sinc function in the time domain.

questions.question: Why is an ideal brick-wall low-pass filter physically unrealizable in practice?

options.text: Because its frequency response is zero everywhere
Because it requires infinite power gain
Because its impulse response is non-causal (extends to -∞) and infinite in duration
Because it causes zero phase distortion

questions.explanation: The sinc impulse response is non-zero for t < 0, violating causality; practical filters approximate brick-wall behavior with causal rational transfer functions.

questions.question: What is the phase response of a system with pure time delay y(t) = x(t - t_d)?
questions.explanation: H(jω) = e^(-jω t_d), so magnitude |H(jω)| = 1 and phase angle θ(ω) = -ω t_d is strictly linear with frequency.

questions.question: What is the primary benefit of a filter having a LINEAR PHASE response?

options.text: It introduces a constant group delay across all frequencies, preventing waveform shape distortion
It provides the sharpest cutoff with minimum order

questions.explanation: Linear phase ensures all frequency components are delayed by the exact same amount of time, preserving pulse shapes.

questions.question: What is the group delay τ_g(ω) of a filter with phase response θ(ω)?
questions.explanation: Group delay measures the transit delay of the signal envelope and is defined as the negative derivative of phase with respect to frequency.

questions.question: How is the Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) related to the DTFT?

options.text: The DFT is continuous in frequency
The DFT cannot be computed with FFT
The DFT is formed by uniformly sampling the DTFT at N discrete frequency points around the unit circle
The DFT is identical to the Laplace transform

questions.explanation: The N-point DFT samples X(e^(jΩ)) at Ω_k = 2π k / N for k = 0, 1, ..., N-1.

questions.question: What is the computational complexity of computing an N-point DFT directly versus using the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT)?

options.text: O(N) directly versus O(N^2) with FFT
O(N log N) directly versus O(N) with FFT
O(N^3) directly versus O(N^2) with FFT
O(N^2) directly versus O(N log_2 N) using FFT

questions.explanation: Cooley-Tukey FFT algorithm reduces computational operations from N^2 complex multiplications down to (N/2) log_2 N.

questions.question: What is a minimum-phase system?

options.text: A causal, stable system whose transfer function has both all poles and all zeros inside the unit circle (or in LHP)
A system with zero phase response
A system with the minimum number of poles

questions.explanation: Minimum-phase systems have stable and causal inverses because both poles and zeros reside strictly in the stability region.

questions.question: What is an all-pass filter?

options.text: A filter that passes all frequencies with zero phase shift
A filter that has constant magnitude |H(jω)| = 1 for all frequencies but modifies phase
A filter with no poles or zeros

questions.explanation: All-pass filters maintain flat unity magnitude across the entire spectrum, serving as pure phase equalizers or delay synthesizers.

questions.question: What is the relationship between the impulse response h(t) and the step response s(t) of an LTI system?
questions.explanation: By the derivative property of LTI systems, differentiating the step response yields the impulse response.

questions.question: What is the 3-dB cutoff frequency of a first-order low-pass system with transfer function H(s) = 1 / (1 + s τ)?
If the input x(t) to an LTI system is periodic with period T_0, the output y(t) will be:

options.text: Periodic with the exact same fundamental period T_0

questions.explanation: LTI systems preserve periodicity; each harmonic is simply scaled and phase shifted by H(j k ω_0).

questions.question: What happens in time domain when zero-padding is performed on a discrete signal prior to DFT?

options.text: Frequency spectrum is interpolated with finer resolution (sinc interpolation) without changing underlying spectral content

questions.explanation: Zero-padding increases DFT length N, evaluating the DTFT at denser frequency grid points without adding new information.

questions.question: What is the Bilinear Transform used for in digital signal processing?

options.text: Mapping analog s-plane transfer functions into digital z-plane filters via s = (2/T)(1 - z^(-1))/(1 + z^(-1))

questions.explanation: The bilinear transform maps the entire left-half s-plane into the interior of the unit circle, avoiding aliasing.

questions.question: What artifact is introduced by the Bilinear Transform that requires pre-warping?

options.text: Nonlinear frequency warping between analog and digital frequency axes (ω and Ω)

questions.explanation: The nonlinear mapping Ω = 2 arctan(ω T / 2) compresses high frequencies; pre-warping ensures critical frequencies match.

questions.question: What is Gibbs phenomenon in Fourier series approximations?

options.text: An overshoot of approximately 9% near step discontinuities that does not vanish as the number of terms approaches infinity
A decay of high frequency components

questions.explanation: Truncating Fourier series of a discontinuous signal produces a persistent ~8.95% ripple adjacent to the jump discontinuity.

questions.question: What is the z-transform of the ramp sequence x[n] = n * u[n]?
questions.explanation: Using the differentiation property -z d/dz [z/(z-1)] gives z / (z - 1)^2.

questions.question: What does the circular convolution of two N-point sequences correspond to in the DFT domain?

options.text: Point-wise multiplication of their N-point DFTs

questions.explanation: The DFT multiplication property corresponds strictly to circular (periodic) convolution in the time domain, not linear convolution.

questions.question: How can linear convolution of two sequences of lengths L and M be computed using circular convolution / FFT?

options.text: By computing N-point FFT where N = max(L, M)
By zero-padding both sequences to a length of at least L + M - 1 before taking FFTs

questions.explanation: Zero-padding to at least L + M - 1 prevents circular aliasing (wrap-around), making circular convolution identical to linear convolution.

questions.question: What is the fundamental difference between an open-loop and a closed-loop control system?

options.text: Closed-loop systems utilize feedback to compare output against input reference, whereas open-loop systems do not
Open-loop systems have higher accuracy in presence of disturbances

questions.explanation: Closed-loop systems measure actual output and feed it back to reduce error, making them robust against disturbances and parameter variations.

questions.question: What is a transfer function of a linear time-invariant system?

options.text: The ratio of output to input in the time domain
The ratio of the Laplace transform of the output to the Laplace transform of the input, assuming zero initial conditions
The Fourier transform of the steady state
The ratio of input to output with non-zero initial state

questions.explanation: By definition, Transfer Function G(s) = Y(s) / X(s) with all initial conditions set to zero.

questions.question: For a negative feedback closed-loop system with forward transfer function G(s) and feedback transfer function H(s), the closed-loop transfer function T(s) is:
questions.explanation: Closed-loop transfer function with negative feedback is T(s) = G(s) / [1 + G(s)H(s)]. With positive feedback, the denominator becomes 1 - GH.

questions.question: In Mason's Gain Formula, what does the term Δ (determinant of the graph) represent?

options.text: The product of all forward path gains
The sum of all node voltages
The characteristic frequency of the system
1 - (sum of all individual loop gains) + (sum of gain products of two non-touching loops) - ...

questions.explanation: Δ = 1 - Σ L_i + Σ L_j L_k - Σ L_m L_n L_p ..., representing the system characteristic equation.

questions.question: What are two loops in a signal flow graph defined as 'non-touching'?

options.text: When they do not share any common node
When their loop gains are equal
When they both touch the input node

questions.explanation: Non-touching loops are completely isolated from each other, sharing no common node or branch.

questions.question: What is the time constant τ of a first-order system with transfer function G(s) = 1 / (s + 5)?
questions.explanation: Writing in standard form G(s) = K / (τ s + 1) = (1/5) / ((1/5)s + 1) gives time constant τ = 1/5 = 0.2 s.

questions.question: For a first-order system subjected to a unit step input, the output reaches approximately what percentage of its final steady-state value after one time constant (t = τ)?
For a standard first-order system, what is the settling time T_s for the 2% criterion?
questions.explanation: The 2% settling criterion requires e^(-t/τ) ≤ 0.02, which yields t = -ln(0.02) τ ≈ 3.91 τ ≈ 4 τ.

questions.question: In the standard second-order transfer function G(s) = ω_n^2 / (s^2 + 2 ζ ω_n s + ω_n^2), what does ζ represent?
questions.explanation: ζ (zeta) is the dimensionless damping ratio that characterizes the transient oscillation behavior.

questions.question: A second-order system is described as UNDERDAMPED if its damping ratio ζ satisfies:
questions.explanation: When 0 < ζ < 1, the characteristic roots are complex conjugates, producing decaying oscillatory responses.

questions.question: A second-order system is described as CRITICALLY DAMPED if:
questions.explanation: Critical damping (ζ = 1) yields two identical real poles, providing the fastest response without overshoot.

questions.question: A second-order system is described as OVERDAMPED if:
questions.explanation: When ζ > 1, the poles are real and unequal, resulting in a sluggish, non-oscillatory response.

questions.question: What is the damped natural frequency ω_d of an underdamped second-order system?
questions.explanation: The imaginary part of the complex conjugate poles is ω_d = ω_n √(1 - ζ^2).

questions.question: What is the peak time T_p of an underdamped second-order step response?
questions.explanation: The first derivative of step response vanishes at t = π / ω_d, which is the time to reach the first maximum peak.

questions.question: What is the formula for the maximum percent overshoot (%OS) of a second-order underdamped system?
questions.explanation: Percent overshoot depends exclusively on the damping ratio ζ: %OS = 100 * exp(-π ζ / √(1 - ζ^2)).

questions.question: What is the approximate settling time T_s (2% criterion) for an underdamped second-order system?
questions.explanation: The envelope decays as e^(-ζ ω_n t); reaching 2% residual requires ζ ω_n t ≈ 4 => T_s ≈ 4 / (ζ ω_n).

questions.question: For a unity feedback control system, what is the system 'Type' number?

options.text: The number of pure integrators (poles at s = 0) in the open-loop transfer function G(s)
The order of the closed-loop characteristic equation
The number of zeros in G(s)
The value of damping ratio ζ

questions.explanation: System Type is defined by the number of open-loop poles located exactly at the origin s = 0: G(s) = K / (s^N ...).

questions.question: What is the steady-state error e_ss of a Type 0 system subjected to a unit step input?

options.text: e_ss = 1 / (1 + K_p), where K_p = lim_{s->0} G(s)

questions.question: What is the steady-state error of a Type 1 system subjected to a unit step input?
questions.explanation: A Type 1 system has a pole at s=0, giving position error constant K_p = ∞, hence e_ss = 1 / (1 + ∞) = 0.

questions.question: What is the steady-state error of a Type 1 system subjected to a unit ramp input r(t) = t u(t)?

options.text: e_ss = 1 / K_v, where K_v = lim_{s->0} s G(s)

questions.explanation: For ramp input, e_ss = 1 / K_v where velocity error constant K_v = lim_{s->0} s G(s) is finite for Type 1.

questions.question: According to the Routh-Hurwitz stability criterion, a system is stable if and only if:

options.text: All elements in the first column of the Routh array are strictly positive (no sign changes)
The determinant of the matrix is zero
All roots of the characteristic equation are real
The number of sign changes is greater than 1

questions.explanation: The number of sign changes in the first column equals the number of roots in the right-half s-plane. Zero sign changes => strictly stable.

questions.question: If there are two sign changes in the first column of the Routh array, how many poles lie in the right-half of the s-plane?
questions.explanation: Routh's theorem states that the number of right-half plane (RHP) roots equals the number of sign variations in column 1.

questions.question: What does an entire row of zeros in a Routh array indicate?

options.text: Symmetric roots with respect to the origin (pairs on jω axis or quad pairs)

questions.explanation: A row of zeros arises from an auxiliary polynomial possessing roots that are symmetric about the origin, such as purely imaginary jω poles.

questions.question: How do you resolve a row of zeros when constructing a Routh array?

options.text: Form an auxiliary polynomial from the preceding row and replace the zeros with its derivative coefficients

questions.explanation: Construct auxiliary polynomial A(s) from the row above, differentiate dA(s)/ds, and substitute its coefficients into the zero row.

questions.question: What is the characteristic equation of a closed-loop system?
questions.explanation: The closed-loop denominator 1 + G(s)H(s) set to zero gives the characteristic equation whose roots are the closed-loop poles.

questions.question: In the s-plane, moving poles further to the left of the imaginary axis causes the transient response to:
questions.explanation: Real part -σ determines the exponential decay envelope e^(-σ t). More negative real parts yield faster decay.

questions.question: In the s-plane, moving poles vertically further away from the real axis causes:
questions.explanation: The imaginary coordinate corresponds directly to the damped oscillation frequency ω_d.

questions.question: What does a pole located in the right-half s-plane (Re{s} > 0) produce in the time domain?
questions.explanation: Positive real part gives an exponential factor e^(+σ t) that grows without bound as t -> ∞.

questions.question: A system has poles at s = ±j 4. What is its unforced natural response?

options.text: Sustained sinusoidal oscillation at 4 rad/s (marginally stable)

questions.explanation: Pure imaginary poles generate sustained sinusoids cos(4t) and sin(4t) with constant amplitude.

questions.question: What is the rise time T_r of an underdamped second-order system commonly defined as?

options.text: The time to reach the first peak
The time required for the response to rise from 10% to 90% (or 0% to 100%) of its final value
The duration of the input pulse

questions.explanation: Rise time measures initial speed of response, commonly taken as the time from 0 to 100% (or 10% to 90%) of final value.
