questions.question: In a C++ implementation of a singly linked list, what does the 'head' pointer store?

options.text: The data value of the last node
The memory address of the first node in the list (or nullptr if empty)
The address of the middle node

questions.explanation: In linked list data structures, head is a pointer to the first ListNode; an empty list has head == nullptr.

questions.question: What is the time complexity to insert a new node at the BEGINNING (head) of a singly linked list?
questions.explanation: Inserting at the head requires allocating a node, setting its next pointer to head, and updating head, which executes in constant O(1) time.

questions.question: What is the time complexity to access the k-th element by index in a singly linked list?
questions.explanation: Linked lists do not support random access; retrieving the k-th node requires traversing k-1 pointers sequentially from head.

questions.question: In C++, what operator is used to dynamically allocate memory on the heap for a new struct or class node?
questions.explanation: C++ uses the 'new' operator to dynamically allocate heap memory and invoke class constructors.

questions.question: What must be called in C++ to prevent memory leaks when removing a node from a dynamically allocated linked list?
questions.explanation: Each node created with 'new' must be explicitly deallocated using 'delete' to prevent memory leakage.

questions.question: In a doubly linked list, what pointers does each node contain?

options.text: Only a pointer to next node
Two data fields and one pointer
A pointer to head and tail only
Pointers to both the NEXT node and the PREVIOUS node

questions.explanation: Doubly linked list nodes contain a data field, a 'next' pointer, and a 'prev' pointer, enabling bidirectional traversal.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of pushing an element onto a stack implemented using a dynamic array (std::vector)?
questions.explanation: Pushing to a dynamic array is O(1) on average; when reallocation is triggered, elements are copied, giving O(1) amortized.

questions.question: Which data structure operates on a Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) principle?
questions.explanation: Stacks enforce LIFO ordering: the most recently pushed element is the first element popped.

questions.question: Which data structure operates on a First-In, First-Out (FIFO) principle?
questions.explanation: Queues enforce FIFO ordering: elements are enqueued at the rear and dequeued from the front.

questions.question: In a circular array implementation of a queue with capacity N, how is the rear index updated when enqueuing?
questions.explanation: Modulo arithmetic wraps the index around from N-1 back to 0, preventing false overflow in circular queues.

questions.question: How is an arithmetic expression in Infix notation (e.g. 'A + B * C') converted to Postfix notation ('A B C * +') programmatically?

options.text: Using Dijkstra's Shunting-Yard algorithm with an operator Stack

questions.explanation: The Shunting-Yard algorithm processes tokens sequentially, using a stack to buffer operators based on precedence.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of searching for a value in a balanced Binary Search Tree (AVL tree) with n nodes?
questions.explanation: Each comparison in a balanced BST halves the search space, yielding O(log n) worst-case time complexity.

questions.question: In a Binary Search Tree (BST), what property must be satisfied by every node X?

options.text: All keys in X's left subtree are strictly less than X, and all keys in X's right subtree are strictly greater than X
Keys in left subtree must be greater than X
All nodes must have exactly two children
All leaves must be at the same depth

questions.explanation: The BST invariant requires left_subtree < root < right_subtree for every node.

questions.question: Which tree traversal of a Binary Search Tree visits nodes in strictly ASCENDING sorted order?
questions.explanation: In-order traversal visits Left subtree, current Node, then Right subtree, producing sorted output for any BST.

questions.question: What is the balance factor of a node in an AVL tree, and what are its allowed values?

options.text: Depth of node; any positive integer
Height(left subtree) - Height(right subtree); allowed values are -1, 0, +1
Degree of root; allowed values 0 or 1

questions.explanation: AVL trees maintain strict self-balancing: the height difference between left and right subtrees must not exceed 1 (|BF| ≤ 1).

questions.question: What rotation is performed to rebalance an AVL tree node that experiences a Left-Left (LL) imbalance?
questions.explanation: When a node's left child has a left-heavy subtree insertion, a single right rotation at the unbalanced node restores balance.

questions.question: What is a Min-Heap binary tree property?

options.text: The value of each parent node is less than or equal to the values of its children, with minimum element at the root
The root holds the maximum element
Every left child must be greater than right child
It must be an AVL tree

questions.explanation: A Min-Heap is a complete binary tree where every node satisfies parent ≤ children; the minimum key is always at index 0.

questions.question: In an array-based implementation of a binary heap where root is at index 0, what are the indices of the children of node i?

options.text: Left child = i + 1, Right child = i + 2

questions.explanation: 0-indexed heaps store left child at 2i + 1, right child at 2i + 2, and parent at (i - 1) / 2.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of the 'buildHeap' operation that constructs a binary heap from an unsorted array of n elements?
questions.explanation: Floyd's bottom-up heap construction runs in linear O(n) time by sifting down nodes starting from the lowest internal levels.

questions.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of QuickSort, and when does it occur?

options.text: O(n^2), when the pivot is consistently the smallest or largest element (e.g. sorted array with first element as pivot)

questions.explanation: Unbalanced partitions (size 0 and n-1) result in a recursion depth of n, causing O(n^2) quadratic comparisons.

questions.question: What is the average and worst-case time complexity of MergeSort?

options.text: O(n log n) in all cases (best, average, worst)

questions.explanation: MergeSort divides the array into two halves recursively (log n levels) and merges them in linear O(n) time, guaranteeing O(n log n).

questions.question: What is the auxiliary space complexity of standard recursive MergeSort on an array of size n?
questions.explanation: Merging two sorted subarrays requires a temporary auxiliary buffer of size n, resulting in O(n) extra space.

questions.question: What is a 'Collision' in a Hash Table?

options.text: When a key is deleted twice
When two distinct keys produce the exact same hash index via the hash function

questions.explanation: Because the key space is much larger than table size, the pigeonhole principle guarantees collisions (h(k_1) = h(k_2)).

questions.question: How does 'Separate Chaining' resolve collisions in a Hash Table?

options.text: By probing the next consecutive array slot
By rehashing with a new table size
By storing all elements that hash to the same bucket in a linked list attached to that bucket

questions.explanation: Separate chaining maintains a linked list (or balanced tree) at each bucket index to store colliding key-value pairs.

questions.question: In Open Addressing with Linear Probing, what formula determines the probe sequence for key k?
questions.explanation: Linear probing checks sequential buckets (h(k) + 1, h(k) + 2, ...) circularly until an empty slot is located.

questions.question: What is 'Primary Clustering' in Hash Tables using Linear Probing?

options.text: The clustering of nodes in a BST
The tendency for occupied slots to build long contiguous blocks, causing probe sequences to lengthen and degrading performance
A collision between two hash functions

questions.explanation: Long runs of occupied slots attract more colliding keys, creating a cascading snowball effect that degrades search time toward O(n).

questions.question: What is the Load Factor (λ) of a Hash Table with n stored elements and m table buckets?
questions.explanation: The load factor measures fullness: λ = n/m. Tables typically rehash and double size when λ exceeds 0.7 to 0.75.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of Breadth-First Search (BFS) on a graph with V vertices and E edges using an adjacency list?
questions.explanation: BFS visits each vertex once and inspects each incident edge once, executing in linear O(V + E) time using a FIFO queue.

questions.question: Which data structure is primarily used to implement Breadth-First Search (BFS) on a graph?
questions.explanation: BFS explores nodes level by level using a FIFO queue to buffer discovered neighbors.

questions.question: Which data structure is primarily used to implement Depth-First Search (DFS) iteratively on a graph?
questions.explanation: DFS plunges deep into branch paths using a LIFO stack (or programmatic function recursion call stack).

questions.question: What algorithm finds the Single-Source Shortest Paths in a graph with non-negative edge weights?
questions.explanation: Dijkstra's greedy algorithm extracts the minimum unvisited distance node using a priority queue in O((V + E) log V) time.

questions.question: What algorithm finds a Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) by sorting all edges by weight and adding them greedily using a Disjoint Set Union (Union-Find) structure?
questions.explanation: Kruskal's algorithm sorts all edges in O(E log E) and adds non-cycle edges greedily using Union-Find to form an MST.

questions.question: In 8086 DOS programming, which DOS interrupt service is invoked to print a '$'-terminated string located at DX to the console?
questions.explanation: DOS service AH = 09h of INT 21h prints a string whose offset is in DX, terminated by '$'.

questions.question: Which instruction sequence properly terminates an assembly program and returns control cleanly to the DOS command prompt?
questions.explanation: Function 4Ch of INT 21h exits with return code (AL), cleanly terminating execution.

questions.question: In EMU8086 / DOSBox assembly experiments, what DOS interrupt service call is used to print a '$'-terminated string located at DX to the console?
questions.explanation: INT 21h with AH = 09h prints a character string from DS:DX up to the terminator character '$'. (AH = 02h prints a single character in DL).

questions.question: When nesting two loops in x86 assembly where both use the CX register as a loop counter, how should the outer loop counter be preserved during inner loop execution?

options.text: PUSH CX before starting the inner loop, and POP CX immediately after the inner loop terminates
Set CX = 0 inside the inner loop
Copy CX into the code segment register CS

questions.explanation: Since the LOOP instruction automatically decrements CX, nesting loops requires saving the outer loop CX onto the runtime stack using PUSH CX, and restoring it with POP CX after the inner loop finishes.

questions.question: In 8086 microprocessor assembly, what is the size of the general-purpose registers (AX, BX, CX, DX)?
questions.explanation: The Intel 8086 is a 16-bit processor; AX, BX, CX, and DX are 16-bit registers, divided into 8-bit halves (e.g. AH and AL).

questions.question: What are the two 8-bit components that make up the 16-bit accumulator register AX in 8086?
questions.explanation: AX is split into AH (bits 15-8) and AL (bits 7-0), each addressable independently as 8-bit registers.

questions.question: How is a 20-bit physical memory address computed from Segment and Offset registers in 8086 real mode?
questions.explanation: The 8086 shifts the 16-bit segment register left by 4 bits (multiplying by 16) and adds the 16-bit offset to address 1 MB of memory.

questions.question: What is the maximum addressable physical memory capacity of the 8086 microprocessor with its 20-bit address bus?
questions.explanation: A 20-bit address bus can access 2^20 distinct memory locations = 1,048,576 bytes = 1 Megabyte.

questions.question: Which register pair is used by default to fetch machine instructions in the 8086 processor?
questions.explanation: Instruction Pointer (IP) holds the offset of the next instruction within the Code Segment (CS).

questions.question: Which register pair points to the current top of the runtime stack in 8086 memory?
questions.explanation: Stack Pointer (SP) holds the offset of the top of the stack within the Stack Segment (SS).

questions.question: What does the instruction 'MOV AX, [BX]' do in 8086 assembly?

options.text: Copies the address BX into AX
Moves AX into memory at BX
Copies the 16-bit word from memory at offset address BX (in DS) into register AX

questions.explanation: Square brackets denote memory indirection: [BX] dereferences the memory location pointed to by data segment register BX.

questions.question: What is the effect of the 'PUSH AX' instruction in 8086 assembly?

options.text: Increments SP by 2, then stores AX
Stores AX at SP, then decrements SP
Decrements SP by 2, then stores the 16-bit content of AX at memory address SS:[SP]

questions.explanation: The 8086 stack grows downward toward lower memory; PUSH decrements SP by 2 and writes the word to the new top of stack.

questions.question: What is the effect of the 'POP BX' instruction in 8086 assembly?

options.text: Loads the 16-bit word from SS:[SP] into BX, then increments SP by 2
Decrements SP by 2, then loads BX

questions.explanation: POP reads the top of stack into the destination register and increments SP by 2, restoring stack space.

questions.question: What does the instruction 'LEA SI, [BX + DI + 4]' do?

options.text: Loads the data value at that address into SI
Calculates the effective memory address (BX + DI + 4) and loads the resulting address number into SI without accessing memory

questions.explanation: Load Effective Address (LEA) calculates pointer offsets without performing any memory data read.

questions.question: In 8086 assembly, what does the instruction 'LOOP target_label' do?

options.text: Decrements CX by 1; if CX != 0, jumps to target_label; otherwise falls through
Decrements AX and jumps if zero

questions.explanation: LOOP uses register CX as a hardware loop counter: it executes CX = CX - 1 and branches if CX is non-zero.

questions.question: Which flag in the 8086 FLAGS register is set when an arithmetic operation produces a result of zero?
questions.explanation: ZF is set (ZF = 1) if the ALU result is zero, and cleared (ZF = 0) if non-zero.

questions.question: What is the difference between the Carry Flag (CF) and the Overflow Flag (OF) in 8086?

options.text: CF indicates unsigned arithmetic carry/borrow out of MSB; OF indicates signed two's complement arithmetic overflow
CF is for signed; OF is for unsigned

questions.explanation: CF tracks unsigned arithmetic out-of-range conditions; OF triggers when adding two numbers of like sign produces a result of opposite sign.

questions.question: What does the instruction 'TEST AL, 01H' do?

options.text: Performs a bitwise AND between AL and 01H to set flags (ZF) without modifying the content of AL

questions.explanation: TEST performs a non-destructive bitwise AND, updating Zero, Sign, and Parity flags while leaving operand values untouched.

questions.question: What does the instruction 'CMP AX, BX' do?

options.text: Performs subtraction (AX - BX) internally to update CPU flags without altering the value of AX or BX

questions.explanation: CMP executes internal subtraction (AX - BX) to set CF, ZF, SF, and OF flags for subsequent conditional jumps.

questions.question: Which conditional jump instruction branches if the Carry Flag is set (CF = 1)?

options.text: JC (Jump if Carry) / JB (Jump if Below)

questions.explanation: JC (and its alias JB for unsigned comparisons) branches when CF = 1.

questions.question: Which conditional jump branches if register AX is EQUAL to register BX after 'CMP AX, BX'?

options.text: JE (Jump if Equal) / JZ (Jump if Zero)

questions.explanation: Equal values yield AX - BX = 0, setting the Zero Flag (ZF = 1); JE/JZ jumps when ZF = 1.

questions.question: In DOS programming using INT 21h, what function number must be placed in AH to display a single character stored in DL?
questions.explanation: INT 21h with AH = 02h outputs the ASCII character loaded in register DL to the standard console display.

questions.question: In DOS INT 21h, what function number in AH outputs a '$'-terminated string whose address is in DX?
questions.explanation: Function 09h writes a character string pointed to by DS:DX to the screen, terminating when it encounters the '$' delimiter character.

questions.question: In DOS INT 21h, what function number terminates the program and returns control to the operating system?
questions.explanation: MOV AH, 4Ch followed by INT 21h gracefully exits the executable and returns an exit status code in AL to DOS.

questions.question: In 8086 assembly, what is the purpose of the 'XCHG' instruction?

options.text: Exchanges the contents of two registers, or a register and a memory location

questions.explanation: XCHG swaps operands without requiring a temporary third register.

questions.question: What is the result of executing 'XOR AX, AX' in 8086 assembly?

options.text: Sets all bits of AX to 1 (FFFFh)
Clears AX to 0000h efficiently and sets the Zero Flag (ZF = 1)

questions.explanation: XORing any value with itself produces all zeros; 'XOR AX, AX' is a compact 2-byte instruction commonly used to zero a register.

questions.question: What does the instruction 'SHL AX, 1' do?

options.text: Shifts all bits of AX left by 1 position, inserting 0 into LSB and moving MSB into Carry Flag (equivalent to multiplying by 2)

questions.explanation: Shift Logical Left moves bits toward MSB, filling empty low bits with 0; each shift by 1 doubles unsigned values.

questions.question: What does the instruction 'SAR AX, 1' (Shift Arithmetic Right) do?

options.text: Shifts bits right by 1 while preserving the original sign bit (MSB) to perform signed division by 2

questions.explanation: SAR maintains the sign of negative numbers by replicating the MSB during rightward shifts.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 8086 'CALL' and 'RET' instructions in subroutines?

options.text: CALL pushes the return address (IP) onto the stack and jumps to procedure; RET pops the return address back into IP
CALL jumps unconditionally; RET halts CPU
CALL clears registers; RET restores them

questions.explanation: CALL saves the next instruction address on stack before branching; RET restores IP to resume execution immediately after the CALL.

questions.question: What is the difference between a NEAR call and a FAR call in 8086 assembly?

options.text: A Near call branches within the same code segment (modifies IP only); a Far call branches to a different segment (modifies both CS and IP)
Far call does not use stack

questions.explanation: Intra-segment (Near) calls modify only IP (saving 2 bytes on stack); inter-segment (Far) calls modify both CS and IP (saving 4 bytes).

questions.question: What does the 'IN' instruction do in x86 architecture?

options.text: Reads data from an I/O peripheral port (specified by DX or an 8-bit port number) into AL or AX

questions.explanation: The x86 architecture has isolated I/O address space; IN transfers data from external port addresses into accumulator registers.

questions.question: What does the 'OUT' instruction do in x86 architecture?

options.text: Writes data to hard drive directly
Transmits data from AL or AX out to an I/O peripheral port address

questions.explanation: OUT transfers byte or word data from AL or AX to an external device register at port DX.

questions.question: What is an Interrupt Vector Table (IVT) in the 8086 processor?

options.text: A 1024-byte table located at physical address 00000h containing 256 4-byte pointers (CS:IP) for Interrupt Service Routines (ISRs)
A table of CPU register names
A hardware lookup table in BIOS chip

questions.explanation: Each of the 256 interrupts has a 4-byte entry (2-byte IP, 2-byte CS) in the IVT spanning 00000h to 003FFh.

questions.question: What happens when the 8086 CPU acknowledges an interrupt request?

options.text: Pushes FLAGS, pushes CS, pushes IP, clears IF and TF, then loads the ISR vector (CS:IP) from the IVT

questions.explanation: Hardware saves context (FLAGS, CS, IP) on stack, disables maskable interrupts (IF=0), and transfers execution to the interrupt handler.

questions.question: Which instruction is used at the end of an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) to return to the interrupted program?
questions.explanation: IRET pops IP, CS, and the original FLAGS register from stack, completely restoring machine state prior to interrupt.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 8255 Programmable Peripheral Interface (PPI) chip commonly interfaced with 8086 in lab experiments?

options.text: To act as a secondary CPU
To provide 24 programmable I/O pins organized into three 8-bit parallel ports (Port A, Port B, Port C)

questions.explanation: The 8255 PPI provides flexible parallel digital I/O for switches, LEDs, keyboards, and stepper motors via control word programming.

questions.question: In processor simulation tools (like Logisim or ModelSim), what is the function of a Program Counter (PC)?

options.text: A register that holds the memory address of the next instruction to be fetched and executed
An accumulator that stores ALU results
A stack pointer for function returns

questions.explanation: The Program Counter holds the memory address of the next instruction in sequence.

questions.question: In a single-cycle MIPS datapath simulation, how many clock cycles does each instruction take to execute?
questions.explanation: In a single-cycle datapath, the clock cycle period is fixed to accommodate the slowest instruction, taking exactly 1 long cycle per instruction.

questions.question: In Logisim or ModelSim simulation of a single-cycle MIPS CPU datapath, what control signal determines whether the second ALU input operand comes from Register rt or from the Sign-Extended Immediate field?

options.text: ALUSrc (0 for Register rt, 1 for Immediate)

questions.explanation: The ALUSrc multiplexer control line selects between read data 2 from the register file (ALUSrc=0) and the sign-extended 32-bit immediate constant (ALUSrc=1) for load, store, and addi instructions.

questions.question: In a pipelined MIPS processor datapath simulation, what is the function of the Hazard Detection Unit when a "Load-Use Data Hazard" occurs?

options.text: It inserts a pipeline stall (bubble/NOP) by disabling PC and IF/ID write, and clearing control signals in the ID/EX register
It doubles the ALU clock speed
It writes unverified data to the memory buffer

questions.explanation: When an instruction tries to read a register immediately loaded by the preceding lw instruction, forwarding cannot solve it in time. The Hazard Detection Unit stalls the pipeline for 1 clock cycle by inserting a bubble.

questions.question: In Computer Architecture simulations using Logisim, what does a multiplexer's select bit width S determine regarding its data inputs D?
questions.explanation: An S-bit binary select signal can choose between exactly 2^S distinct input data lines.

questions.question: In an ALU design lab, which control signals determine whether the ALU performs Addition or Subtraction?

options.text: ALUOp control lines (using 2's complement inverter and Carry-In = 1 for subtraction)

questions.explanation: Subtraction A - B is performed by adding A to the 1's complement of B with Carry-In asserted to 1.

questions.question: In a 32-bit MIPS processor, how many general-purpose registers are in the register file ($zero through $ra)?
questions.explanation: MIPS R2000/R3000 architectures contain thirty-two 32-bit general-purpose registers numbered $0 to $31.

questions.question: In MIPS architecture, what is the special property of register $zero ($0)?

options.text: It is hardwired to constant 0 and writes to it are discarded

questions.explanation: Register $0 always returns 0, providing a convenient constant operand for comparisons and moves.

questions.question: What is the size of all MIPS instructions in memory?
questions.explanation: A core RISC principle in MIPS is that all instructions are strictly 32 bits wide and aligned on 4-byte boundaries.

questions.question: What are the three primary instruction formats in MIPS architecture?
questions.explanation: MIPS classifies instructions into R-format (register arithmetic), I-format (immediates, loads, stores, branches), and J-format (unconditional jumps).

questions.question: In MIPS R-type instructions (e.g. 'add $t0, $t1, $t2'), what is the opcode field value in bits [31:26]?

options.text: 000000 (0x00, with actual operation specified by the 6-bit 'funct' field)

questions.explanation: All standard MIPS R-type ALU instructions share opcode 0; the ALU operation is decoded from the 'funct' field in bits [5:0].

questions.question: What are the fields of a MIPS R-type instruction format?

options.text: Opcode (6 bits), Rs (5 bits), Immediate (21 bits)
Opcode (6 bits), Rs (5 bits), Rt (5 bits), Rd (5 bits), Shamt (5 bits), Funct (6 bits)

questions.explanation: Total 32 bits: 6 (opcode) + 5 (source 1) + 5 (source 2) + 5 (destination) + 5 (shift amount) + 6 (function code).

questions.question: What are the fields of a MIPS I-type instruction format?

options.text: Opcode (6 bits), Rs (5 bits), Rt (5 bits), Immediate / Offset (16 bits)
Opcode (6 bits), Rs (13 bits), Rt (13 bits)

questions.explanation: I-type uses 6 bits for opcode, two 5-bit register specifiers (Rs, Rt), and a 16-bit immediate constant or branch/load offset.

questions.question: How does a MIPS 'lw' (load word) instruction compute the memory address to access?

options.text: Effective Address = Register(Rs) + Sign-Extended(16-bit Immediate offset)

questions.explanation: The 16-bit offset is sign-extended to 32 bits and added to base register Rs via the ALU to form the memory byte address.

questions.question: In a Single-Cycle MIPS processor, what determines the minimum clock period?

options.text: The latency of the fastest R-type instruction
The clock speed of the bus
The latency of the longest (critical) path in the datapath (typically the 'lw' load word instruction)

questions.explanation: In single-cycle execution, each instruction completes in one clock cycle, forcing clock cycle time to accommodate the slowest instruction ('lw').

questions.question: What are the 5 standard pipeline stages in a classic RISC (MIPS) processor?

options.text: IF (Instruction Fetch), ID (Instruction Decode), EX (Execute), MEM (Memory Access), WB (Write Back)

questions.explanation: The classic Hennessy-Patterson 5-stage RISC pipeline breaks instruction processing into Fetch, Decode, Execute, Memory, and Writeback.

questions.question: What is a 'Structural Hazard' in a pipelined processor?

options.text: Hardware resource conflict where multiple instructions attempt to access the same physical hardware component simultaneously

questions.explanation: Structural hazards occur when hardware cannot support all pipeline stage overlaps (e.g. single-ported memory accessed for both instruction fetch and data load).

questions.question: How is the structural hazard for memory access resolved in the classic 5-stage pipeline?

options.text: By using separate Instruction Memory (I-Cache) and Data Memory (D-Cache) (Harvard architecture)

questions.explanation: Separating instruction and data caches allows IF and MEM stages to access memory concurrently without structural collision.

questions.question: What is a 'Data Hazard' (Read-After-Write - RAW) in a pipelined CPU?

options.text: An instruction depends on the result of an earlier instruction that is still in the pipeline and not yet written to the register file

questions.explanation: When instruction j reads a register before earlier instruction i writes its result back in WB stage, reading stale data creates a RAW hazard.

questions.question: What hardware optimization eliminates data hazard stalls when an ALU result from EX stage is needed immediately by the next instruction?
questions.explanation: Forwarding routes the ALU output directly from EX/MEM or MEM/WB pipeline registers back to the ALU inputs, avoiding stall cycles.

questions.question: In which case can Data Forwarding CANNOT completely eliminate a stall in the 5-stage MIPS pipeline?

options.text: Load-Use Data Hazard (an instruction immediately uses the result of a 'lw' load instruction)

questions.explanation: A load does not retrieve data until the end of MEM stage; an instruction needing that data in EX stage must stall 1 cycle even with forwarding.

questions.question: What is a 'Control Hazard' (Branch Hazard) in a pipelined CPU?

options.text: Uncertainty about which instruction to fetch next because the branch condition and target address are not yet resolved

questions.explanation: Branches change the PC; until the branch condition is evaluated, the pipeline does not know whether to fetch sequential or branch target code.

questions.question: How does 'Branch Prediction' reduce the performance penalty of control hazards?

options.text: By executing both paths simultaneously in hardware
By predicting whether a branch is taken or not taken before it evaluates, continuing pipeline fetch speculatively
By stalling 10 cycles on every branch

questions.explanation: Predictors (static or dynamic 2-bit saturating counters) guess branch outcomes; if correct, zero stalls occur; if mispredicted, speculative instructions are flushed.

questions.question: What is a 'Pipeline Flush'?

options.text: Discarding instructions currently in early pipeline stages when a branch misprediction or exception occurs

questions.explanation: Flushing converts incorrect speculative instructions into no-ops (NOPs), preventing corrupted state writes.

questions.question: What is the CPI (Cycles Per Instruction) of an ideal 5-stage pipelined processor with no hazard stalls?
questions.explanation: Once the pipeline fills, one instruction completes every clock cycle, achieving an ideal throughput of CPI = 1.

questions.question: What is the speedup of an N-stage pipeline over an unpipelined processor under ideal conditions?
questions.explanation: Assuming balanced stages and no stalls, throughput increases by factor N because clock cycle time is divided by N.

questions.question: What is 'Direct-Mapped Cache' organization?

options.text: Any block can go into any line
Each block of main memory maps to exactly one specific line (set) in the cache based on index bits

questions.explanation: In direct mapping, Cache Line = (Block Address) mod (Number of Cache Lines), allowing fast, simple hardware lookup with potential conflict misses.

questions.question: What is a 'Fully Associative Cache' organization?

options.text: Blocks can only go in line 0
A memory block can be placed in ANY cache line; all tags are searched in parallel using content-addressable memory (CAM)

questions.explanation: Fully associative caches eliminate conflict misses completely but require complex, power-hungry parallel tag comparison hardware.

questions.question: What is an 'N-Way Set-Associative Cache'?

options.text: The cache is divided into sets, each containing N lines; a block maps to a specific set and can reside in any of the N lines within that set
A cache with N separate CPU cores
A cache with N levels (L1 to LN)
A cache accessible by N threads

questions.explanation: Set-associative architectures balance hit speed and miss rate: Set Index = (Block Address) mod (Number of Sets), with N-way parallel tag search.

questions.question: What are the 'Three C's' of cache misses categorized by Mark Hill?

options.text: Compulsory (Cold) misses, Capacity misses, and Conflict (Collision) misses

questions.explanation: Compulsory misses occur on first reference; capacity misses occur when working set exceeds cache size; conflict misses arise from non-fully-associative mapping.

questions.question: What is the difference between Write-Through and Write-Back cache policies?

options.text: Write-Through updates both cache and main memory simultaneously on every write; Write-Back updates only cache, marking line 'dirty' until replaced

questions.explanation: Write-Through keeps memory coherent but consumes high bus bandwidth; Write-Back reduces memory traffic by writing modified dirty blocks only upon eviction.

questions.question: What is a 'Dirty Bit' in a Write-Back cache line?

options.text: A status bit set to 1 when a cache line has been modified by a write, indicating it must be written back to main memory upon eviction

questions.explanation: Dirty bits prevent unnecessary memory writes: clean lines can be silently overwritten, while dirty lines must be written back to backing memory.

questions.question: What is the Least Recently Used (LRU) cache replacement policy?

options.text: When a set is full, the line that has not been accessed for the longest time is evicted

questions.explanation: LRU exploits temporal locality: data accessed recently is likely to be accessed again soon, making oldest unaccessed blocks best eviction candidates.

questions.question: What is Amdahl's Law for theoretical speedup S when a fraction f of a program is enhanced by factor k?
questions.explanation: Amdahl's law demonstrates that overall speedup is fundamentally limited by the serial fraction (1 - f) that cannot be accelerated.

questions.question: What is the difference between Spatial Locality and Temporal Locality in memory accesses?

options.text: Spatial is about time; Temporal is about space
Locality applies only to disk drives
Temporal locality: recently accessed data is likely to be accessed again soon; Spatial locality: data items with nearby addresses are likely to be accessed soon

questions.explanation: Caching leverages temporal locality by keeping recently used data in fast SRAM, and spatial locality by fetching multi-word cache blocks.

questions.question: What is Virtual Memory and what is the role of the MMU (Memory Management Unit)?

options.text: Virtual memory is a fast USB drive
Virtual memory provides an illusion of vast contiguous memory per process; the MMU translates virtual addresses to physical RAM addresses via Page Tables

questions.explanation: Virtual memory isolates processes, enables paging between RAM and disk, and translates Virtual Page Numbers (VPN) to Physical Frame Numbers (PFN).

questions.question: When using a Vernier caliper, if the main scale reads 12 mm and the 6th Vernier division aligns (with resolution 0.05 mm), what is the total measured reading?
questions.explanation: Reading = Main Scale + (Aligned Division * Resolution) = 12 mm + (6 * 0.05 mm) = 12 mm + 0.30 mm = 12.30 mm.

questions.question: In the simple pendulum lab experiment, what is the formula relating the period T to pendulum length L and gravitational acceleration g?
questions.explanation: The period of a simple pendulum for small oscillations is T = 2π √(L/g).

questions.question: In a Simple Pendulum experiment measuring local gravitational acceleration g, the period of oscillation is measured as T = 2.0 s for a pendulum length L = 1.0 m. Using the formula T = 2*pi*sqrt(L/g), what is the calculated experimental value of g? (Take pi ≈ 3.1416)

In an electrical resistivity laboratory experiment, a wire of length L = 2.0 m, cross-sectional area A = 1.0 x 10^-6 m^2, has measured resistance R = 3.4 Ohms. What is the wire material resistivity (rho)?
questions.explanation: From resistance formula R = rho * L / A => rho = R * A / L = 3.4 * (1.0e-6) / 2.0 = 1.7 x 10^-6 Ohm.m.

questions.question: When using a vernier caliper to measure cylinder diameter, how is the reading obtained?

options.text: Main scale reading + (Vernier scale coinciding mark * Vernier least count)
Multiplying main scale by vernier scale

questions.explanation: The caliper reading is the last main scale mark before the zero line plus the coinciding vernier division multiplied by resolution (e.g. 0.02 mm or 0.05 mm).

questions.question: What is the least count (precision) of a standard micrometer screw gauge with 0.5 mm pitch and 50 circular scale divisions?
questions.explanation: Least Count = Pitch / Total Circular Divisions = 0.5 mm / 50 = 0.01 mm.

questions.question: What is a 'Zero Error' in a micrometer screw gauge, and how is it corrected?

options.text: A systematic offset when anvils touch; corrected by subtracting the zero error (with sign) from measured readings

questions.explanation: If circular zero does not align with datum line when closed, measured values are systematically shifted; Correct Reading = Observed Reading - Zero Error.

questions.question: In a simple pendulum experiment to determine acceleration due to gravity g, what is the theoretical period T?
questions.explanation: For small angle oscillations (sin θ ≈ θ), simple harmonic motion gives period T = 2π √(L/g), meaning T^2 is linear with length L.

questions.question: In the simple pendulum experiment, what is plotted on the axes to determine g from the slope of a straight line?

options.text: T^2 versus L (Slope = 4π^2 / g => g = 4π^2 / Slope)

questions.explanation: Linearizing T^2 = (4π^2/g) L: plotting T^2 on the y-axis against L on the x-axis yields slope m = 4π^2/g, so g = 4π^2/m.

questions.question: Does the period of a simple pendulum depend on the mass of the bob (for small amplitudes)?

options.text: Period is directly proportional to mass
No, period is independent of bob mass

questions.explanation: In the equation T = 2π√(L/g), mass m cancels out because inertial mass equals gravitational mass.

questions.question: What is Hooke's Law for an ideal spring within its elastic limit?

options.text: F = -k * x (restoring force is directly proportional to displacement)

questions.explanation: Within the proportional elastic limit, restoring force F is proportional to extension x: F = -k x, where k is spring stiffness (N/m).

questions.question: In a spring oscillation experiment, what is the oscillation period T of mass m attached to a spring of constant k?
questions.explanation: Simple harmonic oscillation of a mass-spring system gives angular frequency ω = √(k/m), yielding period T = 2π/ω = 2π√(m/k).

questions.question: In an experiment verifying Newton's Second Law (F = m * a) using an air track, how is friction minimized?

options.text: By supporting the glider on a thin cushion of compressed air escaping through tiny track holes
By polishing the track with sandpaper

questions.explanation: Air tracks eject pressurized air from perforations, lifting gliders on a near-frictionless air film to simulate ideal dynamic motion.

questions.question: In a conservation of linear momentum experiment with two colliding carts, what condition must hold for momentum to be strictly conserved?

options.text: The net external horizontal force on the system must be zero (isolated system)
The collision must be perfectly elastic

questions.explanation: By Newton's third law and momentum theorem, total momentum Σ p is conserved in any system where external forces sum to zero.

questions.question: What distinguishes an ELASTIC collision from an INELASTIC collision in the physics lab?

options.text: Inelastic collisions conserve kinetic energy only
Elastic collisions do not conserve momentum
Elastic collisions conserve both total kinetic energy and momentum; inelastic collisions conserve momentum but lose kinetic energy to heat/deformation

questions.explanation: Total mechanical kinetic energy is conserved strictly in elastic collisions; in inelastic collisions, energy converts into thermal and sound energy.

questions.question: In a projectile motion experiment, what is the shape of the trajectory of a ball launched horizontally from a table edge?
questions.explanation: Horizontal velocity v_x is constant, while vertical motion accelerates as y = 1/2 g t^2; eliminating t gives parabolic equation y = (g / 2v_x^2) x^2.

questions.question: What is the formula for the horizontal range R of a projectile launched with speed v_0 at angle θ over flat ground?
questions.explanation: Neglecting air resistance, range R = v_x * t_flight = (v_0 cos θ)(2 v_0 sin θ / g) = (v_0^2 sin 2θ) / g.

questions.question: At what launch angle θ is the theoretical horizontal range of a projectile maximized on flat ground?
questions.explanation: Range formula R = (v_0^2 sin 2θ)/g is maximized when sin(2θ) reaches its peak value of 1, occurring at 2θ = 90° => θ = 45°.

questions.question: In a standing wave experiment on a vibrating string of length L fixed at both ends, what is the wavelength λ_n of the n-th harmonic?
questions.explanation: Boundary nodes at x = 0 and x = L require L = n (λ/2), giving allowed wavelengths λ_n = 2L / n for harmonics n = 1, 2, 3...

questions.question: What is the wave speed v on a stretched string of tension T and linear mass density μ (kg/m)?
questions.explanation: Wave velocity in a flexible string depends on restoring tension and inertia: v = √(T/μ).

questions.question: In the resonance tube experiment using a tuning fork of frequency f, what is the distance between consecutive resonance air column lengths (L_2 - L_1)?
questions.explanation: Resonance in a closed-end acoustic pipe occurs at odd quarter-wavelengths (λ/4, 3λ/4, 5λ/4...); the gap between adjacent nodes is exactly λ/2.

questions.question: How is the speed of sound v in air calculated from the resonance tube experiment?
questions.explanation: Since λ/2 = L_2 - L_1 => λ = 2(L_2 - L_1), wave speed is v = f λ = 2 f (L_2 - L_1), automatically eliminating tube end-correction errors.

questions.question: In a centripetal force experiment, what is the centripetal acceleration a_c of an object of mass m moving with speed v in circle of radius r?
questions.explanation: Radial acceleration directing toward the center of curvature is a_c = v^2 / r = ω^2 r.

questions.question: What is the coefficient of static friction μ_s measured on an inclined plane when a block just begins to slide at angle θ?
questions.explanation: At the verge of slipping: mg sin θ = f_s_max = μ_s N = μ_s mg cos θ => μ_s = sin θ / cos θ = tan θ.

questions.question: What is the rotational analog of Newton's second law (F = m * a) in rotational dynamics?

options.text: τ = I * α (Torque equals Moment of Inertia times Angular Acceleration)

questions.explanation: Torque τ (N·m) accelerates rotational inertia I (kg·m^2) by angular acceleration α (rad/s^2), analogous to force and mass in linear motion.

questions.question: What is the moment of inertia I of a solid uniform cylinder or disk of mass M and radius R about its central axis?
questions.explanation: Integrating dm r^2 across a continuous solid cylinder gives moment of inertia I = 1/2 M R^2.

questions.question: In an experiment measuring the viscosity of a liquid using Stokes' Law, what is the drag force F_d on a spherical bead of radius r falling at terminal velocity v?
questions.explanation: Sir George Stokes proved that low Reynolds number viscous drag on a sphere is F_d = 6π η r v, where η is dynamic viscosity.

questions.question: When a sphere reaches 'Terminal Velocity' falling through a viscous fluid, what is its acceleration?

options.text: 0 m/s^2 (downward gravity equals sum of upward buoyancy and viscous drag)

questions.explanation: At terminal velocity, net vertical force is zero (F_g - F_b - F_drag = 0), so acceleration vanishes and velocity remains constant.

questions.question: What does Archimedes' Principle state regarding buoyant force F_b on a submerged object?

options.text: The buoyant force equals the weight of the fluid displaced by the object: F_b = ρ_fluid * V_sub * g
F_b equals the weight of the object
F_b depends on the depth of the ocean

questions.explanation: Buoyant upward force arises from hydrostatic pressure differential and equals the weight of displaced liquid mass.

questions.question: In a thermal expansion experiment, what is the linear expansion formula for a metal rod of initial length L_0 subjected to temperature change ΔT?
questions.explanation: Fractional elongation ΔL/L_0 is proportional to temperature increase ΔT: ΔL = α L_0 ΔT, where α is the coefficient of linear expansion (1/°C).

questions.question: In an electric field mapping lab, how are equipotential lines oriented relative to electric field lines?

options.text: Equipotential lines are always PERPENDICULAR (orthogonal, at 90°) to electric field lines

questions.explanation: Because no work is done moving along an equipotential surface (dV = -E · dr = 0), electric field vectors E are everywhere normal to equipotential lines.

questions.question: In an Ohm's Law verification experiment, what does the slope of a Voltage versus Current (V vs I) graph represent?
questions.explanation: From V = I · R, plotting V on y-axis and I on x-axis produces a straight line through the origin whose slope is resistance R.

questions.question: In a magnetic field experiment, what is the magnetic field B inside an ideal long solenoid of n turns per unit length carrying current I?
questions.explanation: By Ampere's Law, the magnetic flux density inside a tightly wound solenoid is uniform and directed along the axis: B = μ_0 n I.

questions.question: In a focal length experiment using a thin convex lens, what is the Thin Lens Equation relating object distance d_o, image distance d_i, and focal length f?
questions.explanation: The Gaussian thin lens equation states: 1/f = 1/d_o + 1/d_i (with standard real-is-positive Cartesian sign convention).

questions.question: What is the magnification m of an image formed by a thin lens?
questions.explanation: Linear magnification is the ratio of image height to object height: m = h_i / h_o = -d_i / d_o; negative m indicates an inverted real image.

questions.question: In a diffraction grating experiment with laser light of wavelength λ and grating line spacing d, what is the condition for interference maxima?

options.text: d * sin(θ_m) = m * λ, where m = 0, ±1, ±2, ...

questions.explanation: Constructive interference occurs when path difference between adjacent slits equals an integer number of wavelengths: d sin θ = m λ.

questions.question: In an acid-base titration experiment, what indicator is commonly used to observe the endpoint transition between colorless in acid and pink in basic solution?
questions.explanation: Phenolphthalein is clear in acidic and neutral solutions and turns distinct pink around pH 8.2–10.0.

questions.question: Which volumetric glassware provides the highest volumetric precision for dispensing variable volumes of titrant liquid?
questions.explanation: A burette is calibrated to dispense finely controlled volumes with readability up to ±0.01 mL.

questions.question: During an acid-base titration experiment in the laboratory, how should the liquid level in a volumetric burette be read accurately to prevent parallax error?

options.text: At eye level, aligning with the BOTTOM of the curved liquid meniscus for clear aqueous solutions
Aligning with the top edge of the meniscus
Viewing from a 45-degree angle above the burette
Estimating the midpoint between the top and bottom meniscus

questions.explanation: Standard analytical chemistry protocol requires reading the graduation line directly aligned with the bottom of the concave meniscus at exact eye level to eliminate parallax error.

questions.question: What is the fundamental laboratory safety rule when preparing a diluted solution of concentrated sulfuric acid (H2SO4) in water?

options.text: ALWAYS add ACID slowly to WATER with continuous stirring, NEVER add water to concentrated acid
Add water rapidly into the acid container
Boil the acid before mixing with water
Mix both liquids in equal volumes simultaneously in a sealed flask

questions.explanation: The dissolution of concentrated sulfuric acid in water is violently exothermic. Adding water to concentrated acid causes localized boiling and violent acid splattering; adding acid slowly to a large volume of water dissipates heat safely.

Accelerate evaporation of the porcelain material
Prevent condensation on the clay triangle

questions.question: What is the proper laboratory technique when diluting concentrated sulfuric acid with water?

options.text: Always add water to acid quickly
Mix both simultaneously in a closed container
Always add ACID to WATER slowly while stirring (never add water to acid)

questions.explanation: Dissolving concentrated acid is highly exothermic; adding water to acid causes localized boiling, splashing concentrated acid violent into the air.

questions.question: What laboratory glassware is designed specifically to deliver an accurately measured variable volume of liquid in a titration experiment?
questions.explanation: A buret features precise graduation markings and a stopcock valve for delivering dropwise titrant volumes with high precision (±0.01 mL).

questions.question: What is the proper way to read the volume of a liquid that wets glass (like water) in a graduated cylinder or buret?

options.text: Read at the BOTTOM of the concave meniscus at eye level
Read at the top of the meniscus

questions.explanation: Surface tension creates a concave meniscus; parallax error is avoided by aligning sight horizontally with the bottom curve of the meniscus.

questions.question: What is the primary function of an analytical balance in the chemistry laboratory?

options.text: To measure mass with high precision (typically to ±0.0001 g / 0.1 mg)
To weigh objects up to 50 kg

questions.explanation: Analytical balances use electromagnetic force restoration within glass draft shields to weigh chemicals accurately to 0.1 mg.

questions.question: What does the 'Tare' button on an electronic laboratory balance do?

options.text: Calibrates the balance with factory weights
Zeroes the balance display, subtracting the mass of the container (weigh boat or beaker)

questions.explanation: Taring sets current load to 0.000 g, allowing direct measurement of chemical mass added into the vessel.

questions.question: What personal protective equipment (PPE) is mandatory at all times in an academic chemistry laboratory?

options.text: Safety goggles, laboratory coat, closed-toe shoes, and suitable protective gloves

questions.explanation: Chemical splash goggles, flame-resistant lab coats, and closed-toe footwear provide essential barrier protection against spills and shattering glassware.

questions.question: In an acid-base titration of strong acid (HCl) with strong base (NaOH), what is the equivalence point pH at 25 °C?
questions.explanation: Neutralization of a strong acid by a strong base yields neutral water and spectator ions (NaCl), giving pH = 7.00 at 25 °C.

questions.question: What indicator is commonly used in strong acid - strong base titrations that turns from colorless in acid to pale pink in base?
questions.explanation: Phenolphthalein is colorless in acidic and neutral solutions (pH < 8.2) and turns vivid pink in basic solutions (pH > 10.0).

questions.question: In a titration experiment, what is the difference between the 'Equivalence Point' and the 'End Point'?

options.text: Equivalence point is the stoichiometric theoretical point where moles of acid equal moles of base; End point is where the indicator physically changes color
They are identical in every titration
End point occurs before equivalence point always
Equivalence point is determined by eye

questions.explanation: The experimental end point estimates the stoichiometric equivalence point; selecting an indicator whose pK_In matches equivalence pH minimizes titration error.

questions.question: What is a 'Primary Standard' in analytical chemistry?

options.text: Any chemical purchased from a store
A highly stable, pure, non-hygroscopic substance of known high molecular weight used to standardize titrant solutions

questions.explanation: Primary standards (e.g. Potassium Hydrogen Phthalate KHP, Na2CO3) must have high purity (>99.9%), high equivalent weight, and air stability.

questions.question: Why must sodium hydroxide (NaOH) solutions be standardized before use in quantitative titrations?

options.text: Solid NaOH is hygroscopic, absorbs atmospheric moisture and CO2, preventing accurate direct mass weighing

questions.explanation: NaOH pellets absorb water vapor and react with air CO2 to form Na2CO3; solutions must be standardized against a primary standard like KHP.

questions.question: In gravimetric analysis of sulfate (SO4^2-), which reagent is added to precipitate barium sulfate (BaSO4)?
questions.explanation: Adding BaCl2 to a warm, acidic sulfate solution precipitates insoluble white barium sulfate: Ba^2+(aq) + SO4^2-(aq) -> BaSO4(s).

questions.question: What is the formula for Molarity (M) of a solution?

options.text: M = Moles of solute / Liters of solution (mol / L)
M = Grams of solute / Liters of solvent
M = Moles of solute / Kilograms of solvent
M = Volume of solute / Volume of solution

questions.explanation: Molarity expresses concentration as moles of dissolved solute per total volume of solution in liters.

questions.question: How many grams of NaOH (Molar mass = 40.0 g/mol) are required to prepare 500 mL of a 0.10 M NaOH solution?
questions.explanation: Moles = M * V = 0.10 mol/L * 0.500 L = 0.050 mol. Mass = moles * MW = 0.050 mol * 40.0 g/mol = 2.0 g.

questions.question: What is the dilution equation used to calculate required stock volume V_1 of concentration M_1 to prepare volume V_2 of concentration M_2?
questions.explanation: Because the amount of solute remains constant upon adding solvent: moles = M_1 V_1 = M_2 V_2.

questions.question: What does Beer-Lambert's Law state in spectrophotometric analysis?

options.text: Absorbance A = ε * b * c (Absorbance is directly proportional to path length b and solute concentration c)

questions.explanation: Beer-Lambert Law governs optical absorption: A = -log(T) = ε b c, where ε is molar absorptivity and b is cuvette path length (typically 1 cm).

questions.question: In spectrophotometry, why is a 'Blank' cuvette filled with solvent used before measuring samples?

options.text: To zero the spectrophotometer, calibrating for absorbance and reflections caused by solvent and cuvette walls

questions.explanation: The blank contains everything except the analyte; zeroing against it ensures that measured absorbance is due solely to the absorbing solute.

questions.question: In a calorimetry experiment, how is heat q absorbed or released by solution calculated from mass m, specific heat c, and temperature change ΔT?
questions.explanation: Sensible heat transfer is given by q = m c ΔT, where c is specific heat capacity (e.g. 4.184 J/g·°C for water).

questions.question: In an endothermic chemical reaction occurring inside a coffee-cup calorimeter, what happens to the measured water temperature?
questions.explanation: Endothermic processes absorb heat from the surrounding solution, causing the water temperature to drop.

questions.question: In a chemical kinetics experiment, what is the rate law for a reaction A + B -> Products if doubling [A] quadruples the rate, and doubling [B] doubles the rate?
questions.explanation: Rate is proportional to [A]^m [B]^n; 2^m = 4 => m = 2 (second order in A); 2^n = 2 => n = 1 (first order in B).

questions.question: In a graphical kinetics analysis, a plot of ln[A] versus time t yields a straight line with slope -k. What is the reaction order with respect to A?
questions.explanation: Integrated rate laws: Zero order is [A] vs t; First order is ln[A] vs t (slope = -k); Second order is 1/[A] vs t (slope = +k).

questions.question: What is the half-life t_1/2 formula for a first-order chemical reaction with rate constant k?
questions.explanation: For first order, half-life is independent of initial concentration: t_1/2 = ln(2) / k = 0.693 / k.

questions.question: According to Le Chatelier's Principle, what happens to the exothermic equilibrium N2(g) + 3 H2(g) <=> 2 NH3(g) + heat when temperature is INCREASED?

options.text: The equilibrium shifts to the right
The equilibrium shifts to the LEFT (reactants favored), decreasing NH3 yield

questions.explanation: Adding heat to an exothermic reaction drives the system in the reverse endothermic direction to absorb excess thermal energy.

questions.question: What is the pH of a 0.0010 M HCl strong acid solution at 25 °C?
questions.explanation: HCl fully dissociates: [H+] = 0.0010 M = 1.0 * 10^-3 M. pH = -log[H+] = -log(10^-3) = 3.00.

questions.question: What is the pH of a 0.010 M NaOH strong base solution at 25 °C?
questions.explanation: NaOH fully dissociates: [OH-] = 1.0 * 10^-2 M => pOH = -log(10^-2) = 2.00. Since pH + pOH = 14: pH = 14 - 2 = 12.00.

questions.question: What is a chemical 'Buffer Solution'?

options.text: A solution of strong acid and strong base
A solution containing a weak acid and its conjugate base (or weak base and conjugate acid) that resists changes in pH upon addition of small amounts of acid or base
A solution that changes color with temperature

questions.explanation: Buffers absorb added H+ or OH- ions via conjugate pair equilibria: HA + OH- -> A- + H2O and A- + H+ -> HA.

questions.question: What is the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation used to calculate buffer solution pH?
questions.explanation: The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation relates solution pH directly to the acid dissociation constant pK_a and conjugate base/acid concentration ratio.

questions.question: In an oxidation-reduction (redox) titration, what is the oxidation state change of manganese when purple permanganate (MnO4^-) is reduced in acidic solution?

options.text: Mn(+7) is reduced to colorless Mn(+2)

questions.explanation: In acidic media, MnO4^- + 8H+ + 5e- -> Mn^2+ + 4H2O; deep purple permanganate acts as its own self-indicator, turning colorless upon complete reduction.

questions.question: In a galvanic (voltaic) electrochemical cell, at which electrode does OXIDATION take place?
questions.explanation: Mnemonic 'An Ox and Red Cat': Oxidation occurs at the Anode; Reduction occurs at the Cathode.

questions.question: What is the function of the 'Salt Bridge' in a galvanic cell?

options.text: To maintain electrical neutrality by allowing ion migration between half-cells while preventing solution mixing

questions.explanation: Cations migrate toward the cathode and anions migrate toward the anode through the salt bridge agar gel, preventing charge buildup that would halt cell current.

questions.question: What does the Nernst Equation calculate for an electrochemical cell under non-standard conditions?

options.text: Cell potential E = E° - (RT / nF) * ln(Q) = E° - (0.0592 / n) * log(Q) at 25 °C

questions.explanation: The Nernst equation quantifies how voltage E varies with reaction quotient Q away from standard 1.0 M state E°.

questions.question: When qualitative analysis precipitates white silver chloride (AgCl), what happens upon adding aqueous ammonia (NH3)?

options.text: It forms an insoluble yellow precipitate
AgCl dissolves by forming the soluble diamminesilver(I) complex ion: [Ag(NH3)2]^+

questions.explanation: Complex ion formation AgCl(s) + 2 NH3(aq) -> [Ag(NH3)2]^+(aq) + Cl^-(aq) dissolves the precipitate, confirming presence of silver ions.

questions.question: In MATLAB/Simulink control system modeling, which built-in function creates a continuous-time transfer function object from numerator and denominator polynomial vectors?
questions.explanation: tf(num, den) creates a transfer function model in MATLAB (e.g. sys = tf([1], [1, 2, 1])).

questions.question: When analyzing a second-order underdamped step response in the lab, the Peak Time (Tp) is observed at 0.5 s. The damped natural frequency ω_d is:
questions.explanation: Peak time formula is Tp = π / ω_d => ω_d = π / Tp = π / 0.5 = 2π rad/s.

questions.question: In MATLAB / Simulink control lab simulation, what effect does increasing the Proportional Gain (Kp) of a PID controller typically have on the closed-loop system step response?

options.text: Reduces rise time and steady-state error, but increases percent overshoot and potential oscillation
Eliminates steady-state error completely without integral action
Decreases overshoot and increases system damping
Makes the system infinitely stable under all conditions

questions.explanation: Higher Kp produces a stronger control effort, reducing rise time and steady-state offset, but decreases relative stability, leading to increased peak overshoot and ringing.

questions.question: In the Ziegler-Nichols closed-loop PID tuning method, the integral and derivative gains are set to zero while proportional gain Kp is increased until the system exhibits:

options.text: Sustained, continuous marginal oscillations with constant amplitude at critical gain Kcr
Zero steady-state error with critical damping

questions.explanation: The Ziegler-Nichols closed-loop test increases Kp until the closed-loop system reaches the boundary of stability, exhibiting sustained harmonic oscillations at critical gain Kcr and ultimate oscillation period Pcr.

questions.explanation: Phase margin is defined as PM = 180° + ∠G(jω_gc) evaluated at the gain crossover frequency where |G(jω)| = 0 dB (gain of 1).

questions.question: On a system open-loop frequency response Bode plot, what is the definition of the "Gain Margin" (GM)?

The bandwidth frequency where magnitude drops by 3 dB

questions.question: In a control lab experiment using MATLAB / Simulink, which command is used to define a continuous-time transfer function G(s) = 5 / (s + 2)?
questions.explanation: The Control System Toolbox function tf(num, den) creates transfer functions from numerator and denominator polynomial coefficient vectors.

questions.question: In MATLAB, which command computes and plots the time-domain unit step response of a transfer function sys?
questions.explanation: The 'step(sys)' command automatically generates the transient step response plot, displaying settling time, rise time, and peak overshoot.

questions.question: In MATLAB, which command calculates and plots the impulse response of a dynamic system?
questions.explanation: The 'impulse(sys)' function plots the response of a dynamic LTI system to a unit Dirac delta function input.

questions.question: In MATLAB, which command plots the open-loop poles and zeros in the complex s-plane?
questions.explanation: The 'pzmap(sys)' command plots poles as 'x' markers and zeros as 'o' markers in the complex plane.

questions.question: What does the MATLAB command 'feedback(G, H)' compute?

options.text: The closed-loop transfer function: G / (1 + G * H) assuming negative feedback

questions.explanation: By default, feedback(sys1, sys2) assumes negative feedback and evaluates the closed-loop system sys1 / (1 + sys1 * sys2).

questions.question: What does the MATLAB command 'series(G1, G2)' compute?

options.text: G1 * G2 (cascade connection of two transfer functions)

questions.explanation: 'series(sys1, sys2)' multiplies two transfer functions representing cascaded blocks in block diagram algebra.

questions.question: Which MATLAB command interactively displays the Root Locus of an open-loop system and lets users inspect closed-loop pole locations for varying gain K?
questions.explanation: 'rlocus(sys)' plots root locus trajectories in the complex plane, allowing users to click along branches to view gain, damping, and frequency.

questions.question: Which MATLAB command plots the frequency response as Bode Magnitude (in dB) and Phase (in degrees) versus frequency?
questions.explanation: 'bode(sys)' computes and plots asymptotic and exact Bode magnitude and phase curves across a logarithmic frequency scale.

questions.question: Which MATLAB command calculates and annotates both the Gain Margin and Phase Margin on a Bode plot?
questions.explanation: 'margin(sys)' plots the Bode response and displays exact values for Gain Margin, Phase Margin, and their crossover frequencies.

questions.question: Which MATLAB command plots the frequency response of a system in the complex plane (Nyquist plot)?
questions.explanation: 'nyquist(sys)' creates polar plots of Re{G(jω)} versus Im{G(jω)} for frequencies from -∞ to +∞.

questions.question: Which MATLAB command is used to simulate the time response of an LTI system to an ARBITRARY user-defined input signal u(t)?
questions.explanation: 'lsim(sys, u, t)' simulates linear system response to arbitrary inputs (e.g. ramps, chirps, random noise) defined over time vector t.

questions.question: In Simulink, which basic block is used to integrate a signal x_dot(t) to obtain x(t)?
questions.explanation: The continuous Integrator block (1/s) computes the time integral of its input, foundational to modeling state variables.

questions.question: In Simulink, which block is used to multiply a signal by a constant factor K?
questions.explanation: The Gain block multiplies its input signal by a constant scalar, vector, or matrix value.

questions.question: In a servomotor position control lab, what physical sensor is commonly mounted on the motor shaft to measure angular position θ(t)?
questions.explanation: Incremental optical shaft encoders generate quadrature digital pulses representing shaft angular position and direction.

questions.question: In a DC motor speed control experiment, what physical sensor produces an analog voltage proportional to motor angular velocity ω(t)?
questions.explanation: A DC tachometer is a permanent magnet generator whose output voltage is directly proportional to rotational shaft speed: V_tach = K_tach * ω.

questions.question: What is an LVDT (Linear Variable Differential Transformer) used to measure in a control lab?

options.text: Linear displacement / position with sub-millimeter precision

questions.explanation: An LVDT converts mechanical linear displacement of a movable ferromagnetic core into differential AC voltage across two secondary windings.

questions.question: What type of power amplifier circuit is used in the control lab to drive a DC servomotor in both clockwise and counterclockwise directions from a single DC supply?

options.text: H-Bridge circuit (four switching MOSFETs or transistors)

questions.explanation: An H-bridge allows bidirectional current flow through the motor armature by switching diagonal pairs of transistors.

questions.question: What modulation technique is used by microcontrollers (e.g. Arduino, DSP) to control the average voltage and speed of a DC motor efficiently?
questions.explanation: PWM varies the duty cycle (on-time ratio) of a constant-frequency pulse train, controlling average delivered power with minimal transistor thermal dissipation.

questions.question: In a PID tuning experiment on a DC motor, what is the initial symptom observed when Proportional gain K_p is increased too high?

options.text: The system exhibits large overshoot, high-frequency oscillations, and approaches instability

questions.explanation: Excessive proportional gain reduces damping and drives closed-loop poles toward the imaginary axis, producing underdamped ringing.

questions.question: In a closed-loop speed control experiment, why is an Integral (I) controller action added to the proportional controller?

options.text: To eliminate steady-state error caused by motor friction and physical load torque

questions.explanation: P-only controllers require a continuous non-zero error to generate drive voltage against load torque; the integrator accumulates error until steady-state error is zero.

questions.question: What is the effect of adding Derivative (D) control action when tuning a position servomechanism?

options.text: It adds damping, decreases peak overshoot, and reduces settling time
It slows down response speed completely

questions.explanation: Derivative action responds to rate of change (velocity error), introducing predictive damping that counteracts excessive overshoot.

questions.question: What practical limitation occurs when tuning the Derivative (D) gain in physical analog or digital controllers?

options.text: High-frequency measurement noise from sensors is amplified, causing actuator jitter
System enters saturation at steady state

questions.explanation: The mathematical operation s amplifies high-frequency noise spikes; practical PID controllers always include a low-pass filter on the derivative term.

questions.question: What is the Ziegler-Nichols Continuous Cycling (Ultimate Gain) tuning method in the control lab?

options.text: Set K_i = K_d = 0, increase K_p until the system exhibits sustained marginal oscillations at ultimate gain K_u, then calculate PID gains from K_u and period T_u

questions.explanation: The closed-loop Ziegler-Nichols method determines ultimate gain K_u and oscillation period T_u, using empirical formulas to select initial PID parameters.

questions.question: What is the Ziegler-Nichols reaction curve (open-loop step response) tuning method based on?

options.text: Measuring the delay time L and time constant T of the S-shaped step response of the open-loop plant

questions.explanation: For stable self-regulating processes, the S-shaped step response yields apparent dead time L and time constant T, mapped to PID formulas.

questions.question: In an inverted pendulum on a cart experiment, what makes the system an attractive benchmark for advanced control design?

options.text: It is inherently non-linear, open-loop unstable, and underactuated (one motor input controls both cart position and pendulum angle)
It is linear and always stable

questions.explanation: The inverted pendulum has an open-loop right-half plane pole and fewer control actuators than degrees of freedom, requiring active balancing feedback.

questions.question: What state-space control technique is commonly used to balance an inverted pendulum around its upright vertical position?

options.text: Linear Quadratic Regulator (LQR) state-feedback control after linearizing the system about θ = 0

questions.explanation: LQR computes optimal state feedback matrix K (u = -Kx) minimizing a quadratic cost function of state error and control effort.

questions.question: What is an anti-windup circuit/algorithm used for in practical PID motor controllers?

options.text: To prevent the integrator from accumulating huge error values when the motor amplifier reaches physical saturation (voltage limits)

questions.explanation: When actuators saturate, normal feedback is broken; anti-windup suspends or clamps integration, preventing massive overshoot upon desaturation.

questions.question: In digital control lab experiments, what does the zero-order hold (ZOH) block represent?

options.text: Holding a discrete digital sample constant as an analog voltage over one sampling period T

questions.explanation: D/A converters hold the converted analog value constant between sampling clock edges, imparting a zero-order hold transfer function (1 - e^(-sT))/s.

questions.question: What rule of thumb is used in the control lab to select the digital sampling frequency f_s relative to the closed-loop system bandwidth f_bw?

options.text: f_s should be at least 10 to 20 times the closed-loop bandwidth (f_s ≥ 20 * f_bw)

questions.explanation: While Shannon-Nyquist requires f_s > 2 f_max for signal reconstruction, digital control requires f_s = 10 to 30 times bandwidth to prevent phase lag from degrading stability.

questions.question: What happens to the transient response of a DC motor position control loop when an analog velocity feedback tachometer loop is wrapped inside the position loop?

options.text: Damping ratio increases, drastically reducing position overshoot without altering steady-state position gain

questions.explanation: Inner velocity feedback adds effective viscous damping, allowing high forward position gain with rapid, non-overshooting settling.

questions.question: What does the MATLAB command 'c2d(sys_c, Ts, 'zoh')' perform?

options.text: Converts a continuous-time system sys_c into an equivalent discrete-time system at sampling period Ts using Zero-Order Hold discretization

questions.explanation: 'c2d' transforms analog s-domain transfer functions or state-space models into digital z-domain transfer functions for DSP implementation.

questions.question: What is a Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL) simulation in control engineering?

options.text: Soldering electronic components on a breadboard
Measuring motor temperature with a thermometer
A technique where real physical hardware (e.g. a microcontroller or ECU) is connected to a computer running real-time simulated models of the physical plant

questions.explanation: HIL tests embedded control firmware against high-fidelity real-time mathematical plant simulations, validating safety and edge cases before real machine deployment.

Analyzing network traffic logs requires specialized packet sniffing software.

questions.question: What is the meaning of the Latin abbreviation 'e.g.' (exempli gratia)?

questions.question: What is the meaning of the Latin abbreviation 'i.e.' (id est)?

Writing a comprehensive bibliography in APA format.
Synthesizing ideas from multiple peer-reviewed papers.

questions.question: In academic research writing, what constitutes "Patchwriting"?

Translating a text verbatim into another language
